The following [[Outline (list)|outline]] is provided as an overview of and topical guide to World War I:

'''[[World War I]]''' – [[World war|major war]] centred in Europe that began on 28 July 1914 and lasted until 11 November 1918. It involved all the world's [[great powers]],<ref>{{harvnb|Willmott|2003|pp=10–11}}</ref> which were assembled in two opposing alliances: the [[Allies of World War I|Allies]] (centred on the [[Triple Entente]] of [[United Kingdom|Britain]], [[France]] and [[Russia]]) and the [[Central Powers]] (originally centred on the [[Triple Alliance (1882)|Triple Alliance]] of [[Germany]], [[Austria-Hungary]] and [[Italy]]).<ref name=Willmott15>{{harvnb|Willmott|2003|p=15}}</ref> More than 70 million military personnel, including 60 million Europeans, were mobilised in one of the largest wars in history.<ref>{{harvnb|Keegan|1998|p=8}}</ref><ref>{{harvnb|Bade|Brown|2003|pp=167–168}}</ref> More than 9 million combatants [[World War I casualties|were killed]], largely because of great technological advances in firepower without corresponding advances in mobility. It was the sixth deadliest conflict in world history, subsequently paving the way for various political changes such as revolutions in the nations involved.<ref>{{harvnb|Willmott|2003|p=307}}</ref>

== Nature of World War I ==
World War I can be described as all of the following:

** [[Total war#World War I|Total war]]
** [[World war]]

* [[Armoured warfare#World War I|Armoured warfare]]
* [[Asymmetric warfare#World War I|Asymmetric warfare]] (in some cases)
* [[Attrition warfare]]
* [[Chemical weapons in World War I|Chemical warfare]]
* [[Ground warfare]]
* [[Modern warfare]]
* [[Naval warfare]]
** [[Submarine warfare#World War I|Submarine warfare]]

title: 1914 French mobilization
wikitext:
{{Short description|French mobilization procedures at the start of WWI}}
{{Broader|World War I}}
{{See also|Plan XVII}}
{{use mdy dates|date=February 2025}}

[[File:Affiche “ordre de mobilisation générale” 1 - Archives Nationales - AE-II-3598.jpg|thumb|"General mobilization order" poster dated August 2, 1914, held by the [[Archives Nationales (France)|French National Archives]].]]
[[File:Detaille Le Rêve.jpg|thumb|[[Édouard Detaille]], ''[[The Dream (Detaille)|Le Rêve]] (The dream)'', 1888: painting showing Third Republic conscripts on maneuvers, dreaming of their predecessors. This patriotic painting, measuring three by four meters and winning a prize at the 1888 [[Salon (Paris)|Salon]], was purchased by the French government and reproduced in large numbers.]]
[[File:66e RI (2).JPG|thumb|Soldiers of the 66th Infantry Regiment march with flags at the end of their rifles towards the station in [[Tours]] on the morning of August 5, 1914, arriving at [[Flavigny-sur-Moselle]] (near [[Nancy, France|Nancy]]) on August 6.]]

The '''1914''' '''French [[mobilization]]''' was the set of operations at the very start of [[World War I]] that put the [[French Army]] and [[French Navy|Navy]] in a position for war, including the theoretical call to arms of all Frenchmen fit for [[Conscription in France|military service]]. Planned long before 1914 (via [[Plan XVII]]), each man's assignment was based on his age and residence.

It was triggered in response to equivalent measures taken by Germany, the French [[mobilization]] took place over 17 days, from August 2 to 18, 1914, and involved transporting, clothing, equipping and arming more than three million men in all French territories, both in [[metropolitan France]] and in some of the [[List of French possessions and colonies|colonies]], and then transporting them by rail to the potential theater of war, which at the time was considered to be the [[France–Germany border|Franco-German border]].

Such event had political ([[Sacred Union]]), socio-economic (due to the departure of almost all young men) and, of course, military consequences (the start of the [[Battle of the Frontiers]]). It was the first time that a general mobilization was declared in France (in 1870, only the professional army was mobilized); [[French mobilization in 1939|the second took place in 1939]]. In August 1914, 3,780,000 men were mobilized; in total, throughout the war, some 8,410,000 French soldiers and sailors were mobilized, including 7% indigenous soldiers.<ref name=":8">{{Cite journal |last=J.P |year=1921 |title=Les pertes des nations belligérantes au cours de la Grande Guerre |trans-title=Casualties of the belligerent nations in the Great War |url=https://gallica.bnf.fr/ark:/12148/bpt6k5441824j |journal=Les Archives de la Grande Guerre |language=fr |publisher=Éd. Chiron |issue=7 |pages=41–44 |issn=0982-2062}}</ref>

== Preparation ==
The [[Industrial Revolution]] transformed the art of warfare, not only through the development of weapons and equipment, but above all through the ability of states to effectively mobilize armies with million of men. Since it was economically and socially impossible to keep them all permanently in uniform, they were left to live civilian lives during peacetime, and states mobilized them in the event of conflict,<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Martin |first=Michel |year=1981 |title=Le déclin de l'armée de masse en France: Note sur quelques paramètres organisationnels |trans-title=The decline of the mass army in France: A note on some organizational parameters |url=http://www.persee.fr/web/revues/home/prescript/article/rfsoc_0035-2969_1981_num_22_1_3390 |journal=Revue française de sociologie |language=fr |volume=22 |issue=1 |pages=87–115 |doi=10.2307/3321186 |jstor=3321186 |archive-url=https://archive.wikiwix.com/cache/index2.php?url=http%3A%2F%2Fwww.persee.fr%2Fweb%2Frevues%2Fhome%2Fprescript%2Farticle%2Frfsoc_0035-2969_1981_num_22_1_3390 |archive-date=January 20, 2014}}</ref> hoping to keep it short.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Porte |first=Rémy |year=2006 |title=Mobilisation industrielle et guerre totale: 1916, année charnière |trans-title=Industrial mobilization and total war: 1916, a pivotal year |url=http://rha.revues.org//index4072.html |journal=Revue historique des armées |language=fr |issue=242 |pages=26–35 |doi=10.3917/rha.242.0026 |archive-url=https://archive.wikiwix.com/cache/index2.php?url=http%3A%2F%2Frha.revues.org%2F%2Findex4072.html#federation=archive.wikiwix.com&tab=url |archive-date=February 12, 2025}}</ref>
[[File:Caserne Colbert 1911.jpg|alt=An entrance gate between two gatehouses, opening onto a vast courtyard, the latter enclosed in the background by a four-storey building.|thumb|Most French towns served as garrisons: here, the entrance to the Colbert barracks in [[Reims]] in 1911 (home to the 132nd infantry regiment).]]
From the end of the 19th to the end of the 20th century, the French army was a [[conscription]] army, like all the armies of the great European continental powers of the time: A small cadre of volunteer career officers and NCOs would be supplemented by millions of reservists, who had received training through their mandatory two-year-service at age 20 and periodic refresher trainings.
Only a small proportion of its units were fully composed of professional soldiers (notably some of the [[Troupes coloniales|colonial troops]] and the [[French Foreign Legion|Foreign Legion]]).

This was in line with the egalitarian ideology of some Republicans under the [[French Third Republic|Third Republic]], in a more [[Militarism|militaristic]] and [[Patriotism|patriotic]] context: after 1871, conscript societies (whose members practiced gymnastics, shooting and military instruction from adolescence)<ref>{{Cite book |title=Les Athlètes de la République: gymnastique, sport et idéologie républicaine, 1870/1914 |date=1987 |publisher=Editions Privat |isbn=978-2-7089-5323-9 |editor-last=Arnaud |editor-first=Pierre |series=Bibliothèque historique Privat |location=Toulouse |pages=423 By 1913, 221 provincial towns had garrisons,<ref>{{Cite book |last=Lejeune |first=Dominique |title=La France de la Belle époque: 1896-1914 |publisher=A. === Legislation ===
[[File:French Maneuvers 1800.jpg|alt=Company firing a salvo in line.|thumb|French infantry unit on maneuvers, 1889. Each capable man is trained during his service, then later returns to uniform for training "periods".]]
Following the [[Franco-Prussian War]] of 1870, the [[French Third Republic|Third Republic]] organized the recruitment for its armies with the law of July 27, 1872 (or the [[Ernest Courtot de Cissey|Cissey]] law): "{{lang|fr|tout Français peut être appelé, depuis l'âge de vingt ans jusqu'à celui de quarante}}" ("any Frenchman may be called up, from the age of twenty to that of forty"),<ref>Army Recruitment Act of July 27, 1872, published in the [[Journal officiel de la République française|Journal Officiel]] of August 17, 1872. {{Gallica|id=bpt6k210062f/f115|t=Bulletin des lois, n° 101, p.97}} (In French).</ref> service was for five years, with selection by lottery, but with the possibility of being discharged (short stature, deformity, respiratory illness, etc.), replaced or exempted (family responsibilities, clergymen, teachers, etc.). Service was reduced from five to three years by the law of July 15, 1889 (or the [[Charles de Freycinet|Freycinet]] law).<ref>Army Recruitment Act of July 15, 1889, published in the ''Journal Officiel'' of July 17, 1889. {{Gallica|id=bpt6k2141260/f104|t=Bulletin des lois, n° 1263, p. 73}} (In French).</ref> This situation was reformed by the law of March 21, 1905 (or the [[Henri Maurice Berteaux|Berteaux]] law),<ref group="Note">The 1905 law on universal service is explained partly by the warmongering and [[Anti-German sentiment|Germanophobic]] climate that culminated in the [[First Moroccan Crisis|Tangier crisis]] that same year, but also by the domestic policies of the Rouvier government (which was predominantly [[Radical Party (France)|radical]]) with the [[1905 French law on the Separation of the Churches and the State|law on the separation of Church and State]] that same year.</ref> which abolished the drawing of lots, replacements and exemptions: henceforth, all men could be called up for two years.<ref>Law of March 21, 1905 amending the law of July 15, 1889 on Army recruitment and reducing to two years the length of service in the active Army, promulgated in the Journal Officiel of March 23, 1905, {{Gallica|id=bpt6k215437x/f1280|t=Bulletin des lois, n° 2616, p. 1265}} (In French).</ref> Finally, the [[Law of Three Years|law of August 7, 1913]] (or the [[Louis Barthou|Barthou]] law) increased military service from two to three years.<ref>Law of August 7, 1913, amending the laws concerning the infantry, cavalry, artillery and engineers, with regard to the size of units and setting the conditions for recruitment into the active army and the duration of service in the active army and its reserves, promulgated in the Journal officiel of August 8, 1913, {{Gallica|t=Bulletin des lois, n° 110, p. 2077|id=bpt6k220779v/f335}} (In French).</ref>
{{See also|Conscription in France}}
The theoretical consequence of these laws was that, between 1905 and 1914, every French male who reached the age of 20 (just before the [[age of majority]] at the time) had to be registered on a nomination list, then do his [[military service]] for two, then three years in the active army (from age 21 to 23), before being returned to civilian life. For the eleven years following his service, men were assigned to the [[military reserve force]] (from age 24 to 34), then to the [[Territorial Army (France)|Territorial Army]] for seven years (from age 35 to 41), and finally to the Territorial Army Reserve for another seven years (from age 42 to 48).<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |title=Les lois de recrutement |url=http://combattant.14-18.pagesperso-orange.fr/Pasapas/E302Lois.html |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130604141730/http://combattant.14-18.pagesperso-orange.fr/Pasapas/E302Lois.html |archive-date=2013-06-04 |website=combattant.14-18.pagesperso-orange.fr |language=fr}}</ref> Men doing their service were transferred to active regiments, theoretically recruited locally; after their service, they were called up three times for maneuvers and exercises, two times for reservists (each one for four weeks) and one time for territorial army reservists (of only two weeks).<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |year=1999 |title=Rapport de la commission des Affaires étrangères sur le projet de loi portant création de la réserve militaire |trans-title=Report of the Foreign Affairs Committee on the bill to create the military reserve |url=http://www.senat.fr/rap/l98-355/l98-3553.html |archive-url=https://archive.wikiwix.com/cache/?url=http%3A%2F%2Fwww.senat.fr%2Frap%2Fl98-355%2Fl98-3553.html |archive-date=February 7, 2014 |website=senat.fr |language=fr}}</ref> In theory, men declared unfit for service due to physical incapacity were still subject to military obligations, in the form of auxiliary service (in offices, depots, the health service, etc.). A final case is that of the "special assigned", i.e. customs officers, forest hunters, men in field railway sections, and post and telegraph officers.
[[File:Detaille - Infantry of the Line, inspection in the rooms, 1885.jpg|alt=Painting showing officers checking conscripts' rooms.|thumb|[[Édouard Detaille]], ''Inspection des chambres'' (Room Inspection), 1885.]]Each year, a "class" of conscripts was recruited: a class is a group of men born in the same year and fit for service. The number of a class corresponds to the year of its census, generally taken in December of the year in which they turned twenty; conscription took place the year after the census, in autumn. When mobilized, men from the active forces and the youngest reservists formed the units sent into combat, while older reservists were destined to form reserve regiments kept behind the front or to fill depots while waiting to replace casualties. The men of the territorial army formed units for tasks behind the front, such as the garrisoning of squares or entrenchment work. Finally, men from the Territorial Army Reserve were to be used to guard railroads and the coast.<ref name=":0" />

The [[French Navy]] recruited its personnel in a different way, based on maritime recruitment: men engaged in maritime or river navigation were required to serve in the "army of the sea",<ref>Regulation of November 7, 1866 and law of December 24, 1896 on maritime registration, published in the Journal officiel of December 27, 1896, {{Gallica|id=bpt6k214889c/f1507|t=Bulletin des lois, n° 1825, p. 1473}} (In French).</ref> with a five-year term of service in peacetime. However, as the fleet needed a large number of qualified technicians, recruitment was nationwide, with maritime enrollment providing only half of the fleet's manpower in the event of mobilization.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Vers la fin de l'Inscription maritime, au XXe siècle |trans-title=Towards the end of the 20th-century maritime inscription |url=http://www.unicaen.fr/ufr/histoire/cimarconet/inscription_maritime/historique6.php |archive-url=https://archive.wikiwix.com/cache/index2.php?url=http%3A%2F%2Fwww.unicaen.fr%2Fufr%2Fhistoire%2Fcimarconet%2Finscription_maritime%2Fhistorique6.php#federation=archive.wikiwix.com&tab=url |archive-date=September 16, 2022 |website=unicaen.fr |language=fr}}</ref>

=== Planning ===
[[File:Joffre and Messimy.jpg|alt=The general in simple uniform, the civilian in jacket and bowler hat, both wearing binoculars and boots.|thumb|The two main leaders of the French armed forces in 1914: on the left, [[Joseph Joffre]] ( Commander-in-chief of the Army); on the right, [[Adolphe Messimy]] (Minister of War).]]
{{Main|Plan XVII}}The [[entire mobilization]] was planned by the [[Staff (military)|General Staff]] of the Army, headed since 1911 by [[Divisional general|Major General]] [[Joseph Joffre|Joffre]], in particular its 1st bureau (organization and mobilization of the army, headed in 1914 by [[Lieutenant colonel]] Émile Giraud) and 4th bureau (stages, railroads, troop transport by rail and water, headed by Lieutenant-Colonel Camille Ragueneau).<ref name=":2">{{Cite book |title=Répartition et emplacement des troupes de l'armée française |date=May 1, 1914 |publisher=Imprimerie nationale |location=Paris |language=fr |trans-title=Distribution and location of French army troops}}</ref>

The plan applied in 1914 was [[Plan XVII]], prepared in 1913 by the General Staff and validated by the [[Conseil supérieur de la guerre|Superior War Council]]. It provided for the mobilization of men, their concentration on the borders, their organization into several armies and the direction of the first offensives. But as all this would take around a fortnight, some of the active troops also needed to cover this mobilization. The role entrusted to the [[French Navy|navy]], which was outclassed by the [[Imperial German Navy|German navy]], was simply to protect troop convoys from Algeria and Morocco (in the hope that Italy would be neutral) and to block the English Channel to German ships (in the hope of British support).<ref>{{Harvtxt|Valluy|Dufourcq|1968|pp=130–131|loc=Volume 1}}</ref>

==== Troops organization ====
In the event of partial mobilization (motivated by the "threat of aggression characterized by the gathering of armed foreign forces"),<ref name=":1" /> only the two youngest reserve units were called up. In the event of general mobilization, everyone was called up, without any individual notification. In his military brochure, each man was given a route sheet ("''fascicule de mobilisation''", or mobilization booklet, model A was pink if he needed to use the railroads, model A1 was light green if he had to march<ref name=":7">{{Cite book |title=Note ministérielle du 5 juillet 1897 portant adoption d'un nouveau modèle de fascicule A et modifiant certaines dispositions de l'instruction du 28 décembre 1895, sur l'administration des hommes des différentes catégories de réserve dans leurs foyers |publisher=H. Charles-Lavauzelle |year=1898 |location=Paris |language=fr |trans-title=Ministerial note of July 5, 1897 adopting a new model for booklet A and amending certain provisions of the instruction of December 28, 1895, on the administration of men in the various reserve categories in their homes.}} {{Gallica|id=bpt6k6101232d}}</ref>) with his call-up date and route (free of charge) to his [[Main operating base|base]], where he was dressed, equipped and armed.<ref>{{Cite book |title=L'infanterie en un volume: manuel d'instruction militaire à l'usage des élèves-caporaux, sous-officiers, élèves-officiers de réserve candidats aux écoles de Saint-Maixent ou de Saint-Cyr |publisher=Librairie Chapelot |year=1914 |location=Paris |pages=926 |language=fr |trans-title=The infantry in one volume: a military instruction manual for cadets, non-commissioned officers and reserve officer cadets applying to the Saint-Maixent or Saint-Cyr schools.}}</ref><gallery mode="packed" caption="The four pages of the mobilization brochure (model A)">

[[File:12e compagnie du 1er RI, 1911.jpg|alt=Infantry company souvenir photo.|thumb|The 12th [[Company (military unit)|company]] of the [[1st Infantry Regiment (France)|1st infantry regiment]] in 1911, stationed in [[Cambrai]]. Units were generally recruited locally, particularly in the infantry: soldiers of the 1er RI mainly come from the [[Arrondissement of Cambrai|Cambrai district]].]]

The different types of unit, theoretically recruited locally, were housed in the same [[barracks]]:<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Valluy |first1=Jean Étienne |title=La première guerre mondiale |last2=Dufourcq |first2=Pierre |publisher=Larousse |year=1968 |volume=1 |location=Paris |pages=72 |language=fr |trans-title=The First World War}}</ref>

* Men doing their military service formed the backbone of the active [[regiment]]s, mainly the 173 [[French Infantry regiments|infantry regiments]] (numbered from 1 to 173), plus the 59 colonial and indigenous infantry regiments, the 89 [[cavalry]] regiments, the 87 [[artillery]] regiments, the 11 [[Military engineering|engineer regiments]], as well as the service units (crew, management, health, aeronautics corps, etc.){{refn|group="Note"|In May 1914, the French army comprised: 173 infantry regiments, 31 foot chasseur battalions, 4 Zouave regiments, 9 Algerian tirailleurs regiments, 2 foreign regiments, 5 African light infantry battalions, 24 colonial infantry regiments, 6 colonial infantry marching regiments, one Annamite tirailleurs regiment, 4 Tonkinois tirailleurs regiments, 4 Senegalese tirailleurs regiments, 2 indigenous regiments (from Gabon and Chad), 3 Madagascan infantry regiments, 11 colonial battalions, 12 cuirassier regiments, 32 dragoon regiments, 21 chasseur regiments, 14 hussar regiments, 6 African chasseur regiments, 4 [[spahi]] regiments, 11 foot artillery regiments, 62 field artillery regiments, 5 heavy artillery regiments, 2 mountain artillery regiments, 7 colonial artillery regiments and 11 engineer regiments.<ref name=":2">{{Cite book |title=Répartition et emplacement des troupes de l'armée française |date=May 1, 1914 |publisher=Imprimerie nationale |location=Paris |language=fr |trans-title=Distribution and location of French army troops}}</ref>}}
* On Day 2, the arrival at the depots of the three youngest classes of reservists must bring all active regiments up to full wartime strength
* They were then replaced by the remaining reservists, who were to form reserve infantry regiments created during mobilization (numbered 201 to 421) in infantry regiment depots (numbered by adding 200 to the number);
* Finally, the territorial infantry, who formed 145 territorial infantry regiments, at least one in each [[military district]] subdivision.

Each [[infantry]] [[Main operating base|depot]] completes an active regiment (with three [[battalion]]s), increasing it from 2,000 men to just over 3,200, then sets up a reserve regiment (with two battalions, numbered 5 and 6), followed by a territorial regiment. Finally the guard posts for communication routes (railroads, canals, telephone and telegraph lines). Each [[cavalry]] depot reinforces its cavalry regiment with two reserve [[Squadron (army)|squadrons]]; each artillery depot completes its [[artillery]] regiment and creates a reserve group (composed of several [[Artillery battery|batteries]]); each [[Military engineering|engineer]] depot reinforces its regiment with new [[Company (military unit)|companies]]. A few hundred reservists are maintained in each depot to replace future losses.

The vote by the [[Chamber of Deputies]] on the [[Law of Three Years]] in 1913 was requested by the Army Staff, which wanted to have as many active units as its German counterpart, the ''[[Imperial German Army|Deutsches Heer]]'' (for fear of a possible sudden attack). Thanks to this law, the peacetime army grew from 520,000 to 736,000 men in uniform, each company from 90 to 140 men, with ten new infantry regiments (nos. 164 to 173). This force was structured into 22 [[corps]],{{refn|group="Note"|In 1914, each French [[Corps|army corps]] was theoretically composed of two infantry [[Division (military)|divisions]] (each with four infantry [[regiment]]s, i.e. twelve [[battalion]]s) supported by divisional artillery. The theoretical maximum strength of a corps is therefore 40,000 men (plus 8,900 horses and 120 [[Canon de 75 modèle 1897|75 mm cannon]]), an infantry division 16,000, a regiment 3,400 and a battalion 1,100.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Composition des unités |trans-title=Unit composition |url=http://www.pages14-18.com/C_PAGES_DOCUMENTS/DOC/unit%C3%A9s_1914.pdf |website=pages14-18.com |language=fr}}</ref>}} each assigned to a military region (or "corps region": in 1914 there were twenty in Metropolitan France, plus one in Algeria).

Between 1914 and 1918, the core tactical element was the [[Division (military)|infantry division]]. On August 2, 1914, France mobilized 93 divisions, including 45 active, 25 reserve, 11 territorial, 2 [[Troupes coloniales|colonial]] and 10 cavalry divisions. By November 11, 1918, France had 119 infantry divisions.

==== Transportation to the border ====
[[File:Concentration 1914.png|alt=Northern part of France, crossed by several concentric lines all leading to the Franco-German border.|thumb|Diagram showing the various lines used to transport army corps.]]
Mobilization was determined by [[Rail transport in France|rail resources]] and by the strategy planned for the start of the conflict. The transport of all troops, known as "concentration", mobilized the majority of rolling stock, requisitioned on the advice of the Minister of War:<ref>Decree of February 5, 1889 organizing military service on the railroads and decree of December 8, 1913 regulating strategic transport by rail, {{Gallica|id=bpt6k62248326/f9}}</ref> one train was needed for a battalion, three trains for an infantry regiment,<ref>{{Harvtxt|Naërt|al.|1936|p=61}}</ref> four for a cavalry regiment, seven for an infantry brigade, 26 for an infantry division and 117 for an army corps.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Mallouy |first=Jean |date=June 14, 1914 |title=Les Transports stratégiques |trans-title=The strategic transport |journal=Armée et Marine: Revue hebdomadaire illustrée des armées de terre et de mer |language=fr |issue=24 |pages=615}} {{Gallica|id=bpt6k57308394/f6}}</ref> These trains were made up of 34 (for a [[Squadron (army)|squadron]]) to 47 (for a [[battalion]]) wagons, making for 400-meter-long convoys, with [[Passenger railroad car|passenger carriages]], [[Covered goods wagon|goods wagons]] (at a rate of eight horses or forty men per wagon)<ref group="Note">After the First World War, the OCEM (''Office central d'études de matériel de chemins de fer'', or Central Office for Railway Material Design) standardized the wagons with the words "''Hommes 40 - Chevaux en long 8''" (Men 40 - Horses in length 8) on them.</ref> and [[flat wagon]]s (for vans and cannons),{{refn|group="Note"|For example, the 125th infantry regiment from Poitiers embarked in three parts, the first (a battalion and a machine-gun section) on August 5 in a train of 49 wagons: 2 for officers, 30 for troops, 10 for horses and 7 for carriages.<ref>{{Cite web |title=125e régiment d'infanterie, Journal de Marche du 5 août 1914 au 31 décembre 1916 |trans-title=125th Infantry Regiment, March Diary from August 5, 1914, to December 31, 1916 |url=http://www.memoiredeshommes.sga.defense.gouv.fr/jmo/img-viewer/26_N_685_001/viewer.html |website=memoiredeshomme.sga.defense.go |page=6 |language=fr}}</ref>}} as required.

As a result, railroads were extensively developed for military reasons, each subprefecture was connected ([[Freycinet Plan|Freycinet plan]] from 1879 to 1914), double tracks led eastwards (notably those from [[Paris-Est–Strasbourg-Ville railway|Paris to Nancy]] and [[Paris-Est–Mulhouse-Ville railway|Paris to Belfort)]] with [[ring road]]s between them, while some stations were enlarged (e.g. [[Gare de l'Est|''Gare de Paris-Est'']]). Ten lines crossing metropolitan France were prepared by the General Instruction on the execution of the concentration (''l'instruction générale sur l'exécution de la concentration)'' of February 15, 1909, rectified on April 4, 1914,<ref>{{Harvtxt|Naërt|al.|1936|p=56}}</ref> each line designed to transport two army corps from their military regions to landing stations behind the concentration zone. From the 2nd to the 4th day of mobilization, these lines were to carry the second stage of the covering corps (the army corps stationed near the German border); on the 3rd and 4th days, the cavalry; from the 4th to the 10th day, all the army corps, starting with the "hasty" divisions of the 2nd, 5th and 8th corps (from the 4th to the 6th day); for day 13, all reserve divisions must be deployed; on day 16, the [[Army of Africa (France)|Army of Africa]] (part of the [[19th Army Corps (France)|19th Army Corps]]) arrived; finally, for day 17, all territorial divisions, fleets and logistics must be in place.<ref>{{Harvtxt|Naërt|al.|1936|pp=57–58}}</ref>

Overseas troops were a special case: the [[19th Army Corps (France)|19th Army Corps]] (mainly recruited and stationed in [[French Algeria|Algeria]]) had to supply two divisions (the [[37th Infantry Division (France)|37th]] and [[38th Infantry Division (France)|38th]]), which had to cross the [[Mediterranean Sea|Mediterranean]] on requisitioned ships and under the protection of French squadrons to land at [[Sète]] and [[Marseille]]. [[Troupes coloniales|Colonial troops]] in the colonies were not included in the mobilization and concentration plan.

==== Precautionary measures ====
Troops were stationed directly along the Franco-German border to protect mobilization from the very first day, relying on [[Séré de Rivières system|fortifications in the East]].<ref name=":2" /> In the event of diplomatic tension, The instruction for preparing for mobilization (''l'instruction sur la préparation de la mobilisation)'' provided for six groups of measures to be taken successively:

* group A (precautionary measures), recall of officers, volunteers and troops on the move;
* group B (surveillance measures), surveillance of the border and telegraph and telephone offices;
* group C (protective measures), guarding fortified structures and engineering works;
* group D, coastal surveillance and protection;
* group E (preparatory organizational measures), call-up for exercise of gendarmes, certain reservists and territorial guards of border communication routes, as well as the location of necessary horses;
* group F (preparatory measures for operations), loading of mine devices (to destroy border engineering structures), firing on suspicious aircraft, mobilization exercises for border garrisons, interruption of international power lines.<ref>Instruction on the preparation of mobilization of February 15, 1909, updated on April 4, 1914, appendix 2, cited in {{Harvtxt|Naërt|al.|1936|p=94}}</ref>
The "cover" (protection) of the mobilization was provided by five [[Corps|army corps]], the first echelon of which was almost fully manned in peacetime,{{refn|group="Note"|For example, the 152nd regiment was stationed at [[Gérardmer]], with its depot at [[Langres]], and belonged to the 7th corps ([[41st Infantry Division (France)|41st]] [[Remiremont]] division): its active manpower was 2,296, with mobilization adding 994 reservists, bringing the total to 3,290 men.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Journal des marches & opérations du 152e Régiment d'Infanterie pendant les marches de reconnaissances, grandes manœuvres, tirs de guerre, etc. du 16 juillet 1913 au 20 juin 1915, « 26 N 697/13 » |trans-title= Diary of marches & operations of the 152nd Infantry Regiment during reconnaissance marches, major maneuvers, firing in war, etc. from July 16, 1913 to June 20, 1915, "26 N 697/13" |url=http://www.memoiredeshommes.sga.defense.gouv.fr/jmo/img-viewer/26_N_697_013/viewer.html |website= memoiredeshommes.sga.defense.gouv.fr |language=fr}}</ref>}} prepositioned along the Franco-German border: part of the [[2nd Army Corps (France)|2nd corps]] at [[Charleville-Mézières|Mézières]], the 6th corps at [[Verdun]] and [[Saint-Mihiel]], the 20th corps at [[Toul]] and [[Nancy, France|Nancy]], the 21st corps at [[Épinal]] and [[Saint-Dié-des-Vosges|Saint-Dié]] and the 7th corps at [[Remiremont]] and [[Belfort]].<ref name=":2" /> Their mission under the XVII plan was "initially, to stop enemy reconnaissance or detachments seeking to penetrate the territory, and subsequently, to delay the march of larger corps that could disrupt the landing and concentration of armies". These corps were theoretically available in two echelons: the first between the 3rd and 8th hour of mobilization, the second from the 2nd to the 4th day; [[12th Infantry Division (France)|the 12th Reims division]] was to serve as reserve. Between days 4 and 6, the cover was to be reinforced by three "hasty" divisions (cover reinforcements) provided by the 2nd corps (the 3rd Amiens division), the 5th corps ([[9th Motorized Division|the 9th Orléans division]], temporarily transferred to the 6th corps) and the 8th corps ([[15th Infantry Division (France)|the 15th Dijon division]], loaned to the 21st corps).<ref>{{Harvtxt|Naërt|al.|1936|pp=83–84}}</ref>

== Outbreak ==
[[France–Germany relations|Relations between Germany and France]] at the start of the 20th century were marked by a series of diplomatic tensions, most notably the two Moroccan crises: [[First Moroccan Crisis|the Tangier crisis]] of 1905 and the [[Agadir Crisis|Agadir crisis]] of 1911. However, it was through the alliances that these two states were forced to declare their mobilization.

=== July Crisis ===
{{Main|July Crisis}}
The ''[[casus belli]]'' of the [[Assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand]]t triggered a succession of [[ultimatum]]s, [[mobilization]]s and [[Declaration of war|declarations of war]] that quickly spread to Germany and then France. On July 25, 1914, the [[Kingdom of Serbia]] decreed its mobilization in response to the [[Ultimatum of July 23, 1914|Austro-Hungarian ultimatum]]; on the same day, [[Austria-Hungary]] announced partial mobilization from the 28th. On the 29th, the [[Russian Empire]] followed with a partial mobilization due to start on July 30.<ref>{{Harvtxt|Le Naour|2012|p=95}}</ref> On the 30th, the Tsar ordered general mobilization,<ref>{{Harvtxt|Le Naour|2012|p=109}}</ref> which had no other consequences than the inevitable Austrian (from the 31st) and German mobilizations. In France, at 7 a.m. on July 30, Chief of Staff [[Joseph Joffre|Joffre]] asked [[Minister of the Armed Forces (France)|War Minister]] [[Adolphe Messimy|Messimy]] for an order to mobilize, or at least to cover the borders, but did not receive it. The General warned the Minister: "If what we know of German intentions proves true, the enemy will enter our territory without firing a shot."<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Cartier |first1=Raymond |title=La première guerre mondiale |date=1982 |publisher=[[Presses de la Cité]] |others=Jean-Pierre Cartier |isbn=978-2-258-01101-4 |series=Coup d'oeil |location=Paris |pages=64 |language=fr |trans-title=The First World War}}</ref>
[[File:Paris, Baron Von Schon, German Amb. (LOC).jpg|alt=Baron's standing portrait|thumb|Baron [[Wilhelm von Schoen|von Schoen]], German ambassador to France.]]
On the 31st, the [[German Empire]] decreed ''Kriegsgefahrzustand'' (a state of war danger: requisitions, border closures, etc.): Joffre again called for mobilization: "It is absolutely necessary that the government should know that, from this evening onwards, any delay of twenty-four hours in calling up reservists and sending the covering telegram will result in a retreat of our concentration force, i.e. in the initial abandonment of part of our territory"<ref>{{Harvtxt|Cartier|1982|loc=v. 1|p=65}}</ref> He obtained the covering order, but not the mobilization order: he sent the order by [[Telegram services|telegram]] at 5:40 p.m. to the various units, with application from 9 p.m. At 7 p.m., the German ambassador to France, [[Wilhelm von Schoen|Schoen]], met the [[President of the Council of Ministers|President of the Council]], [[René Viviani|Viviani]], and under the orders of the German Chancellor<ref>{{Cite web |title=Télégramme du chancelier du Reich au baron von Schoen, ambassadeur d'Allemagne à Paris le 31 juillet 1914 |trans-title=Telegram from the Reich Chancellor to Baron von Schoen, German Ambassador to Paris, July 31, 1914 |url=https://fr.wikisource.org/wiki/Ultimatum_de_l%27Allemagne_%C3%A0_la_France_en_1914 |website=Wikisource |language=fr}}</ref> asked him whether France would remain neutral in the event of a Russo-German war: the Frenchman procrastinated ("allow me time to think").<ref>{{Harvtxt|Cartier|1982|loc=v. 1|pp=66–67}}</ref>

=== Mobilization order ===
At 11 a.m. on August 1, Schoen met Viviani again to obtain the reply that "France will be guided by its interests". At 3:45 p.m., the French government<ref group="Note">Viviani did not sign the order, which was signed only by the Ministers of War and the Navy.</ref> decreed the start of general mobilization on August 2.<ref name=":3">{{Harvtxt|Cartier|1982|p=70|loc=v. 1}}</ref> By 5:00 p.m. Kaiser Wilhelm II ordered the [[German mobilization]], then declared war on Russia at 7 p.m.<ref>{{Harvtxt|Cartier|1982|pp=71–73|loc=v. 1}}</ref> On the evening of the 2nd, Germany told the Belgian government not to oppose the passage of German troops through Belgium.<ref>{{Harvtxt|Cartier|1982|pp=79–80|loc=v. 1}}</ref> On the 3rd, the German ambassador transmitted the declaration of war to France to the head of the French government at 6:45 p.m. (on the basis that French aircraft had attacked German territory)<ref>{{Cite web |title=Déclaration de guerre de l'Allemagne à la France |trans-title=German declaration of war on France |url=https://fr.wikisource.org/wiki/D%C3%A9claration_de_guerre_de_l%E2%80%99Allemagne_%C3%A0_la_France |website=Wikisource |language=fr}}</ref> and left Paris, while Belgium refused to let German troops through.<ref name=":9">{{Harvtxt|Cartier|1982|p=83|loc=v. 1}}</ref>

The mobilization order was issued by the "Decree ordering the mobilization of the Army and Navy on August 1, 1914", published in the ''[[Journal officiel de la République française|Journal Officiel]]'' on August 2.<ref>{{Gallica|id=bpt6k2207815/f430|t=Bulletin des lois, n° 133, p. 2228}}</ref> The telegram giving the mobilization order was sent from Paris at 3:55 p.m. on August 1 to [[corps]], [[Division (military)|division]] and [[regiment]] commanders, as well as to [[Prefect (France)|prefects]], who relayed it to sub-prefects and mayors; isolated rural communes were informed by [[National Gendarmerie|gendarmes]] (on horseback or by car), then to hamlets by messengers sent by the mayors.<ref name=":10">{{Cite book |last=Petit-Dutaillis |first=Charles |author-link=Charles Petit-Dutaillis |url=https://gallica.bnf.fr/ark:/12148/bpt6k5732975z/f11 |title=Annales de l'Université de Grenoble |publisher=Allier Frères |year=1915 |location=Grenoble |pages=5–10 |language=fr |trans-title=Annales of the University of Grenoble |chapter=L'appel de guerre en Dauphiné: 1er-2 août 1914 |trans-chapter=The call to war in Dauphiné: August 1–2, 1914}} (notes taken by village teachers in Isère, Drôme and Hautes-Alpes).</ref> The first poster was put up on August 1 at 4pm on the corner of [[Place de la Concorde|Concorde]] and [[Rue Royale, Paris|Rue Royale.]]<ref name=":3" /> The entire population was informed on the same day by posters, printed since 1904<ref name=":11">{{Cite web |title=L'affiche de mobilisation, 1914 |trans-title=Mobilization poster, 1914 |url=http://horizon14-18.eu/wa_files/affiche_20mobilisation.pdf |website=horizon14-18.eu |language=fr}} ([[Army Museum (Paris)|Army Museum]], educational brochure)</ref> (only the date needed to be completed), posted on public roads in each commune<ref>Law of March 19, 1875 on Mobilization by means of posters and publicity, published in the ''Journal officiel'' of March 26, 1875, {{Gallica|id=bpt6k210067b/f430|t=Bulletin des lois, n° 251, p. 408}}</ref> and then by the [[Bell|tocsin]] sounded by church and belfry bells.<gallery mode="packed">

== First reactions ==

=== Astonishment then enthusiasm ===
The announcement of mobilization did not trigger widespread enthusiasm:<ref name=":4">{{Cite book |last=Becker |first=Jean-Jacques |title=La Première guerre mondiale |date=1985 |publisher=M.A |isbn=978-2-86676-197-4 |series=Le Monde de |location=Paris |pages=137 |language=fr |trans-title=The First World War}}</ref> as historian [[Jean-Jacques Becker]] points out, "probably the most widespread feeling among all sections of the population was one of surprise",<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Becker |first1=Jean Jacques |author-link1=Jean-Jacques Becker |title=La France en guerre: 1914-1918: la grande mutation |last2=Becker |first2=Annette |date=1988 |publisher=Editions Complexe |isbn=978-2-87027-261-9 |series=Questions au XXe siècle |location=Bruxelles |language=fr |trans-title=France at war: 1914–1918: the great transformation}}</ref> particularly in rural areas where the press was less widely distributed than in cities. The astonishment expressed at the time clearly indicates that the mobilization initially took the population by surprise,<ref name=":4" /> as in [[Charente]] village [[Aignes-et-Puypéroux|Aignes]]:
{{Translated blockquote
| quote = « le premier août 1914, vers cinq heures du soir, la plupart des gens furent avertis, par le son de la cloche, que la mobilisation générale était décrétée. En effet quelques instants auparavant, la gendarmerie de Blanzac était venue en apporter la nouvelle au maire. Plus tard, la nouvelle fut confirmée dans tous les villages, par le tambour, qui apposait également les affiches spéciales. La première impression fut, pour tout le monde, une profonde stupéfaction car personne ne croyait la guerre possible. Néanmoins, les jours suivants, les départs s'effectuèrent avec la plus grande régularité. Les femmes retrouvèrent leur calme et les hommes, pleins d'enthousiasme, partaient en chantant »
| translation = "On August 1, 1914, at around five o'clock in the evening, most people were warned by the sound of the bell that general mobilization had been decreed. Indeed, a few moments earlier, the Blanzac gendarmerie had come to bring the news to the mayor. Later, the drummer confirmed the news in all the villages, who also put up the special posters. Everyone's first impression was one of profound amazement, for no one thought war was possible. Nevertheless, in the days that followed, the departures took place with the greatest regularity. The women regained their composure and the men, full of enthusiasm, set off singing"<ref>{{Cite web |title=La mobilisation à Aignes, par M. Léger (instituteur) |trans-title=Mobilization in Aignes, by M. Léger (teacher) |url=http://www.archives16.fr/arkotheque/arkotheque_visionneuse_archives.php?arko=YTo0OntzOjQ6ImRhdGUiO3M6MTA6IjIwMTMtMDItMTEiO3M6MTA6InR5cGVfZm9uZHMiO3M6MTE6ImFya29fc2VyaWVsIjtzOjQ6InJlZjEiO2k6MjtzOjQ6InJlZjIiO2k6NDM7fQ== |language=fr}}</ref>
| language = fr
| class = 
}}
Similarly, in [[Nyons]], a town in the [[Drôme|Drôme region]], a schoolteacher testifies: "The population, although prepared for the war for several days by the press, learned the unfortunate news with a sort of stupor. I saw some women crying. The men looked sad, but determined."<ref>Testimony of M. Roux, schoolteacher in Nyons, quoted in {{Harvtxt|Petit-Dutaillis|1915|p=22}} {{Gallica|id=bpt6k5732975z/f28}}</ref>

Analyzed by Jean-Jacques Becker, these documents show the different stages of popular reaction. The initial astonishment was often followed by a certain despondency: "consternation, sadness and anguish were widespread, far more so than feelings dictated by the patriotic impulse",<ref name=":5">{{Harvtxt|Becker|1985|p=138}}</ref> and expressions of enthusiasm were rare. President [[Raymond Poincaré]]'s proclamation, posted and published in the newspapers on August 2, was reassuring, emphasizing "mobilization is not war; on the contrary, in the present circumstances, it appears to be the best means of ensuring peace with honor. The government, strengthened by its ardent desire to reach a peaceful solution to the crisis and shielded by these necessary precautions, will continue its diplomatic efforts and still hopes to succeed. It is counting on the composure of the noble nation not to give way to unjustified emotion; it is counting on the patriotism of all Frenchmen, and knows that there is not one who is not ready to do his duty. At this hour, there are no more parties, there is an eternal, peaceful and resolute France. There is the entire country of law and justice, united in calm, vigilance and dignity".<ref>{{Cite web |last=Poincaré |first=Raymon |date=August 2, 1914 |title=Proclamation du Président de la République |url=https://fr.wikisource.org/wiki/Proclamation_du_Pr%C3%A9sident_de_la_R%C3%A9publique_(Le_Figaro) |website=Wikisource}}</ref>

However, the mood had changed by the time the soldiers left for their barracks, as described above in Aignes. Whereas before, expressions of enthusiasm had been infrequent, now they were more spectacular, particularly at the embarkation stations for mobilized soldiers, demonstrating a genuine patriotic impulse imbued with seriousness and a determination to do one's duty, despite the frequent tears shed by the women or the more or less heart-rending farewells.<ref name=":5" /> How can this change in mood be explained? According to Jean-Jacques Becker, revanchist sentiments linked to the [[Franco-Prussian War|1870 war]] and the loss of [[Alsace–Lorraine|Alsace-Lorraine]] played little part. French [[public opinion]] was dominated by the idea of a peaceful France, obliged to defend itself against outright German aggression. Under these conditions, refusing to fight was out of the question. Men set off, "not with the enthusiasm of a conqueror, but with the resolution of a duty to be fulfilled",<ref name=":5" /> an idea also reflected in the testimony of historian [[Marc Bloch]], who was himself mobilized: "Most of the men were not cheerful: they were resolute, which was better."<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Block |first=Marc |author-link=Marc Bloch |year=1969 |title=Souvenirs de guerre |journal=Cahier des Annales |language=fr |location=Paris |issue=26 |pages=10}}</ref>

=== Xenophobia ===
[[File:Paris -- German Shop smashed by mob (LOC).jpg|alt=Shattered store window.|thumb|The facade of the ''Appenrodt'' tea house on ''[[Boulevard des Italiens]]'', vandalized.]]
[[File:Magasin Maxim's 1914.jpg|alt=Store window partly covered by a poster.|thumb|Poster for Maxim's store (a shoemaker): "''Vive la France''; French company, sells only French products, Roche, owner, mobilized in Aurillac".]]
This commitment, which was measured if resolute, was not incompatible with displays of [[Patriotism|patriotic]] enthusiasm in the streets, whether in the form of parades, crowds or military songs; nor did it prevent [[Nationalism|nationalist]] and [[Xenophobia|xenophobic]] outbursts, notably the looting of stores with Germanic names<ref name=":6">{{Harvtxt|Valluy|Dufourcq|1968|p=73|loc=Volume 1}}</ref> (on the night of August 2 to 3, 1914, and again the following day, the [[Maggi]] dairy stores, although Swiss-branded, were looted.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Pillage de la boutique Maggi de la rue de la Tombe-Issoire |trans-title=Looting of the Maggi store on rue de la Tombe-Issoire |url=https://www.galerie-roger-viollet.fr/fr/popup-photo.html?photo=8455-5 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131111223828/http://www.parisenimages.fr/fr/popup-photo.html?photo=8455-5 |archive-date=November 11, 2013 |website=parisenimage.fr |language=fr}}</ref> The same company's laboratory was set on fire; the Pschorr tavern on ''[[boulevard de Strasbourg]]'', the Appenrodt food store on ''rue des Italiens'', the Muller brasserie on rue Thorel and the Klein boutique on ''[[boulevard des Italiens]]'' were ransacked); the black veil was removed from the Strasbourg statue on ''[[place de la Concorde]],''<ref>{{Harvtxt|Cartier|1982|p=71|loc=Volume 1}}</ref> etc.). This [[catharsis]] continued in the days that followed, with, for example, the renaming of ''rue de Berlin'' to ''rue de Liège'' on August 15 (in tribute to the Belgian defenders of the [[Battle of Liège|siege of Liège]]), ''avenue d'Allemagne'' to ''avenue Jean-Jaurès'' on August 19 (following a petition from the avenue's residents) and the homonym metro stations ([[Liège station (Paris Métro)|Liège]] and [[Jaurès station|Jaurès]]), the ''café viennois'' was renamed the ''[[café liégeois]]'', berlingots became "''[[Tetra Pak|parigots]]''", German shepherds became Belgian shepherds and ''eau de Cologne'' became "''eau de Pologne''".<ref>{{Harvtxt|Le Naour|2012|p=176}}</ref>

However, these collective manifestations of intense patriotic or even nationalist fervor were very much in the minority, confined to a few towns: as Stéphane Audoin-Rouzeau and [[Annette Becker]] point out, the motivation of rural populations (the majority in France) was clearly distinct from, but not contradictory to, a certain urban enthusiasm, "the leading edge of a general consent centered on resignation and acceptance - sometimes overwhelm - and then the growing resolution of the majority".<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Audoin-Rouzeau |first1=Stéphane |title=14-18, retrouver la guerre |last2=Becker |first2=Annette |author-link2=Annette Becker |publisher=[[Éditions Gallimard]] |year=2000 |isbn=978-2-07-075284-3 |series=Bibliothèque des histoires |location=Paris |pages=113 |language=fr |trans-title=14–18, rediscovering war}}</ref>

=== Sacred union ===
Military and political leaders were worried about the possible refusal to obey by civilians called up as reservists: they feared that the number of ''insoumis'' ([[Desertion|deserters]]) would be significant, and that [[Pacifism|pacifist]] demonstrations would take place. Several opposition unions and political parties, notably the [[General Confederation of Labour (France)|CGT]] and [[French Section of the Workers' International|SFIO]], had taken [[Antimilitarism|anti-militarist]] stances before the crisis broke out, and were planning a general strike (the refusal to obey mobilization orders) to prevent the outbreak of conflict. On July 29 and 30, SFIO leader [[Jean Jaurès]] was in [[Brussels]] for a meeting of the bureau of the [[Second International]] and a meeting with [[Social Democratic Party of Germany|German socialist leaders]], with the aim of coordinating their pacifist actions. Faced with these expected difficulties, the French Ministry of the Interior had planned for the systematic arrest of anti-militarist leaders in the event of mobilization: the [[Carnet B]] was to provide a list of 2,500 individuals "whose attitude and actions may be likely to disturb order and hinder the smooth running of mobilization services".<ref>{{Harvtxt|Lejeune|2007|p=168}}</ref>).

However, the surge of patriotism and the [[Assassination of Jean Jaurès|assassination of Jaurès]] in Paris on July 31 led the Left Party to rally to the "[[Sacred Union]]" called for by [[Raymond Poincaré|President Poincaré]] in his speech on August 4. The CGT announced that it was putting its Paris premises on rue de la Grange-aux-Belles at the disposal of the [[French Armed Forces Health Service|Army Medical Corps]].<ref name=":6" /> [[Léon Jouhaux]], General Secretary of the [[General Confederation of Labour (France)|CGT]], proclaimed at Jaurès's funeral: "In the name of the trade unions, in the name of all those workers who have already joined their regiments, and in the name of those, including myself, who will be leaving tomorrow, I declare that we are going to the battlefield with the determination to repel the aggressor."<ref>{{Harvtxt|Cartier|1982|p=83}}</ref> As a result of these reactions, Interior Minister [[Louis Malvy]] instructed prefects not to use Carnet B, even though a few arrests were made in the [[Nord (French department)|Nord]] and [[Pas-de-Calais]] regions.<ref>{{Harvtxt|Becker|Becker|1988|p=28}}</ref> The SFIO voted for the war loans, then joined the government in the [[Second Viviani government|reshuffle of August 26]], gaining the [[Ministry of War (France)|Ministries of War]] and [[Ministry for Europe and Foreign Affairs (France)|Foreign Affairs]].

== Proceedings ==
The mobilization of 1914 was divided into three periods: the covering period (August 2 to 7), during which reservists were called up under the protection of covering troops; the concentration period (August 8 to 13), during which active and reserve troops were moved to the frontier; and the start of the period of major operations (August 14 to 18), during which territorial troops, fleets, and logistics were put in place.

=== Reservists recalled ===
Not all men were mobilized at the same time, but gradually, depending on their status. The mandatory date of arrival at the depot (indicated in days after the first day of mobilization) appeared on the mobilization booklet (a double sheet) attached by staples to the back cover of the military record booklet,<ref name=":7" />  which each man had to keep for his 28 years of military service (three years in the active service, eleven in the reserve, seven in the territorial service and seven in the territorial reserve), including during his travels, and even if he lived abroad.

The 200,000 men of the Territorial Reserve assigned to guarding transport routes were mobilized on the eve of the first day of mobilization (i.e. August 1), to protect important railroads and engineering structures close to their homes (usually less than ten kilometers away, or 6.2 miles).

The 880,000 men<ref group="Note">Peacetime manpower figures vary according to the men taken into account. The figure of 817,000 provided by MP [[Louis Marin (politician)|Louis Marin]] includes the 766,000 troops in the armed service and the 51,000 in the auxiliary service, excluding indigenous troops and all officers. The total given by Naërt et al. 1936, p. 54 for August 1, 1914 is 882,907 men, including 686,993 in metropolitan France, 62,598 in Algeria-Tunisia, 81,750 in Morocco and 51,566 auxiliaries.</ref> in the active service, i.e. classes 1911, 1912 and 1913 (born between 1891 and 1893, aged 21 to 23)<ref group="Note">This means that the men in class 1911 were drafted in October 1912, with a planned leave in November 1914, the latter not being applied given the state of war. They were demobilized in August 1919 (after eight years in uniform), and released from military service in September 1939. In the navy, some mobilized men from Black Sea units were not discharged until after 1920 (i.e. after more than nine years of continuous service).</ref> were already in depots and barracks. They were joined by the 2,200,000 men in the reserve, i.e. classes 1900 to 1910 (born between 1880 and 1890, aged 24 to 34);<ref>{{Harvtxt|Naërt|al.|1936|p=55}}</ref> then by the 700,000 men in the territorial reserve, i.e. classes 1893 to 1899 (born between 1873 and 1879, aged 35 to 41);<ref name=":12">{{Cite web |title=Tableau de synthèse des informations sur les classes 1886 à 1919 |trans-title=Summary table of information on classes 1886 to 1919 |url=http://combattant.14-18.pagesperso-orange.fr/Pasapas/E302LoisSynthese.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130604113931/http://combattant.14-18.pagesperso-orange.fr/Pasapas/E302LoisSynthese.html |archive-date=June 4, 2013 |website=combattant.14-18 |language=fr}}</ref> the territorial reserve, i.e. classes 1887 to 1892, was not immediately mobilized (it would be incorporated from the youngest from August 16).

The transportation of all these reservists and territorials from their homes to their assignment depots ("mobilization centers") was mainly by rail, hence the first phase, known as "mobilization", was a vast crossroads of 10,000 passenger trains<ref>{{Cite book |last=Miquel |first=Pierre |title=Les Poilus: la France sacrifiée |publisher=Pocket |year=2002 |isbn=978-2-266-11997-9 |series=Pocket |location=Paris |pages=69 |language=fr |trans-title=The French soldiers: France sacrificed}}</ref><ref>{{Harvtxt|Valluy|Dufourcq|1968|p=72|loc=v. 1}}</ref> (including 3,262 trains on the [[Chemins de fer de Paris à Lyon et à la Méditerranée|PLM network]], 3,121 trains on the [[Chemins de fer du Nord|Northern]], 1,500 trains on the [[Compagnie du chemin de fer de Paris à Orléans|PO]] and 1,334 trains in the [[Chemins de fer de l'Est|Eastern]])<ref>{{Harvtxt|Prévot|2014|p=31}}</ref> crossing metropolitan France in all directions and transporting mobilized men in civilian clothes free of charge. "Men who were drafted were advised to set off with two shirts, one pair of boxer shorts, two handkerchiefs and a good pair of shoes; to have their hair cut and to take a day's supply of food with them."<ref>{{Cite web |title=Ville de Versailles: Avis de mobilisation générale |trans-title=Ville de Versailles: notice of general mobilization |url=http://archives.yvelines.fr/apprendre/espace_educatif/ressources_documentaires/images/haute_resolution/francais_et_la_guerre/103J_2_2.jpg |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140102193614/http://archives.yvelines.fr/apprendre/espace_educatif/ressources_documentaires/images/haute_resolution/francais_et_la_guerre/103J_2_2.jpg |archive-date=January 2, 2014 |website=archives.yvelines.fr |language=fr}}</ref> On August 1, the railroads received the general mobilization order; a ministerial decree stated that from August 2, 1914, the railroads were under military control. Immediately, the railways prepared wagons for troop transport.

The youngest reservists (classes 1910, 1909 and 1908) completed the active units, and must join the depots on the 2nd and 3rd days of mobilization, i.e. Monday August 3 and Tuesday August 4. Slightly older reservists (classes 1907, 1906, 1905 and 1904) formed reserve units (supervised by a few officers and men from the active service) and must be present at the depot from the 3rd, 4th or 5th day, depending on the unit, i.e. from Tuesday August 4 or Thursday August 6. As for the oldest reservists (classes 1903 and 1902), they must theoretically remain at the depot to replace future losses.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Au détour des JMO: la mobilisation des régiments d'infanterie d'active et de réserve |trans-title=A look at the JMOs (war diaries): the mobilization of active and reserve infantry regiments |url=http://combattant.14-18.pagesperso-orange.fr/JMO/JMO_026.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130604145818/http://combattant.14-18.pagesperso-orange.fr/JMO/JMO_026.html |archive-date=June 4, 2013 |website=combattant.14-18.pagesperso-orange.fr |language=fr}}</ref> Territorial reservists were called up a little later. In addition, there were 71,000 voluntary enlistees,<ref>"Commitments for the duration of the war are received from the 20th day of mobilization (August 21)". Instruction of August 15, 1914 for the receipt of voluntary commitments from the French, for the duration of the war, {{Gallica|id=bpt6k6204537p/f15|t=Official Bulletin of the Ministry of War, vol. 33, p. 931}}</ref> who were called up early (classes 1914 onwards: [[The Law of Three years]] authorized voluntary enlistment for the duration of the war from the age of 17), re-enlisted (some veterans of the [[Franco-Prussian War|1870 war]]) or were foreigners (26,000 men, including [[Alsace–Lorraine|Alsatians-Lorrains]], [[Poles in France|Poles]] and [[Italians]], who were not all enrolled in the [[French Foreign Legion|Foreign Legion]]).<ref>Decree of August 3, 1914 on the enlistment of foreigners in foreign regiments for the duration of the war, published in the Journal officiel of August 8, 1914, {{Gallica|t=Bulletin des lois, n° 135, p. 2256|id=bpt6k2207815/f458}} and the law of August 5, 1914 concerning the admission of Alsatians-Lorrains into the French army, published in the Journal Officiel of August 6, 1914, {{Gallica|id=bpt6k2207815/f478|t=Bulletin des lois, n° 135, p. 2276}}</ref><gallery mode="packed" caption="Departure of the first mobilized in Paris">

File:Les mobilisés parisiens devant la gare de l'Est le 2 août 1914.jpeg|alt=Crowd in front of the station.|Crowd of mobilized men at the ''[[Gare de l'Est]]''.
File:French heavy cavalry Paris August 1914.jpg|alt=Column of horsemen in Paris.|Regiment of [[cuirassier]]s up one of the boulevards.
File:Volontaires belges 1914.jpg|alt=Crowd flying tricolor flags up a boulevard in northern Paris.|Parade before the departure of Belgian volunteers by train, August 9, 1914.
</gallery>

The ''[[École spéciale militaire de Saint-Cyr]]'' was closed at the start of the mobilization, and all its students were assigned to active service regiments during the August days, most of them becoming [[sub-lieutenant]]s by October (the "[[Battle of Montmirail|Montmirail]]" class of 1912–1914 and the "''Croix du Drapeau''" class of 1913–1914).<ref>{{Cite web |last=Boÿ |first=Jean |title=Historique de la 97e promotion (1912-14), promotion de Montmirail |url=https://www.saint-cyr.org/fr/fichiers/promotions-eteintes/1912-1914-97e-promotion-de-montmirail.pdf |website=saint-cyr.org}}</ref> As for candidates for the 1914 Saint-Cyr entrance examination, who had just taken the written exam in June, their oral exams were abolished: all those eligible were declared successful on August 4 and immediately sent to the depots, where, after four months of training, they became sub-lieutenants or non-commissioned officers (this class of 1914 was dubbed "the Great Revenge" in January 1915).<ref>{{Cite web |last=Boÿ |first=Jean |title=Historique de la 99e promotion (1914), promotion de la Grande Revanche |url=https://www.saint-cyr.org/fr/fichiers/promotions-eteintes/1914-99e-promotion-de-la-grande-revanche.pdf |website=saint-cyr.org}}</ref> The ''[[École polytechnique|École Polytechnique]]'' was also closed for mobilization, and all students from the class of 1913 were transferred to the artillery or engineering corps as sub-lieutenants.<ref>Law of August 5 relating to the immediate appointment, to the rank of second lieutenant, of aspiring students at the École polytechnique and École spéciale militaire who entered these schools in 1913, promulgated in the Journal officiel of August 6, 1914, {{Gallica|id=bpt6k2207815/f476|t=Bulletin des lois, n° 135, p. 2274}}</ref> Students from the ''[[École normale supérieure (Paris)|École normale supérieure]]'', the ''[[National School of Rural Engineering, Water Resources and Forestry|École forestière de Nancy]]'' and the ''[[École nationale supérieure des mines de Saint-Étienne|École des mines de Saint-Étienne]]'' who had been found fit were transferred to the infantry, those from the ''[[École Centrale Paris|École centrale des arts et manufactures]]'' and the ''[[Mines Paris – PSL|École nationale supérieure des mines]]'' joined the artillery, and those from the ''[[École des ponts ParisTech|École des ponts et chaussées]]'' were assigned to the [[Military engineering|engineering corps]] (as provided for by the law of March 21, 1905 or Law of Three Years), while classes resumed for the few who had been exempted.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Mariot |first=Nicolas |year=2012 |title=Pourquoi les normaliens sont-ils morts en masse en 1914-1918 ? Une explication structurale |trans-title=Why did Normaliens die en masse in 1914–1918? A structural explanation |url=http://www.jourdan.ens.fr/~mariot/hopfichiers/PDF/Mariot_Pole_Sud_2012.pdf |journal=Pôle Sud |language=fr |issue=36 |pages=9–30|doi=10.3917/psud.036.0009 }}</ref> Second-year students at the École navale left with the rank of second petty officer of the fleet, but kept their student uniforms.<ref>Decree of August 7, 1914 establishing the status of students at the École navale, published in the Journal officiel of August 8, 1914, {{Gallica|id=bpt6k2207815/f494|t=Bulletin des lois, n° 135, p. 2292}}</ref>

The number of [[Draft evasion|draft dodgers]]{{refn|group="Note"|"Any serviceman at home, recalled to active duty, who, except in the case of force majeure, has not arrived at his destination on the day set by the regularly notified route order, is considered to be insubordinate, after a period of thirty days, and punishable by the penalties laid down in article 230 of the Code of Military Justice."<ref>{{harvtxt|Mingat|1914|p=16}} citing article 83 of the law of March 21, 1905 on army recruitment.</ref>}} was lower (1.5%) than forecast (13%):<ref>{{Harvtxt|Lejeune|2007|p=174}}</ref> the [[National Gendarmerie|gendarmerie]] brigades only had to reduce small underground groups in the [[Loire (department)|Loire]] department<ref>{{Harvtxt|Miquel|2002|p=65}}</ref> and a few self-mutilations (of the left [[index finger]] or [[Calf (leg)|calf]]) were lamented;<ref>{{Harvtxt|Miquel|2002|p=75}}</ref> the men responsible for the incidents (mostly related to drinking) were transferred to disciplinary companies.<ref>{{Harvtxt|Miquel|2002|pp=90–91}}</ref> The [[1st Cuirassier Regiment (France)|1st cuirassier regiment]] was even kept in Paris for three days in the ''[[École militaire|École Militaire]]'' barracks as a precautionary measure, "for reasons of domestic policy",<ref>{{Cite web |last=Defence Historial Service |author-link=Defence Historical Service |title=Journal des marches et opérations du 1er régiment de cuirassiers pendant la Campagne contre l'Allemagne, du 31 juillet 1914 au 19 novembre 1914 |trans-title=Diary of marches and operations of the 1st cuirassiers regiment during the Campaign against Germany, from July 31, 1914 to November 19, 1914 |url=https://www.memoiredeshommes.sga.defense.gouv.fr/fr/article.php?laref=415&titre=page-introuvable |website=memoiredeshommes.sga.defense.gouv.fr |language=fr}}</ref> as reinforcements for the [[Republican Guard (France)|Republican Guard]]. As for rebels and [[Desertion|deserters]] prior to mobilization, they were offered amnesty if they surrendered voluntarily.<ref>Law of August 5, 1914 regarding amnesty for draft dodgers and deserters in the Army and Sea, promulgated in the Journal Officiel of August 6, 1914, {{Gallica|id=bpt6k2207815/f479|t=Bulletin des lois, n° 135, p. 2277}}</ref>

=== Clothing and equipment ===
[[File:Groupe de mobilisés 1914.jpg|alt=A group of five men and one woman, each carrying a travel bag, musette bag or parcel, cap or hat, some in ties, all in jackets.|thumb|Group of five mobilized soldiers at a railway station, before their departure on August 4, 1914.]]
From August 1 to 15, 2,887,000 men were drafted, then 1,099,000 from August 16 to September 30,<ref>{{Cite book |url=https://gallica.bnf.fr/ark:/12148/bpt6k5441824j |title=Archives de la Grande Guerre, t. VII |publisher=Étienne Chiron |year=1921 |location=Paris |pages=43 |language=fr |trans-title=The losses of the belligerent nations in the Great War |chapter=Les pertes des nations belligérantes au cours de la Grande Guerre}}</ref> giving an estimated total of 3,986,000 men (the 1911 [[census]] announced a population of 39.7 million in France, including 19.5 million men, of whom 12.6 million were fitted<ref>{{Cite book |title=Résultats statistiques du recensement général de la population effectué le 5 mars 1911, t. I |publisher=Statistique Générale de la France |year=1917 |location=Paris |language=fr |trans-title=Statistical results of the general population census conducted on March 5, 1911, v. I}}</ref>). In September and October 1914, all those discharged and exempted from the 1887 to 1914 classes were enumerated and then recalled by the draft boards.<ref>Decree of September 9, 1914 on those discharged and exempted, the first of the "recovery laws", quickly followed by the decree of September 26, 1914 on men in auxiliary service, etc.</ref>

Mobilization quadrupled the troops: the crowd had to be dressed in uniform ([[kepi]], jacket, [[overcoat]], pants, suspenders, shirts, tie, underpants, gaiters and socks) and work boots; equip it with a [[backpack]], a bag, a canister, a comb, two handkerchiefs, a grease tin, four brushes, a bar of soap, a sewing kit (scissors, a spool of thread, a thimble, needles and a collection of buttons), a pack of bandages (a feather cushion, a gauze compress, a cotton strip and two safety pins), a mess tin, a spoon, a fork, a quarter of a litre, twelve loaves of war bread (1.5 kg, for two days), a tin of canned food (500 g of [[Corned beef|salted beef]] or condensed soup), sachets of small foodstuffs (200 g of rice or dried vegetables, 72 g of instant coffee, 64 g of sugar and 40 g of salt),<ref>{{Cite book |last=Chapuis |first=F. |url=http://www.gutenberg.org/files/39884/39884-h/39884-h.htm |title=L'instruction théorique du soldat par lui-même: Éducation morale et instruction professionnelle |publisher=Berger-Levrault |year=1913 |location=Paris-Nancy |pages=123 |language=fr |trans-title=Theoretical self-instruction: Moral education and professional training}}</ref> a belt, three cartridge belts and a sword-bayonet holder; for each squad, four large bowls, four cooking pots, two canvas buckets, a coffee grinder, two distribution bags and tools (picks, axes, hacksaws and shovels). Each man wears around his neck an oval aluminum<ref>{{Cite web |title=L'équipement |url=http://www.lesfrancaisaverdun-1916.fr/uniforme-equipement.htm |website=lesfrancaisaverdun-1916.fr |language=fr}}</ref> identity plate (with surname, first name and class on one side, and regional subdivision and regimental number on the other), which is only issued in wartime.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Questionnaire du 28e RI, Service intérieur |trans-title=Questionnaire of the 28th RI, Internal Service |url=http://vlecalvez.free.fr/questionnaire/sercive_interieur.pdf |website=vlecalvez.free.fr |language=fr}}</ref> Stores were emptied for reservists, so the territorials were often dressed and equipped with old clothes and old-fashioned weaponry.<ref>{{Harvtxt|Miquel|2002|pp=74–75}}, citing in particular {{Cite book |last=Barthas |first=Louis |author-link=Louis Barthas |title=Les carnets de guerre de Louis Barthas, tonnelier: 1914-1918 |publisher=F. Maspero |year=1978 |isbn=2-7071-1047-7 |series=Actes et mémoires du peuple |location=Paris |pages=16 |language=fr |trans-title=The war diaries of Louis Barthas, cooper: 1914–1918}}</ref>

In two weeks, the French army went from 686 to 1,636 infantry [[battalion]]s, from 365 to 596 cavalry [[Squadron (army)|squadrons]], from 855 to 1,527 [[Artillery battery|artillery batteries]] and from 191 to 528 engineer units.<ref>{{Harvtxt|Naërt|al.|1936|p=529}}</ref> Its structure grew from 54 [[Division (military)|divisions]] in [[metropolitan France]] (including ten cavalry divisions, not counting units in the [[French North Africa]]) in peacetime to 94 divisions (46 active, 25 [[Military reserve force|reserve]], 13 territorial and 10 cavalry) standing on the ready. In addition, there were 21 army squadrons (each with eight [[Flight (military unit)|aircraft]]), two cavalry squadrons, five [[airship]]s, four companies of local balloonists, and 212 sections of the automotive service (transporting troops, equipment, medical supplies and fresh meat).<ref>{{Harvtxt|Naërt|al.|1936|pp=54–55}}</ref> Departure for the border was on schedule, with the unit theoretically fully manned and equipped.
