juillet 1914 au 13 mars 1915 (cote 26 N 193/1) |url=http://www.memoiredeshommes.sga.defense.gouv.fr/jmo/img-viewer/26_N_193_001/viewer.html |website=memoiredeshommes.sga.defense.gouv.fr. |language=fr}}</ref> (measures to protect communication routes, especially engineering structures). In the middle of the night of the 27th to the 28th, the Ministry of War ordered the recall of those on leave from the interior corps.<ref>''Télégramme du ministre de la Guerre aux différents corps d'armée concernés, 0h 50 le 28 juillet 1914'' (Telegram from the Minister of War to the various army corps concerned, 0.50 am on July 28, 1914) cited in {{Harvtxt|Naërt|al.|1936|p=99}}</ref> On the 29th, the Minister ordered the guarding of fortified structures, military establishments and wireless stations in the six frontier corps (1st in [[Maubeuge]], 2nd in the [[Ardennes]], 6th in [[Verdun]], 20th in [[Toul]], 21st in [[Épinal]] and 7th corps in [[Belfort]]).<ref>''Télégrammes du ministre de la Guerre aux 1er, 2e, 6e, 7e, 20e et 21e corps, vers 13 h le 29 juillet 1914'' (Telegrams from the Minister of War to the 1st, 2nd, 6th, 7th, 20th and 21st Corps, around 1 p.m. on July 29, 1914), cited in {{Harvtxt|Naërt|al.|1936|p=102}}</ref> On the morning of July 31, 1914, the five eastern army corps were ordered to carry out a "full mobilization exercise" (deployment of active units), but ten kilometers behind the border (by order of the government);<ref>''Télégramme du ministre de la Guerre aux 2e, 6e, 7e, 20e et 21e corps, à 16 h 55 le 30 juillet 1914'' (Telegram from the Minister of War to the 2nd, 6th, 7th, 20th and 21st Corps, at 4:55 p.m. on July 30, 1914), cited in {{Harvtxt|Naërt|al.|1936|p=104}}</ref> the governors of the four eastern positions were now ordered to launch defense work (digging trenches, laying barbed wire and setting up batteries).<ref>''Télégramme du ministre de la Guerre aux commandants des places de Verdun, Toul, Épinal et Belfort, entre 18 h 40 et 19 h 10 le 30 juillet 1914'' (Telegram from the Minister of War to the commanders of Verdun, Toul, Épinal and Belfort, between 6.40 p.m. and 7.10 p.m. on July 30, 1914), cited in {{Harvtxt|Naërt|al.|1936|p=104}}</ref>

At 6 p.m. on August 1, the [[colonel]]s of the regiments at stake received the telegram "''Faites partir troupes de couverture''" ("Send out covering troops"), leading to the deployment by train or on foot of units from all five corps and the recall of border reservists,<ref>{{Cite web |last=Defence Historical Service |author-link=Defence Historical Service |title=Journal des marches et d'opérations du 44e régiment d'infanterie pendant la campagne contre l'Allemagne, juillet-août 1914, « cote 26 N 632/1 » |trans-title=Diary of marches and operations of the 44th infantry regiment during the campaign against Germany, July–August 1914, "cote 26 N 632/1". |url=http://www.memoiredeshommes.sga.defense.gouv.fr/jmo/img-viewer/26_N_632_001/viewer.html |website=memoiredeshommes.sga.defense.gouv.fr |language=fr}}</ref> but still ten kilometers behind the border. The 7th Corps (temporarily including the 8th Cavalry Division) deployed in the "[[Vosges#Geography|Higher Vosges]] sector" (from [[Belfort]] to [[Gérardmer]]), the 21st Corps (including the 6th Cavalry Division) in the High [[Meurthe (river)|Meurthe]] sector (from [[Fraize]] to [[Avricourt, Meurthe-et-Moselle|Avricourt]]), the 20th corps (with the 2nd Cavalry Division) in the Low Meurthe sector (from Avricourt to [[Dieulouard]]), the 6th corps (including the 7th Cavalry Division) in the southern [[Woëvre]] (from [[Pont-à-Mousson]] to [[Conflans-en-Jarnisy|Conflans]]) and the [[2nd Army Corps (France)|2nd corps]] (with the 4th Cavalry Division) in the northern Woëvre (from Conflans to [[Givet]]). These covering positions were commanded by generals from the various frontier army corps, under the direct command of the General-in-Chief until the 5th day, when they came under the orders of army commanders. Ahead of the "big ones" several groups were placed, each composed of a [[battalion]] and a [[Squadron (army)|squadron]], with cavalry "scouts" supported by [[customs]] officers and [[forestry hunters]]<ref>{{Harvtxt|Naërt|al.|1936|pp=84–85}}</ref> further forward. Transport of the cover was completed on August 3, thanks to 538 trains; the three early-mobilization divisions were in place by August 5.<ref>{{Harvtxt|Naërt|al.|1936|p=126}}</ref>

The [[French Navy|navy]] was also involved in preventive measures. From July 25, leave-holders were recalled, reserve ships were reconditioned, munitions of war began to be loaded and schools closed. On July 29, the [[battleship]]s concentrated in Toulon filled up with coal. On July 31, [[Fishing trawler|trawlers]] were requisitioned (to be used as auxiliary [[minesweeper]]s) and port defenses were organized. On August 2, the general firing order for the ships' boilers (several hours of heating are needed to build up sufficient steam pressure) is given for 10:15 pm. On August 3, at 4:50 a.m., the [[Squadron (naval)|squadrons]] set sail from [[Toulon arsenal|Toulon]] to protect links with [[French North Africa|North Africa]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Historique du cuirassé Démocratie |trans-title=History of the battleship Démocratie |url=http://navires-14-18.com/fichiers/D/DEMOCRATIE_MN_V3.pdf |website=navires-14-18.com |language=fr}}</ref>
[[File:Leutnant Albert Mayer Grabstein 01 09.jpg|alt=Small stele engraved with the name of the deceased.|thumb|Grave of the first German casualty of 1914: [[Albert Mayer (soldier)|Lieutenant Mayer]], buried at the Deutscher Soldatenfriedhof (German military cemetery) in [[Illfurth]], near [[Mulhouse]].]]
The first border incident occurred on the 2nd of August: a German patrol from the Jäger-Regiment zu Pferde Nr. 5 (5e regiment of cavalrymen, stationed at [[Mulhouse]]) encountered a French squad from the 44th infantry regiment (from [[Montbéliard]]), stationed there for surveillance, at [[Joncherey]] near [[Delle]] (in the [[Territoire de Belfort]]): the exchange of fire killed the two commanders, French corporal [[Jules-André Peugeot|Jules André Peugeot]] (21) and German [[Albert Mayer (soldier)|Albert Mayer]] (22), who became the first to be killed in either country, even before the declaration of war.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Le drame de Joncherey |trans-title=The Joncherey tragedy |url=http://www.joncherey.fr/pages/pages%20patrimoine%20culturel/drame%20de%20joncherey.htm |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131110095056/http://www.joncherey.fr/pages/pages%20patrimoine%20culturel/drame%20de%20joncherey.htm |archive-date=November 10, 2013 |website=joncherey.fr |language=fr}}</ref> Further German reconnaissance near [[Longwy]] and [[Lunéville]] verified the French positions.<ref>{{Cite web |title=The First to Fall: Peugeot and Mayer, 2 August 1914 |url=http://www.westernfrontassociation.com/great-war-people/48-brothers-arms/1515-the-first-to-fall-peugeot-and-mayer-2-august-1914.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131110075502/http://www.westernfrontassociation.com/great-war-people/48-brothers-arms/1515-the-first-to-fall-peugeot-and-mayer-2-august-1914.html |archive-date=November 10, 2013 |website=westernfrontassociation.com}}</ref> On the morning of the 2nd, the Chief of the General Staff sent a note to the [[Ministry of Armed Forces (France)|Minister of War]]: "We have had to abandon positions which were of some importance to the development of our campaign plan. Eventually, we will be obliged to regain these positions, which will not be without sacrifice."<ref>''Note du chef d'État-Major général, à 10 heures le 2 août 1914'' (Note from the Chief of the General Staff, 10 a.m. August 2, 1914), quoted in {{Harvtxt|Naërt|al.|1936|p=116}}</ref> Almost immediately, he obtained "absolute freedom of movement to carry out his plans, even if this means crossing the German border".<ref>''Communication téléphonique reçue à 10 h 10 du ministère de la Guerre, 2 août 1914'' (Telephone communication received at 10.10 a.m. from the War Ministry, August 2, 1914), quoted in {{Harvtxt|Naërt|al.|1936|p=117}}</ref> On August 3, [[Joseph Joffre|Joffre]] called a meeting of his five army commanders in the offices of the Ministry of War, before leaving for his newly created [[Grand Quartier Général (1914–1919)|headquarters]] in [[Vitry-le-François]].

=== Concentration ===

==== Transportation problems ====
[[File:First trains of mobilization (aug 1914).jpg|alt=Wagons full of soldiers pull away from the station platform.|thumb|Departure of a train of mobilized soldiers from [[Gare de l'Est|Gare de Paris-Est]], August 2, 1914.]]
The concentration of almost the entire French army corps (minus the 680,000 men still in depots, the 210,000 men guarding the communication routes, the 821,400 men assigned to strongholds,<ref>''Tableau des effectifs mobilisés'' (Table of mobilized staff), {{Harvtxt|Naërt|al.|1936|p=526}}</ref> the 65,000 men at sea<ref>{{Harvtxt|Valluy|Dufourcq|1968|p=130|loc=v. 1}}</ref> and the units deployed in the colonies) near the Franco-German border was carried out in 1914 by rail. This huge move, organized by the [[Staff (military)|General Staff]], was made possible by the requisitioning of the railroads ([[Chemins de fer du Nord|Nord]], [[Chemins de fer de l'Est|Est]], [[Compagnie du chemin de fer de Paris à Orléans|PO]], [[Chemins de fer de Paris à Lyon et à la Méditerranée|PLM]] and [[Chemins de fer du Midi|Midi]]), which lost all autonomy (except financial) on the evening of July 31.<ref>''Télégramme du ministre de la Guerre à celui des Travaux publics, à 18 h 45 le 31 juillet 1914'' (Telegram from the Minister of War to the Minister of Public Works, 6:45 p.m. on July 31, 1914), cited in {{Harvtxt|Naërt|al.|1936|p=108}}</ref> This requisition was total: personnel, installations and all equipment were under army control. Between August 6 and 18, the concentration of the French army required 4,035 trains running on the ten lines organized by the military.<ref name="Prévot 2014 38">{{Harvtxt|Prévot|2014|p=38}}</ref> Local companies were also affected by the requisition.

A few events disrupted the concentration: the first took place on August 7, when an accident at [[Brienne-le-Château|Brienne]] blocked the E line (from Toulouse) and traffic was redirected to the D line (from Bordeaux); but on August 8, a second incident on the saturated D line caused delays to the landings of the 12th and 17th corps.<ref>{{Harvtxt|Naërt|al.|1936|p=350}}</ref> On August 10, the train carrying the headquarters of the [[55th Infantry Division (France)|55th reserve division]] was hit at [[Sompuis]] at around 5:30 a.m. by one of the 313rd regiment's trains: the collision killed six and injured 25; as for the collision, the officers' wagon was "smashed to pieces", injuring seven, including General Leguay; convoys on the F line were delayed by twenty hours.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Defence Historical Service |author-link=Defence Historical Service |title=Journal des marches et opérations de la 55e division de réserve du 2 août 1914 au 31 décembre 1916, « cote 26 N 369/1 » |trans-title=Diary of marches and operations of the 55th Reserve Division from August 2, 1914, to December 31, 1916, "cote 26 N 369/1" |url=http://www.memoiredeshommes.sga.defense.gouv.fr/jmo/img-viewer/26_N_369_001/viewer.html |website=memoiredeshommes.sga.defense.gouv.fr |page=6 |language=fr}}</ref> There were also wagon fires and a number of accidents: for example, on August 6, a soldier from the 61st infantry regiment in [[Privas]] "perched on the brakeman's cab of a wagon hit a structure and was killed outright" before the Givors-Canal station.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Defence Historical Service |author-link=Defence Historical Service |title=61e Régiment d'Infanterie, Journal des marches et opérations du 1er Bataillon, « cote 26 N 655/12 » |trans-title=61st Infantry Regiment, Diary of marches and operations of the 1st Battalion, "cote 26 N 655/12". |url=http://www.memoiredeshommes.sga.defense.gouv.fr/jmo/img-viewer/26_N_655_012/viewer.html |website=memoiredeshommes.sga.defense.gouv.fr |page=5 |language=fr}}</ref>

As for the French Army of Africa, it provided two divisions from Algeria and Tunisia, as well as a division taken from the Moroccan occupation corps<ref group="Note">The Moroccan occupation corps numbered 82,000 men in 1914, the majority of whom remained in the country.</ref> as planned; but these three divisions, made up of regiments of [[Zouave]]s, [[Tirailleur|Algerian Tirailleurs]], [[French Foreign Legion|Legionnaires]], [[Spahi]]s and [[Chasseur|African ''Chasseurs'']], were vulnerable during their crossing. On August 4, the [[Imperial German Navy|''Kaiserliche'' Navy]] cruisers [[SMS Goeben]] and [[SMS Breslau]] bombarded [[Skikda|Philippeville]] and [[Annaba|Bône]], before fleeing as the [[Mediterranean Fleet|British ships]] approached. The French crossing was uneventful after this surprise, with the two Algerian divisions landing in [[Sète]] and [[Marseille]], while the [[Moroccan Division (France)|Moroccan division]] ("''division de marche d'infanterie coloniale du Maroc''") did so in [[Bordeaux]]. They were then transported by rail, requiring 239 trains.<ref name="Prévot 2014 38"/>

==== Army creation ====
[[File:Un avion de guerre la journée 9 sept.jpg|alt=Autochrome (color photo) of an airplane.|thumb|Military aeronautics in 1914 was no more than a subdivision of the army, with 216 aircraft grouped into squadrons. There were also a few large airships and tethered balloons.<ref>{{Harvtxt|Valluy|Dufourcq|1968|p=71|loc=v. 1}}</ref> Here, a [[Caudron G.3]].]]
The transport lines supplied the troops needed to form, from August 5 onwards, the five maneuver armies of [[Plan XVII]], which foresaw a French offensive towards ''[[Alsace–Lorraine|Elsaß-Lothringen]]'' (German Alsace-Lorraine) and the possibility of a meeting in the Belgian [[Ardennes]]. Three armies were thus massed in Lorraine and around Belfort: the [[1st Army Corps (France)|1st Army]] (commanded by [[Augustin Dubail|General Dubail]] and comprising the 7th, 8th, 13th, 14th and 21st Corps) deployed on the slopes of the [[Vosges]], relying on the [[Fortified region of Belfort|fortified regions of Belfort]] and [[Épinal]] (its mission was to attack to the southeast towards [[Mulhouse]] and above all to the northeast towards [[Sarrebourg]]); the [[2nd Army (France)|2nd Army]] ([[Noël Édouard, vicomte de Curières de Castelnau|General Castelnau]]: 9th, 15th, 16th, 18th and 20th corps) deployed on the Lorraine plateau, relying on the stronghold of [[Toul]] (its mission was to attack to the northeast towards [[Morhange]]); the [[3rd Army (France)|3rd army]] ([[Pierre Ruffey|general Ruffey]]: 4th, 5th and 6th corps) deployed in [[Woëvre]], relying on the fortified town of [[Verdun]] (its more static mission was to guard the German fortifications at Metz-Thionville). In the event of a German violation of Belgian neutrality, a strong French left wing guarded the Ardennes massif: the [[5th Army (France)|5th Army]] ([[Charles Lanrezac|General Lanrezac]]: 1st, 2nd, 3rd, 10th and 11th Corps) was deployed in the [[Ardennes (department)|Ardennes department]] opposite the [[Stenay]] gap, with the [[4th Army (France)|4th Army]] ([[Fernand de Langle de Cary|General Langle de Cary]]: 12th and 17th Corps, as well as the [[Colonial Army Corps|Colonial Corps]]) in reserve astride the [[Forest of Argonne|Argonne]] and in the [[Barrois]], and the Cavalry Corps in reserve around Mézières.

Only the active divisions were placed in the front line, with the reserve divisions held back until they could be properly taken over and further trained. Four "groups of reserve divisions" were therefore concentrated behind the front line: the first group (58th, 63rd and 66th reserve divisions) around [[Vesoul]] (behind the 1st Army), the second group (59th, [[68th Infantry Division (France)|68th]] and 70th divisions) around [[Nancy, France|Nancy]]-[[Toul]] (at the disposal of the 2nd Army), the third group (54th, [[55th Infantry Division (France)|55th]] and 56th divisions) around [[Verdun]] and [[Saint-Mihiel]] (at the disposal of the 3rd Army) and the fourth group (51st, [[53rd Infantry Division (France)|53rd]] and 69th divisions) around [[Vervins]] (behind the 5th Army). The commander-in-chief kept in general reserve the two divisions provided by the 19th corps ([[37th Infantry Division (France)|37th]] and [[38th Infantry Division (France)|38th]], from Algeria), the 44th active division (dispersed in the [[Alps]], facing Italy), the southeastern reservists (the 64th, 65th, 74th and 75th reserve divisions, in the Alps), as well as the divisions assigned to the "mobile defense of the North-East" ([[57th Infantry Division (France)|57th]] at Belfort, [[71st Infantry Division (France)|71st]] at Épinal, [[72nd Infantry Division (France)|72nd]] at Verdun and 73rd at Toul), while the Minister retained control of the 67th (at the Mailly camp) and the [[61st Infantry Division (France)|61st]] and 62nd reserve divisions (in the [[Fortifications of Paris in the 19th and 20th centuries|entrenched camp of Paris]]).<ref>{{Harvtxt|Naërt|al.|1936|loc=p. 77–78, 81–81, and 535–589}}</ref>

The thirteen territorial infantry divisions were the last to be formed, and their concentration continued until August 19. Commanded by [[Joseph Brugère|General Brugère]], nine of these divisions were intended for maneuver, hence their name "territorial field divisions": the 91st at [[Draguignan]] within the Alps army (in case of an Italian threat); the 84th and 88th assigned to the entrenched camp of Paris (for mobile defense); the 81st and 82nd at [[Hazebrouck]] and [[Arras]] (in case of a German naval landing); the 87th concentrated near [[Cherbourg-Octeville|Cherbourg]] (for coastal protection); finally, the 90th and 92nd divisions placed at [[Perpignan]] and [[Bayonne]] to guard the [[France–Spain border|Spanish border]]. The last four divisions, the 83rd, 85th, 86th and 89th, were garrisoned in the entrenched camp of Paris, with limited means of transport, hence their name of "territorial site divisions". As Italian and Spanish neutrality was confirmed at the beginning of August, and the British entry into the war secured the coasts, the field divisions were reassigned to the Northeast, with the exception of the 90th, which was sent to North Africa from August 12.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Recherche:Mobilisation de 1914 — Wikiversité |url=https://fr.wikiversity.org/wiki/Recherche:Mobilisation_de_1914 |access-date= |website=fr.wikiversity.org |language=fr}}</ref>

{{Main|French Army order of battle (1914)}}

==== Modifications ====
The announcement that German troops had entered [[Luxembourg]] on the morning of August 2<ref>Telegram dated August 2, 1914 from the Minister of State of Luxembourg, President of the Government, to the German State Secretary for Foreign Affairs, published in {{Cite book |last1=Kautsky |first1=Karl |title=Documents allemands relatifs à l'origine de la guerre: collection complète des documents officiels, publiés à la demande du ministère allemand des Affaires Étrangères |last2=Montgelas |first2=Max |last3=Schücking |first3=Walther |publisher=Alfred Costes |year=1922 |volume=3 |pages=135 |language=fr |translator-last=Jordan |translator-first=Camille |trans-title=German documents relating to the origins of the war: complete collection of official documents, published at the request of the German Foreign Office.}} {{Gallica|id=bpt6k5490692r/f151}}</ref> confirmed to the French General Staff the hypothesis of a German attack attempting to overrun the French concentration by flanking through Belgium (invaded from the morning of August 4).<ref name=":9" /> On August 2,<ref>''Variantes à la concentration des 5e et 4e armées, ordonnées par Joffre le 2 août 1914 à 19 h 30'' (Variants to the concentration of the 5th and 4th armies, ordered by Joffre on August 2, 1914 at 7:30 pm), cited in {{Harvtxt|Naërt|al.|1936|p=120}}</ref> orders were therefore given to the French left wing to deploy in order to control the outlets of the Ardennes (this was a variant of [[Plan XVII]]):<ref>{{Harvtxt|Naërt|al.|1936|p=79}}</ref> the 4th army, previously in reserve, was to be inserted between the 3rd and 5th armies from [[Sedan, Ardennes|Sedan]] to [[Montmédy]], the 5th army shifted a little further west from [[Hirson]] to [[Charleville-Mézières|Charleville]], half of the 3rd army redeployed from Montmédy to [[Spincourt]], while the cavalry corps was sent to provide cover and reconnaissance ahead of the 5th, in the Belgian [[Ardennes]] (the Belgian government gave the French permission to enter Belgium at 11 p.m. on August 4).<ref>{{Harvtxt|Naërt|al.|1936|p=124}}</ref>

In addition to the French Army's battle corps, the [[British Expeditionary Force (World War I)|British Expeditionary Force]] (commanded by [[Field marshal (United Kingdom)|Field Marshal]] [[John French, 1st Earl of Ypres|John French]]: four infantry divisions and one cavalry division) was secretly foreseen in the French concentration plan.<ref group="Note">The landing of the [[British Expeditionary Force (World War I)|British Expeditionary Force]] was planned by Major-General Henry Wilson, Director of Military Operations at the British [[War Office]] since 1910, who held secret discussions with the French General Staff. The transport plan for the "W Army" was drawn up in March 1913.</ref> The British decision to send their small army to France was taken on August 5, 1914; and the decision to deploy it at Maubeuge only on August 9 ([[Secretary of State for War]] [[Herbert Kitchener, 1st Earl Kitchener|Kitchener]] preferred [[Amiens]]). From August 9 onwards, the various units were embarked in [[Southampton]], [[Cork (city)|Cork]], [[Dublin]] and [[Belfast]], arriving until August 17 in [[Le Havre]], [[Rouen]] and [[Boulogne-sur-Mer|Boulogne]], before being transported (by the W railroad line, created for it) and deployed near [[Maubeuge]], at the left end of the French line.
[[File:Concentration des armées belge, britannique et française, août 1914.png|alt=Deployment of forces along the border, from Maubeuge to Montbéliard.|center|thumb|Map of the concentration of the Belgian, British and French armies in August 1914.]]

== Consequences ==

=== Restriction of freedoms ===
[[File:Contrôle d'identité 1914.jpg|alt=Cars stopped by an infantry picket (territorials in uniform) on a main road.|left|thumb|Identity checks for travelers leaving Paris by car, August 9.]]A "''state de siège''" ([[State of emergency#France|state of emergency]]) was declared on August 2, 1914 (two days before receiving the German declaration of war) in all French departments ([[including Algeria]])<ref>''Décret du 2 août 1914 portant déclaration de mise en état de siège de l'ensemble du territoire'' (Decree of August 2, 1914 declaring the entire country to be under siege) published in the ''Journal officiel'' of August 3, 1914, {{Gallica|id=bpt6k2207815/f450|t=Bulletin des lois, n° 135, p. 2248}} in accordance with {{Cite web |title=loi du 3 avril 1878 relative a l'état de siège |trans-title=law of April 3, 1878 relating to the state of siege |url=https://fr.wikisource.org/wiki/Loi%20du%203%20avril%201878%20relative%20%C3%A0%20l%E2%80%99%C3%A9tat%20de%20si%C3%A8ge |website=Wikisource |language=fr}}</ref> and maintained for the duration of the war.<ref>Loi du 5 août 1914 relative à l'état de siège (Law of August 5, 1914 relating to the state of siege), published in the ''Journal officiel'' of August 6, 1914, {{Gallica|id=bpt6k2207815/f470|t=Bulletin des lois, n° 135, p. 2268}}</ref> The proclamation of a state of emergency did not comply with the 1878 law on states of emergency: on the one hand, it should have set a limited duration (in months or, at worst, years), after which Parliament should have decided whether or not to renew it; on the other hand, Parliament should have continued to sit, instead of absenting itself, until January 1915, immediately after ratifying the state of emergency.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Bathélemy |first=Joseph |author-link=Joseph Barthélemy |year=1915 |title=Notes de droit public sur le droit public en temps de guerre |trans-title=Notes on public law in times of war |journal=Revue du droit public et de la science politique en France et à l'Étrange |language=fr |pages=144}} {{Gallica|id=bpt6k111165z/f145}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Roussellier |first=Nicolas |year=2008 |title=Le Parlement français et la Première Guerre mondiale |trans-title=The French Parliament and the First World War |url=http://www.cairn.info/revue-parlements1-2008-2-page-13.htm |journal=Parlement[s], Revue d'histoire politique |language=fr |publisher=L'Harmattan |issue=10 |pages=13–30}}</ref>

Mayors and prefects immediately lost their police powers to the military authorities, allowing the army to ban meetings, search homes and bring civilians before [[Military justice|military tribunals]] (with highly simplified procedures and immediate execution of sentences). However, the [[Grand Quartier Général (1914–1919)|General Headquarters]] remained accountable to the executive, which in turn was accountable to Parliament, for the duration of the state of siege - which was not lifted until November 1919, more than a year after the armistice.

German and Austro-Hungarian [[Domicile (law)|residents]] were evacuated from the North-East and from the strongholds; all foreigners were required to have a [[residence permit]].<ref>''Décret du 2 août 1914 relatif aux mesures à prendre à l'égard des étrangers stationnés en France'' (Decree of August 2, 1914 on measures to be taken with regard to foreigners stationed in France), published in the ''Journal officiel'' of August 3, 1914, {{Gallica|id=bpt6k2207815/f448|t=Bulletin des lois, n° 135, p. 2246}}</ref> In Paris, exceptional measures were taken: the gates of the [[Thiers wall|fortified city walls]] were closed and guarded from 6 p.m. until 6 a.m.; by order of the Prefecture of Police on July 29, drinking establishments had to close at 8 p.m. and restaurants at 9 p.m.; dances were forbidden; most [[gas burner]]s and electric [[Street light|streetlamps]] were switched off as part of a [[Blackout (wartime)|blackout]].<ref>{{Harvtxt|Le Naour|2012|pp=171–173}}</ref>

Elections were suspended, as the majority of the electorate, including several deputies,<ref group="Note">17 deputies are killed in action during their term of office. The first was Pierre Goujon, radical deputy for Ain and reserve sub-lieutenant in the 229th infantry regiment, who was shot in the head at [[Méhoncourt]] near Lunéville on August 25, 1914.</ref> were in uniform (women and soldiers did not have the right to vote under the [[French Third Republic|Third Republic]]) and part of the country was occupied. On August 2, the [[Senate (France)|Senate]] and [[Chamber of Deputies]] were called into extraordinary session from the 4th to vote on a series of emergency laws.
[[File:Inscription des étrangers 1914.jpg|alt=Queue of men along a sidewalk.|thumb|Registration of foreign residents prior to their forced evacuation to Brittany, Paris, August 5.]]

The freedom and [[secrecy of correspondence]] no longer existed: military mail, which was systematically late (making any indiscretions unusable), was checked before dispatch, and letters that were pessimistic, defeatist or giving precise information were seized or redacted (lines crossed out) by the [[postal censorship]] services. [[Freedom of the press]] was affected by [[censorship]]: initially, "information other than that communicated by the government or the command on operations, the order of battle, the number of troops (including wounded, killed or prisoners), defense work", etc., were forbidden, as well as "any information or article concerning military or diplomatic operations likely to favor the enemy and exert an unfortunate influence on the spirit of the army and the population",<ref>''Loi du 5 août 1914 réprimant les indiscrétions de la presse en temps de guerre'' (Law of August 5, 1914, repressing press indiscretions in wartime), published in the ''Journal Officiel'' of August 6, 1914, {{Gallica|id=bpt6k2207815/f481|t=Bulletin des lois, n° 135, p. 2279}}</ref> and "substantive articles violently attacking the government or army leaders" and those "tending to the cessation or suppression of hostilities."<ref>''Circulaire du ministre de la Guerre Millerand du 19 septembre 1914.'' (Circular from War Minister Millerand, September 19, 1914).</ref> The press was checked before printing, and articles deemed unpatriotic were banned from publication, sometimes leaving the space for white rectangles.

=== Economic difficulties ===
From July 31, the French government took a series of economic decisions to accompany its entry into the war. The export of products that could be used for military purposes was prohibited: arms, munitions and explosives, of course, but also livestock, horses, canned goods, meat, flour, hides, fodder, hay, straw, [[Airplane|aeroplanes]], [[aerostat]]s, cars, [[tire]]s, camping gear, lead,<ref>''Décret du 31 juillet 1914 portant prohibition de sortie et de réexportation en suite d'entrepôt, de dépôt, de transit, de transbordement et d'admission temporaire de certains produits et objets'' (Decree of July 31, 1914 prohibiting the exit and re-export from warehouses, deposits, transit, transshipment and temporary admission of certain products and objects), published in the ''Journal officiel'' of August 1, 1914, {{Gallica|id=bpt6k2207815/f382|t=Bulletin des lois, n° 134, p. 2180}}</ref> etc. The budget allocated to the Ministry of War was increased by a credit of 208 million francs, covering new expenditure on barracks, [[Horse|remounting]], clothing, bedding, furnishings, camping, health equipment, armaments and fortifications.<ref>''Décret du 31 juillet 1914 ouvrant sur l'exercice 1913 un crédit de 208 237 048 francs applicable à des dépenses non renouvelables intéressant la défense nationale'' (Decree of July 31, 1914 opening a credit of 208,237,048 francs from the 1913 fiscal year for non-renewable expenses relating to national defense), {{Gallica|id=bpt6k2207815/f385|t=Bulletin des lois, n° 134, p. 2183}}</ref> To ensure the administration's workload, some civil servants were left on call, and those mobilized were gradually replaced by retired volunteers (later by women and the disabled). Pigeons were kept under surveillance (civilians were forbidden to move or import pigeons).<ref>''Décret du 2 août 1914 portant interdiction d'importation de pigeons voyageurs étrangers'' (Decree of August 2, 1914 prohibiting the import of foreign racing pigeons(, published in the ''Journal officiel'' of August 3, 1914, {{Gallica|id=bpt6k2207815/f446|t=Bulletin des lois, n° 135, p. 2244}}</ref><gallery mode="packed" caption="Army requisitioning of means of transport">
File:Paris - horses taken for war.jpg|alt=Grouping of horses in a street.|Requisition of horses in Paris.
File:Tombereaux réquisitionnés 1914.jpg|alt=Line of horse-drawn carts moving up a street.|Departure for the army of carts of the city of Paris.
File:Réquisition camions 1914.jpg|alt=A line of trucks carrying advertising banners.|Regroupement of [[Large goods vehicle|heavy goods vehicles]] in Paris.
File:Réquisition des autos 1914.jpg|alt=Numerous vehicles lined up in front of the Invalides dome.|Automobile rally on the ''[[Les Invalides|esplanade des Invalides]]'', Paris, August 5, 1914.
</gallery>Mass mobilization had immediate economic and social consequences: young adult men and horses (around 135,000 horses in August,<ref name=":11" /> 600,000 throughout the war, aged between five and fifteen, as well as mules and donkeys)<ref>{{Harvtxt|Miquel|2002|p=71}}</ref> left for the frontiers, completely disrupting the economy and society. Businesses slowed down or closed temporarily. [[Printing press|The press]] greatly reduced its circulation,<ref group="Note">For example, the daily ''[[Le Temps (Paris)|Le Temps]]'' is now printed on only four pages: see the August 3, 1914 edition. {{Gallica|id=bpt6k2418898/f1}}</ref> as mobilization deprived it of some of its staff; mail stopped arriving during the mobilization period; civilian telephone service was suspended;<ref>''Décret interdisant l'usage du language convenu et des langues étrangères pour la rédaction des télégrammes'' (Decree prohibiting the use of agreed language and foreign languages in telegrams), published in the ''Journal officiel'' of August 2, 1914, {{Gallica|id=bpt6k2207815/f389|t=Bulletin des lois, n° 134, p. 2187}}</ref> every day, an official dispatch arrived in prefectures and sub-prefectures by [[Telegraphy|telegraph]] from the [[Minister of the Interior (France)|Ministry of the Interior]], before being posted.<ref>{{Harvtxt|Miquel|2002|p=72}}</ref> Passenger rail traffic was almost totally interrupted during the period of concentration, limited to lines not used by the army. In [[Montbéliard]] on August 5, all non-mobilized workers aged 16 to 60 were called by the municipality to work on fortifications at Fort Lachaux.<ref>{{Cite web |title=La mobilisation des hommes et des femmes |trans-title=Men and women mobilization |url=http://www.montbeliard.fr/fileadmin/Fichiers/Photos/5_Culture_loisirs_et_sport/Archives_municipales/gazette_expositions/mobil_tout.pdf |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131226123514/http://www.montbeliard.fr/fileadmin/Fichiers/Photos/5_Culture_loisirs_et_sport/Archives_municipales/gazette_expositions/mobil_tout.pdf |archive-date=December 26, 2013 |access-date= |website=www.montbeliard.fr |language=fr}}</ref> Households stocked up on provisions as early as July 1914,<ref>{{Cite book |last=Delécraz |first=Antoine |url=https://archive.org/details/1914parispendant00deluoft?view=theater |title=1914, Paris pendant la mobilisation, notes d'un immobilisé, des faits, des gestes, des mots ... 31 juillet - 22 août |publisher=Édition Journal La Suisse |year=1914 |location=Geneva |pages=7 |language=fr |trans-title=1914, Paris during mobilization, notes from an immobilized man, facts, gestures, words... July 31 - August 22}}</ref> fearing supply difficulties, queues formed in front of banks to withdraw savings and exchange them for gold, so much in fact that on the 30th the ''Banque de France'' suspended [[Gold standard|convertibility]],<ref>{{Harvtxt|Le Naour|2012|p=164}}</ref> while some inhabitants evacuated Paris to the south as soon as mobilization was announced.<ref>{{Harvtxt|Delécraz|1914|p=30}}</ref> Under the law of August 5, 1914, a daily allowance of one [[French franc|franc]] and 25 centimes per day was paid to poor families whose "provider" was mobilized.<ref>''Loi du 5 août 1914 tendant à accorder, pendant la durée de la guerre, des allocations aux familles nécessiteuses dont le soutien serait appelé ou rappelé sous les drapeaux'' (Law of August 5, 1914 to grant, for the duration of the war, allowances to needy families whose provider has been called up or recalled to serve in the armed forces), promulgated in the ''Journal officiel'' of August 6, 1914, {{Gallica|id=bpt6k2207815/f471|t=Bulletin des lois, n° 135, p. 2269}}</ref> Fearing a shortage of bread, reserve bakers were granted a 45-day deferment of call-up at the request of mayors, and on August 8 bakery production was limited to a four-[[Pound (mass)|pound]] loaf, while brioches, croissants and pastries were banned.<ref>{{Harvtxt|Le Naour|2012|pp=166–167}}</ref> On August 13, the government ordered the deferment of rents for the duration of the war.<ref>{{Harvtxt|Le Naour|2012|p=170}}</ref>

Some [[Crop yield|harvesting]] and haymaking is still to be done (early August), while the [[Harvest (wine)|grape harvest]] is still to come (September and October), and industry has to supply clothing, equipment, weapons and ammunition to the army. The mobilization plan left only 50,000 workers in armaments factories (powder works, artillery arsenals and thirty private suppliers), with rare call-up deferrals and partial replacement of mobilized workers by auxiliaries and non-mobilizables; other industrial sectors temporarily ceased operations.<ref>{{Harvtxt|Porte|2006|loc=§ 5}}</ref> To feed the troops in the short term, the military authorities requisitioned flour, livestock and wine. From the end of 1914 onwards, solutions included recalling skilled workers to the rear ("''affectés spéciaux''", or special assigned), using female workers ("[[Munitionette|munitionnettes]]"), children, foreigners (notably Africans and Chinese), prisoners of war and the disabled.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Hardarch |first=Gern |title=1914-1918, l'autre front |publisher=Éditions ouvrières |year=1977 |location=Paris |language=fr |trans-title=1914–1918, the other front |chapter=La mobilisation industrielle en 1914-1918 |trans-chapter=The industrial mobilization in 1914–1918 |issn=0338-6252}}</ref>

=== Beginning of military operations ===
[[File:French bayonet charge.jpg|alt=Line of infantrymen.|left|thumb|French infantry advancing in line, [[bayonet]]s drawn, 1913.]]
The main consequences were military: general mobilization provided the French army with the manpower it needed to wage war against Germany and the other [[Central Powers]]. On August 4, covering troops seized the [[Vosges]] passes of [[Col de la Schlucht|La Schlucht]] (two hours after receiving notification of the declaration of war),<ref>{{Cite web |last=Defence Historical Service |author-link=Defence Historical Service |title=Journal des marches & opérations du 152e Régiment d'Infanterie pendant les marches de reconnaissances, grandes manœuvres, tirs de etc. from July 16, 1913 to June 20, 1915 "26 N 697/13". |url=http://www.memoiredeshommes.sga.defense.gouv.fr/jmo/img-viewer/26_N_697_013/viewer.html |website=memoiredeshommes.sga.defense.gouv.fr |page=47 |language=fr}}</ref> [[Bussang Pass|Bussang]] and Oderen.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Defence Historical Service |author-link=Defence Historical Service |title=Journal des marches & opérations de la 41e division d'infanterie pendant la campagne du 31 juillet 1914 au 22 janvier 1915 « 26 N 340/1 » |trans-title=Diary of marches & operations of the 41st infantry division during the campaign from July 31, 1914 to January 22, 1915 "26 N 340/1". |url=http://www.memoiredeshommes.sga.defense.gouv.fr/jmo/img-viewer/26_N_340_001/viewer.html |website=memoiredeshommes.sga.defense.gouv.fr |language=fr}}</ref> On August 6, the cavalry corps entered [[Bouillon, Belgium|Belgium via Bouillon]], [[Bertrix]] and [[Paliseul]].<ref>Message from [[André Sordet|General Sordet]] to the Commander-in-Chief, 7:20 a.m., August 6, 1914 cited in {{Harvtxt|Naërt|al.|1936|p=130}}</ref> On August 7, the French 7th Corps crossed the border into Germany and began the conquest of Haute-Alsace.<ref>Order from Joffre transmitted by telegram to the commander of the 1st Army, at 5:10 p.m. on August 5, cited in {{Harvtxt|Naërt|al.|1936|p=129}}</ref>  On August 14, all units of the 1st and 2nd Armies entered [[Moselle (department)|Moselle]],<ref>{{Harvtxt|Valluy|Dufourcq|1968|pp=78–80|loc=v. 1}}</ref> while the 3rd, 4th and 5th Armies awaited the Germans along the Ardennes section of the [[Meuse]].<ref>Special Instruction No. 6 from General Joffre to the commanders of the 3rd, 4th and 5th armies, August 13, 1914, cited in {{Harvtxt|Naërt|al.|1936|p=166}}</ref>
{{Main|Battle of the Frontiers}}
[[File:Bouvet in Toulon-Agence Rol-3.jpeg|thumb|A French squadron in Toulon harbor: the [[French battleship Bouvet|Bouvet]] seen from another battleship.]]
For the French navy, the entry of the British into the war meant that it no longer had to fear the [[Imperial German Navy|German navy]]. On August 3, 1914, the Franco-British convention of 1913<ref>Franco-British technical agreement of February 10, 1913, repeating that of November 1912 and confirmed by the agreement of August 6, 1914 signed in London. Source: {{Cite book |last=Thomazi |first=Auguste |title=La Marine française dans la Grande Guerre (1914-1918) |publisher=Payot |year=1928 |volume=IV |location=Paris |pages=17 |language=fr |trans-title=The French Navy in The Great War (1914–1918) |chapter=La guerre navale dans la Méditerranée |trans-chapter=Naval war in the Mediterranean}}</ref> came into force, entrusting the [[North Sea]], the [[Strait of Dover|Strait o Dover]] and the [[English Channel]] to the [[Royal Navy]], while the French took charge of the [[Mediterranean Sea|Mediterranean]],<ref>{{Harvtxt|Valluy|Dufourcq|1968|p=131|loc=v. 1}}</ref> with the mission of hunting down enemy cruisers and establishing a naval [[blockade]] off Austrian ports. Consequently, only a light squadron of six [[cruiser]]s was stationed at [[Cherbourg Naval Base|Cherbourg base]] (under the command of Rear Admiral Rouyer), supplemented by flotillas of [[torpedo boat]]s and [[submarine]]s at [[Dunkirk]], [[Calais]] and [[Boulogne-sur-Mer|Boulogne]], while the "naval army" of 19 [[battleship]]s was concentrated at [[Toulon arsenal|Toulon]] (commanded by [[Augustin Boué de Lapeyrère|Admiral Boué de Lapeyrère]]), before moving to [[Valletta]] in September. As the [[Lorient]] [[fusiliers marins]] depot was full, and no landings were initially planned, on August 7 these troops, together with detachments from all the ports, formed two regiments grouped together in a [[Brigade de Fusiliers Marins|fusiliers marins brigade]] (6,400 men, led by naval and marine officers). This brigade, commanded by [[Pierre Alexis Ronarc'h|Rear Admiral Ronarc'h]], was sent to the [[Fortifications of Paris in the 19th and 20th centuries|stronghold of Paris]]<ref>{{Cite web |title=Les fusiliers marins pendant la guerre 1914-1918 |trans-title=Marine fusiliers in the war 1914–1918 |url=http://philippe.millour.free.fr/GrandeGuerre/cadre_BFM.htm |access-date= |website=philippe.millour.free.fr |language=fr}}</ref> from August 17, before being sent to the front on October 7.

== Later drafts ==
[[File:Départ de la classe 18.jpg|alt=Photograph of several cars filled with conscripts leaving the platform.|thumb|Departure of Class 18, 1917. On the wagons: "To [[Berlin]]".]]
French mobilization continued throughout the [[World War I|First World War]], with the successive call-up of the Territorial Army Reserve (classes 1892 to 1888) from December 1914 to April 1915<ref>{{Cite web |title=Tableau de mobilisation durant la grande guerre |trans-title=Mobilization chart for the Great War |url=https://www.abtahistoireboussay.fr/?option=com_content&view=article&id=27:tableau-de-mobilisation:premiere-guerre-mondiale |access-date= |website=abtahistoireboussay.fr |language=fr}}</ref> and, above all, the advance of the classes 1914 (from September 1914, instead of October), 1915 (from December 1914), 1916 (in April 1915), 1917 (in January 1916), 1918 (in April 1917) and 1919 (in April 1918).<ref name=":12" /><ref>The early call-up of a class is discussed in the Chamber of Deputies every time, for example during the {{Cite web |title=séance du 30 novembre 1915 |trans-title=session of November 30, 1915 |url=http://www.assemblee-nationale.fr/histoire/guerre_14-18/classe17_gallieni_30111915.asp |language=fr}} (for the '17 class), or the {{Cite web |title=séance du 28 décembre 1917 |trans-title=session of December 28, 1915 |url=http://www.assemblee-nationale.fr/histoire/guerre_14-18/clemenceau_28dec1917.asp |website=assemblee-nationale.fr |language=fr}} (for the '19 class)</ref> These "rookies" first had to complete their [[Military recruit training|training]] before going into battle; the class of 1919 was only at the front during the last weeks of the war (this was the case for the "[[List of last surviving World War I veterans|last poilus]]" [[Fernand Goux]] and Pierre Picault).<ref>{{Cite web |title=France, derniers poilus de la Guerre 14-18 |trans-title=France, the last poilus of the 14–18 war |url=http://dersdesders.free.fr/france.html |access-date= |website=dersdesders.free.fr |language=fr}}</ref> Even imprisoned criminals and ex-convicts were drafted into the [[Battalions of Light Infantry of Africa]].

[[Conscription]] was gradually applied in the [[French colonial empire|French colonies]], but incorporation was uneven, varying according to status: ''[[pieds-noirs]]'' reservists were mobilized as early as August 1914, and assigned to [[zouave]] units; inhabitants of the "old colonies" ([[Saint Pierre and Miquelon]], [[Guadeloupe]], [[Martinique]], [[French Guiana]], the [[Four Communes|four communes of Senegal]], [[Réunion]], [[French India|the Indies]], [[New Caledonia]] and [[French Polynesia|Polynesia]]) provided the manpower for [[Troupes coloniales|colonial units]] (mainly colonial infantry regiments); [[Indigénat|natives]] (not considered as French citizens, but "subjects") of [[French North Africa|North Africa]], [[French West Africa|West Africa]], [[French Equatorial Africa|Equatorial Africa]], [[Madagascar]], the [[French Somaliland|Somali coast]], [[Comoro Islands|the Comoros]] and [[French Indochina|Indochina]] were more gradually forced into service, a first voluntary service (often encouraged or even forced by local chiefs),<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Antier-Renaud |first1=Chantal |title=Les soldats des colonies dans la Première guerre mondiale |publisher=Éd. "Ouest-France" |others=Christian Le Corre |year=2008 |isbn=978-2-7373-4283-7 |series=Collection Histoire |location=Rennes |pages=32–33 |language=fr |trans-title=Soldiers from the colonies in the First World War}}</ref> completed fairly limited call-ups,<ref>Decree dated February 7, 1912, instituting recruitment by call-up of "black natives of the French West Africa group", providing that they "may in all circumstances be designated to continue their service outside the territory of the colony" and specifying that "the duration of active service is four years". Source: {{Cite book |last=Duval |first=Eugène-Jean |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=evwD-vcHVkMC |title=L'épopée des tirailleurs sénégalais |publisher=L'Harmattan |year=2005 |isbn=978-2-7475-8593-4 |location=Paris |pages=40 |language=fr |trans-title=The epic of the Senegalese riflemen}}</ref> then by mass conscription from 1915<ref>From April 1, 1915 for Indochina and after the decree of October 9, 1915 for [[French West Africa|AOF]]. Source: {{Harvtxt|Antier-Renaud|2008|pp=26–28}}</ref> into units of Algerian, [[Senegalese Tirailleurs|Senegalese]], Moroccan, Tunisian, Malagasy, [[1st Battalion of Somali Tirailleurs|Tonkinese, Annamite]] and Somali tirailleurs. In total, all colonies combined, 583,450 men were gradually drafted,<ref>{{Cite book |last=Sarraut |first=Albert |author-link=Albert Sarraut |title=La mise en valeur des colonies françaises |publisher=Payot |year=1923 |language=fr |trans-title=The development of French colonies}} {{BnF|bnf=341367630}}</ref> leading to several uprisings in the colonies.<ref>{{Harvtxt|Antier-Renaud|2008|pp=34–35}}</ref>

== Historiography ==
Right from the start of the [[World War I|Great War]], the main subject of historical research was not mobilization itself, but the causes and, above all, the people responsible for the conflict.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Becker |first=Jean-Jacques |year=2006 |title=L'évolution de l'historiographie de la Première Guerre mondiale |trans-title=The evolution of First World War historiography |url=http://rha.revues.org//index4152.html |journal=Revue historique des armées |language=fr |issue=242|pages=4–15 |doi=10.3917/rha.242.0004 }}</ref> The first historian to really look into the subject of mobilization was [[Charles Petit-Dutaillis]], medievalist and rector of the Grenoble academy in 1914, who ordered all teachers in the Isère, Drôme and Hautes-Alpes regions to report on the attitude of the local population in the early days.<ref name=":10" /> This rector's initiative was passed on to the Minister of Public Instruction, [[Albert Sarraut]], who decided to send out a circular dated September 18, 1914, instructing all non-mobilized teachers to keep notes on war-related events, starting with mobilization. During and after the conflict, it was the diplomatic aspects (always linked to the question of responsibilities) and military aspects (essentially operations) that dominated historical production, with the work of [[Pierre Renouvin]] in particular.<ref>{{Harvtxt|Becker|2004|loc=153 and 156}}</ref>

The gradual publication of soldiers' testimonies did nothing to change this: for most of the twentieth century, the almost exclusive vision of this entry into the war, printed and taught, was that of general acceptance of the conflict by the population and the departure of the soldiers "''avec'' ''la fleur au fusil''" ,or "[with] the flower on the rifle" (expression used as the title of [[Jean Galtier-Boissière]]'s testimonial, published in 1928),<ref>{{Harvtxt|Galtier-Boissière|1928}}</ref> interpreted as an enthusiastic surge reflecting the spirit of revenge on Germany. The success of this mythical vision of the French entry into the war can be explained by three factors. The first was the immediate usefulness of a mobilization that was presented as enthusiastic, and which was the popular equivalent of the Sacred Union, both of which seemed to emanate from the people as a whole, whereas they were merely the fruit of circumstance. Secondly, the images conveyed by the press and the writings of intellectuals exalting the war contributed powerfully to forging this myth of the flower in the gun. Finally, this representation makes it possible to transfer responsibility for the conflict onto the political leaders, with the crowds letting themselves be carried away by their naivety, without there being any question of their consenting to the war. This consensus was suited to an interwar French population that was both patriotic and pacifist, since it was as compatible with a right-wing opinion (the war was triggered by patriotism and the Germans) as it was with a left-wing opinion (the real perpetrators of the carnage were the politicians and, more generally, the elites).<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Beaupré |first1=Nicolas |title=Les grandes guerres: 1914-1945 |last2=Rousso |first2=Henry |publisher=[[Éditions Belin]] |year=2012 |isbn=978-2-7011-3387-4 |series=Histoire de France |location=Paris |pages=44–45 |language=fr |trans-title=The great wars: 1914–1915}}</ref>

In the early 1960s, [[Jean-Jacques Becker]] made the study of public opinion at the time of the French entry into the war the subject of his thesis, supervised by Renouvin. Since Becker doubted the consensus, he set out to find sources that would show the state of public opinion in 1914, and found Petit-Dutaillis's compilation in the library and archive center ''[[La contemporaine]]''. Using schoolteachers' reports, cross-referenced with other sources (press, prefectoral records, etc.), he challenged the myth of "''la fleur au fusil.''"<ref>{{Harvtxt|Becker|2004|pp=157–160}}</ref> He remained convinced, however, that the French massively embraced the war as a national cause.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Olivera |first1=Philippe |url=http://crid1418.org/espace_scientifique/textes/culture_de_guerre.htm |title=Guerres, paix et sociétés: 1911-1946 |last2=Picard |first2=Emmanuelle |last3=Offenstadt |first3=Nicolas |last4=Rousseau |first4=Frédéric |author-link4=Frédéric Rousseau |publisher=Atlande |year=2004 |location=Neuilly-sur-Seine |pages=669 |language=fr |trans-title=Wars, peace and societies: 1911–1946 |chapter=À propos d'une notion récente: la "culture de guerre" |trans-chapter=On a recent concept: the "culture of war"}}</ref> While Jean-Jacques Becker's thesis is undisputed for the start of the war, other historians such as Jules Maurin and Philippe Boulanger note that, after the first three months, voluntary enlistments abandoned their patriotic character in favor of a survival strategy. Indeed, being called up early enabled volunteers to choose their brach of assignment. Volunteers were more likely to choose the artillery or navy, reputed to be less deadly than the infantry. This observation therefore undermines the idea that the French always consented to war.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Rousseau |first=Frédéric |author-link=Frédéric Rousseau |title=Guerres, paix et sociétés: 1911-1946 |publisher=Atlande |year=2004 |location=Neuilly-sur-Seine |pages=387–388 |language=fr |trans-title=War, peace and societies: 1911–1946 |chapter=De l'acceptation de la guerre à l'acceptation du crime (1914-1945) |trans-chapter=From the acceptance of war to the acceptance of crime (1914–1945)}}</ref>

Historian Nicolas Mariot refutes the idea that the war was the "melting pot of a class union, social inequalities of French society in the 1900s persisted under the uniform" by studying the letters and diaries of intellectuals such as [[Guillaume Apollinaire|Apollinaire]] and the philosopher [[Alain (philosopher)|Alain]], who were either ordinary soldiers or low-ranking soldiers at the front. These intellectuals regretted that their comrades-in-arms from the common people (peasants, craftsmen or workers) did not share their ideals, many of them patriotic. Feeling socially isolated despite an overcrowding that disturbed them, they had little patience for popular swearing or drinking parties. The common soldier looked on them with more suspicion than to the officer, who is often a man designated by rank.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Mariot |first=Nicolas |title=Tous unis dans la tranchée ? 1914-1918, les intellectuels rencontrent le peuple |publisher=[[Éditions du Seuil]] |year=2013 |pages=496 |language=fr |trans-title=All united in the trench? 1914–1918, intellectuals meet the people}}</ref>

'''Angel Down''' is a [[World War I]] novel with a [[narrative structure]] that is a continuously streaming monologue, consisting of one continuous sentence, from the first page of the novel to its last page. The protagonist is a [[Draft evasion|draft dodger]] and then an [[army private]] who encounters an angel on the battlefield. It was written by [[Daniel Kraus (author)|Daniel Kraus]], an American author. It was published by First Atria Books, and imprint of Simon & Schuster, in July 2025.<ref name=nyt-best>[https://www.nytimes.com/2025/12/02/books/review/best-books-2025.html 10 Best Books of 2025].The New York Times</ref><ref name=Winters>{{Cite web|newspaper= The New York Times|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2025/07/26/books/review/angel-down-daniel-kraus.html|title=A Harrowing Tale of War, Told in One Long, Urgent Sentence|date=July 26, 2025}}</ref><ref name=Anders>{{cite news| last = Anders| first = Charlie Jane| title = These sci-fi books ask the most basic question: Are we our memories?ewspaper = The Washington Post| date = July 14, 2025| url = https://www.washingtonpost.com/books/2025/07/14/new-scifi-fantasy-books-haddon-kraus/
| access-date =}}*</ref><ref name=pple>{{Cite web|url=https://people.com/best-2025-books-according-to-nyt-and-people-reviewers-11859861|title=These 14 Books Made The New York Times' and PEOPLE's Best Books of 2025 — See the List!|website=Books|publisher=People Magazine}}</ref><ref name=PubWeek>{{cite web
| url = https://www.publishersweekly.com/9781668068458| title = Review: Angel Down| last = Magazine| first = Staff| date = April 26, 2025| website = Publishers Weekly
| access-date = January 10, 2025| quote =and so Bagger sits up with vision aswirl and shoos away the filthy pelt of air, the pigeon-gray smoke and eyeball-white fog}}</ref><ref name= Polevoi>{{cite web
| url = https://www.highbrowmagazine.com/25946-fall-heaven-wwi-trenches-angel-down
| title = A Fall From Heaven Into WWI Trenches in 'Angel Down'
| last = Polevoi
| first = Lee 
| date =  October 29, 2025
| website = Highbrow Magazine
| access-date = January 10, 2026}}</ref>

==Premise==
Five American soldiers near the end of World War I, during the [[Meuse-Argonne offensive]], are on a bloody battlefield in France.<ref name=Winters/><ref name=PubWeek/>  Major General Reis, who is focused on his own advancement, orders an infantryman, Private First Class Cyril Bagger to investigate an unearthly shrieking sound that is causing the troops to go insane. Bagger is sent out with four other soldiers, a group of misfits. First there is Arno, who is young and innocent. Next is Popkin who is very much a brute. Then there is Goodspeed who is nervously "squirming," and Veck, who is suffering from severe shell shock.<ref name=PubWeek/>

The five men discover the source of the sound is an angel, and she looks like women that each of the men recognize. She is tangled in barbed wire and emitting an very bright aura.<ref name=PubWeek/> They believe Major General Reis will try to exploit the angel for his own benefit and career advancement. Determined to keep her away from Reis, the soldiers desert their post. They carry the angel, dodging artillery fire while arguing with each other. Each man tries to gain favor with the angel hoping she will grant their personal wishes.<ref name=PubWeek/>

==Writing style==
According to ''[[Publishers Weekly]]'', Kraus builds the tension with the rhythm of his writing, creating a sense of non-stop action because the entire story is a single, continuous sentence. Despite the pacing, the writing is also poetic, as there are lyrical passages like "Bagger sits up with vision aswirl and shoos away the filthy pelt of air, the pigeon-gray smoke and eyeball-white fog."<ref name=PubWeek/> Ben H. Winters of ''[[The New York Times]]'' says that this novel starts at the outset in the middle of a sentence and in the middle of a battle, while the narrative ends in a comma indicating that there is no conclusion, only continuation.<ref name=Winters/>

Winters also says that the text shows an exemplary example of the "additive style", in which the "writer's prose is associative and spontaneous, piling up new facts and ideas without necessarily spelling out their relationships. The additive style — as distinct from the precise and ordered subordinating style — suggests that the relationship between events, their quote-unquote 'meaning,' is as uncertain in stories as it is in life."<ref name=Winters/>

According to ''Kirkus Reviews'', Kraus structured the entire novel as one extended run-on sentence, broken up only by paragraph indentation. This structure works by "giving the story a relentless and intense rhythm."<ref name=Kirkus/>

==Themes==
''Kirkus Reviews'' says that in the realm of horror, the novel vividly portrays the violence, and blood and guts of the battlefield. This continuous run-on sentence structure is applied to "keep a story moving." According to ''Kirkus Reviews'', the latter part of the book asks philosophical questions about: Why people seem naturally inclined to wage war. What force or idea might be strong enough to stop this cycle of conflict.<ref name=Kirkus>{{cite web
| url = https://www.kirkusreviews.com/book-reviews/daniel-kraus/angel-down/
| title = Book review: Angel Down
| last = Staff
| date = December 20, 2025
| website = Kirkus Reviews
| access-date =January 10, 2025}}</ref>

==Reception==
According to ''Publishers Weekly'', the novel is a vigorous and fresh take on the war novel genre.<ref name=PubWeek/> Winters, of ''The New York Times'' says, "''Angel Down'', mysterious and full of grace, may work a similar power on its readers, even as it walks the fields of death."<ref name=Winters/>

title: Annie Larsen affair
wikitext:
{{Short description|Gun-running plot in the United States during World War I}}
The '''Annie Larsen affair''' was a [[gun running|gun-running]] plot in the United States during [[World War I]].<ref name=HistoryLink>{{cite web| publisher = HistoryLink.org| url=http://www.historylink.org/essays/output.cfm?file_id=7753| title=U.S. Customs at Grays Harbor seizes the schooner ''Annie Larsen'' loaded with arms and ammunition on June 29, 1915 | access-date=2007-09-22}}</ref> The plot, involving India's [[Ghadar Party]], the [[Irish Republican Brotherhood]], and the German Foreign office, was a part of the larger so-called "[[Hindu–German Conspiracy]]",<ref name="Plowman 2003 90">{{Harvnb|Plowman|2003|p=90}}</ref> and it was the prime offence cited in the 1917 [[Hindu–German Conspiracy Trial]], described at the time as the longest and most expensive trial in American legal history.<ref>{{Harvnb|Plowman|2003|p=85}}</ref>

==Background==
{{Main|Hindu–German Conspiracy}}
{{See also|Ghadar Party|World War I}}

By 1914, plans for a pan-Indian revolution had been hatched. As World War I broke out, Germany decided to actively support the Ghadar plan. For this, links established between Indian and Irish residents in Germany (including [[Roger Casement]]) and the [[Federal Foreign Office|German Foreign office]] were used to tap into the Indo-Irish network in the United States. In September 1914, the German Chancellor [[Theobald von Bethmann Hollweg]] authorised German activity against [[British Raj|British India]]. The German effort was headed by [[Max von Oppenheim]], archaeologist and the head of the newly formed Intelligence bureau for the east. Upon Oppenheim fell the task of arranging the Indian student groups into a cohesive group. Oppenheim also convinced Indian revolutionary [[Har Dayal]] of the feasibility of the project and was able to establish contact with the Ghadar Party in the United States. In an October meeting of the [[German Imperial Naval Office|Imperial Naval Office]], the consulate in San Francisco was tasked to make contact with Ghadar leaders in [[California]]. German military attache to the German consulate [[Wilhelm von Brincken]] was able to establish contact, through [[Tarak Nath Das]] and an intermediary named Charles Lattendorf, with [[Ram Chandra Bharadwaj|Ram Chandra]].

==Arms shipment==
With the approval of San Francisco German vice-consul E.H. von Schack, arrangements for funds and armaments were secured. Ram Chandra was to receive a monthly payment of $1,000. At the same time $200,000 worth of small arms and ammunition was acquired by the German military attaché Captain [[Franz von Papen]] through a [[Krupp]] agent by the name of [[Hans Tauscher]]. In the meantime, Papen arranged for [[Joseph McGarrity]] to make the necessary arrangements for shipping the arms purchase from [[New York City|New York]] to [[Galveston, Texas|Galveston]] via the Mallory Steamship Company, an Irish-American shipping firm. From Galveston the guns were sent by train to [[San Diego]], where they were to be shipped to India via [[Burma]]. However, Charles Martinez, a customs official who had arranged the shipment to San Diego, was not told of the true destination, and hired the [[schooner]] ''[[Annie Larsen]]''.<ref name="Plowman 2003 90"/><ref name="Hoover 1985 252">{{Harvnb|Hoover|1985|p=252}}</ref> For this purpose, an elaborate deception was hatched to convey the idea that the arms were meant for the [[Mexican Revolution|warring factions in Mexico]]. J. Clyde Hizar, a [[Colorado]] attorney in charge of placing the arms on board the ''Annie Larsen'', posed as a representative for the [[Venustiano Carranza|Carranza Faction]]. This ruse was convincing enough to elicit an offer of $15,000 from the rival [[Villistas|Villa faction]] to divert the shipment to a Villa-controlled port.<ref name="Hoover 1985 252"/>

However, the ''Annie Larsen'' was not suitable for a trans-Pacific voyage. Frederick Jebsen, a German reserve naval officer with close connections to the German embassy, arranged for another ship, the [[SS Maverick]], to be purchased under the illusion that it was to be used by the "American-Asiatic Oil Company", a fake oil-trading company, and was to deploy between China and [[Borneo]]. The plan was for the ''Maverick'' to leave empty from [[San Pedro, Los Angeles|San Pedro]] around the same time as the ''Annie Larsen'' leaves [[San Diego]] fully loaded. The two would rendezvous off [[Socorro Island]] near Mexico. The ''Annie Larsen'' would transfer its shipment to the ''Maverick'' which would then proceed towards [[Southeast Asia]].<ref>{{Harvnb|Hoover|1985|p=253}}</ref><ref name="Brown 1948 303">{{Harvnb|Brown|1948|p=303}}</ref> For this purpose, Jebsen established a fake company to hide the true ownership of the ship, taking his attorney Ray Howard as partner.<ref name="Brown 1948 303"/><ref>{{Harvnb|Hoover|1985|p=255}}</ref> The ''Maverick'' received a crew composed of sailors from two German ships interned at San Francisco. An American by the name of John B. Starr-Hunt served as [[supercargo]] on the ''Maverick'', and was under orders to scuttle the ship if challenged by Allied warships.<ref name="Brown 1948 303"/> The impression at the docks was that the ship was to relieve congestion in the East Indian Coconut industry, in [[Java]] and Borneo.

The ''Annie Larsen'' sailed for [[Topolobampo]] on 8 March 1915 under Captain Paul Schlueter for rendezvous with the SS ''Maverick''. Also placed on board was a person by the name of Walter Page as supercargo. Page's real identity was L. Othmer, the captain of the German [[Barque|bark]] ''Atlas'', which had earlier been interned by the U.S. government in San Francisco. Page was given complete authority over the ship's movement and he set sail for [[Socorro Island]], off [[Baja California]].<ref name="HistoryLink"/><ref name="Hoover 1985 256">{{Harvnb|Hoover|1985|p=256}}</ref>

However, at this stage the plan started falling apart. The ''Maverick'', which was in [[drydock]] at the time, could not sail for another month. Even during this time, rumours abounded that it was to be used to smuggle arms into Southeast Asia. The ship was searched a number of times by customs and security agents, who only found the ship's empty hold. Immediately before it left, it received an additional crew of five Indian Ghadar activists carrying fake [[Iran|Persian]] passports. They carried with themselves large amounts of Ghadarite literature, and were tasked by Ram Chandra to establish contacts with Indian revolutionaries and arrange for the arms to be transported inland.<ref name="Brown 1948 303"/><ref name="Hoover 1985 256"/> However, awaiting the ''Maverick'' for nearly a month, the ''Annie Larsen'' ran out of fresh water and, without a condenser on board, was forced to head for the mainland of Mexico. Arriving at the rendezvous point, the ''Maverick'' was informed of the ''Annie Larsen''<nowiki>'</nowiki>s departure by a two-man crew left behind by Page. The ''Maverick'' waited for twenty-nine days for the Schooner's return. During this time, it was visited by [[HMS Kent (1901)|HMS ''Kent'']]. The Ghadar agents were forced to burn the revolutionary literature in the boiler room while the ''Kent''{{'s}} crew searched the ship. A subsequent visit by an American warship also revealed nothing save the ship's empty hold.<ref name="Brown 1948 303"/><ref name="Hoover 1985 256"/>

The ''Annie Larsen'' sailed to [[Acapulco]] to replenish its supplies. However, it faced trouble as three of the crew members refused to sail the ship, claiming it was not seaworthy. Captain Sheultzer was able to successfully appeal for help from the {{USS|Yorktown|PG-1|6}} which was in the area. Its contraband cargo was not discovered by the ''Yorktown's'' boarding party. Allowed to use the ''Yorktown's'' wireless, the German crew were able to notify the German Consulate of their position and of the failed rendezvous.<ref name="Brown 1948 304">{{Harvnb|Brown|1948|p=304}}</ref> Sailing from Acapulco, the ''Annie Larsen'' made for Socorro Island again. However, in adverse weather, this attempt failed as well, and after twenty-two days Scheultzer gave up, choosing to make for the northern port of [[Hoquiam, Washington]].<ref name=HistoryLink/><ref name="Brown 1948 304"/>

Returning to San Diego after failing to meet the ''Annie Larsen'', the ''Maverick'' was directed by Fred Jebsen to proceed to [[Hilo, Hawaii]], where it was redirected to [[Johnston Island]] by the German consulate for a second effort to rendezvous with the ''Annie Larsen''. However, this failed too and it was subsequently directed to [[Anjer]], [[Java]].<ref name="Hoover 1985 256"/><ref name="Brown 1948 304"/> At Anjer, a German operative named Theodore Helfrichs was instructed to dispose of the ship. However, it was seized by Dutch authorities. Starr-Hunt and four of the Ghadarites attempted to flee in a ship, but were captured by the British cruiser {{HMS|Newcastle|1909|6}}. Taken to [[Singapore]], Starr-Hunt confessed his role in the plot.<ref name="Brown 1948 304"/>

==Resolving the plot==
In the United States, the conspiracy was successfully infiltrated by British intelligence through both the Irish, as well as Indian channels. The activities of Ghadar on the Pacific coast were noted by W. C Hopkinson, who had grown up in India and spoke fluent Hindi.<ref>{{cite web | publisher = UC, Berkeley, Bancroft Library| url=http://www.lib.berkeley.edu/SSEAL/echoes/chapter7/chapter7.html| title=Echoes of Freedom:South Asian pioneers in California 1899-1965| access-date=2007-11-11| archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20071116202006/http://www.lib.berkeley.edu/SSEAL/echoes/chapter7/chapter7.html| archive-date= 16 November 2007 | url-status= live}}</ref> In the meantime, through [[Hindu–German Conspiracy#Counter-intelligence|intelligence sources]] arising from British, Irish, European, and Mexican sources, the [[United States Department of Justice|Justice Department]] had a clear picture of the conspiracy and the true purposes of the ''Maverick'' and the ''Annie Larsen''.<ref name="Hoover 1985 256"/> The Home department of the British Indian government had begun the task of actively tracking Indian seditionists on the [[East Coast of the United States|East Coast]] as early as 1910. Francis Cunliffe Owen, the officer heading the Home Office agency in New York, had become thoroughly acquainted with George Freeman and Myron Phelps posing as members of the Clan-na-Gael. Owens' efforts were successful in thwarting the SS ''Moraitis'' plan.<ref>{{Harvnb|Popplewell|1995|p=147}}</ref> The Ghadar Party was incidentally established after Irish Republicans, sensing infiltration, encouraged an exclusively Indian society.<ref name="Popplewell 1995 148">{{Harvnb|Popplewell|1995|p=148}}</ref> Following this, a number of approaches were adopted, including instituting a "Native" Indian intelligence officer to infiltrate the movement, as well as the use of the famous American [[Pinkerton's]] detective agency.<ref name="Popplewell 1995 148"/>

An Irish double agent by the name of Charles Lamb is said to have passed on the majority of the information that compromised the conspiracy and ultimately helped the construction of the prosecution. An Indian operative, codenamed "''C''" and described most likely to have been [[Chandra Kanta Chakraverty]] (later the chief prosecution witness in the trial), also passed on the details of the conspiracy to British and American intelligence.
On 29 June 1915, the ''Annie Larsen'' was raided at Hoquiam and its contraband cargo seized.<ref name=HistoryLink/><ref name="Hoover 1985 256"/> However, Page was able to escape and later made for Germany. The ''Annie Larsen''{{'s}} cargo was sold at an auction despite the German Ambassador Count [[Johann von Bernstoff]]'s attempts to take possession insisting they were meant for [[German East Africa]].<ref name="Brown 1948 304"/> Additionally, some of the plans involving the Indian [[Berlin Committee]] leaked out through [[Czechoslovakia|Czech]] revolutionaries and spy networks who were in touch with their counterparts in the United States.<ref>{{Harvnb|Voska|Irwin|1940|p=98,108,120,122,123}}</ref><ref>{{Harvnb|Masaryk|1970|p=50,221,242}}</ref><ref>{{Harvnb|Bose|1971|p=2332,233}}</ref>  The American network of the Czech organisation, headed by [[E. V. Voska]], was a counter-espionage network spying on [[German Empire|German]] and [[Austria-Hungary|Austrian]] diplomats. Voska, being pro-American, pro-British and anti-German, on learning of the plot from the Czech European network, spoke of it to [[Tomáš Masaryk]], who then passed the information to the American authorities. The Americans informed British intelligence.

==Trial==
The [[Hindu–German Conspiracy Trial]] commenced in the [[United States District Court for the Northern District of California|District Court]] in [[San Francisco]] on November 12, 1917, following the uncovering of the ''Annie Larsen''{{'s}} cargo. One hundred and five people, including the former Consul-General and vice consul, members of the [[Ghadar Party]], and members of the German consulate in [[San Francisco]] were tried. The trial lasted from November 20, 1917, to April 24, 1918. The trial was also sensationally notable for the assassination of the chief conspirator Ram Chandra.  Chandra was assassinated on the last day of the trial in a packed courtroom by one of his fellow accused, Ram Singh. Singh himself was also immediately shot dead by a [[United States Marshals Service|United States Marshal]]. In May 1917, eight [[Indian nationalism|Indian nationalists]] of the Ghadar Party were indicted by a federal grand jury on a charge of conspiracy to form a military enterprise against Britain. The trial in later years has been criticised for being largely a [[show trial]] to appease the British government.<ref name=Fraser257>{{Harvnb|Fraser|1977|p=257}}</ref> In addition, the jury during the trial was carefully selected to exclude Irish persons with republican views or associations.<ref name=Jensen65>{{harvnb|Jensen|1979|p=65}}</ref> The British authorities hoped that the conviction of the Indians would result in their deportation from the United States back to India. However, in the face of strong public support in favor of the Indians, officials of the U.S. Department of Justice chose not to do so.

==Impact on Anglo-American relations==
{{See also|Anglo-American relations}}
By 1916, the majority of the resources of the American department of the British Foreign office were related to the Indian seditionist movement. Before the outbreak of the war, [[Cecil Spring Rice|Sir Cecil Spring Rice]], the Ambassador to United States at the time of the war, is known to have urged the [[British Foreign office]] not to make this a diplomatic issue. Spring Rice's dispatches cite concerns with regards to American tolerance of the [[Anarchism|Anarchist movements]] in American soil, the American government's inactions despite concrete knowledge (in Spring Rice's opinion) of the conspiracies, as well as concerns regarding the image of Britain in American public opinion if Britain were seen to persecute oppressed people. Further, Spring Rice was particularly wary of the political commitments of American [[Woodrow Wilson|President Wilson's government]],<ref name=Fraser260>{{Harvnb|Fraser|1977|p=260}}</ref> especially given that the [[United States Secretary of State|Secretary of State]] [[William Jennings Bryan]] had eight years previously written the highly critical pamphlet ''British Rule in India''. This pamphlet had been classified as seditionist by the Indian and Imperial governments.

Following Bryan's departure, the British secretary of state, [[Robert Crewe-Milnes, 1st Marquess of Crewe|Robert Crewe-Milnes]], attempted to persuade Spring Rice to raise the issue in front of the United States government. American authorities in the Philippines were also more cooperative at this time, and assured Britain they would have foreknowledge of any plans against Hong Kong. Following the conclusion of the [[Lahore Conspiracy Case trial]], and as more evidence of German complicity came to light, Foreign Secretary [[Edward Grey, 1st Viscount Grey of Fallodon|Edward Grey]] was forced to override Spring Rice's hesitation; in February 1916, the British government officially presented its concerns regarding the conspiracy and German complicity to the American government. Although the new secretary of state [[Robert Lansing]] was initially as uncooperative as Bryan, the first investigations of the conspiracy opened with the raid of the Wall Street office of [[Wolf von Igel]]. The papers seized were later presented as evidence in the [[Hindu–German Conspiracy trial]]. Much to the chagrin of the British government, however, it was not pursued further at the time.

The issue did precipitate a more general Anglo-American neutrality dispute. This was aggravated by belligerent preventive measures taken by the British far-eastern fleet that threatened the sovereignty of American vessels. In particular, HMS ''Laurentic'' seized German and Turkish passengers on the American vessel ''China'' at the mouth of the [[Yangtze]], the British government accusing them of planning to foment an armed uprising in India. This incident provoked outrage from the American government, and was followed by a number of incidents including the SS ''Henry S'' incident.{{clarify|date=June 2016}} The [[US Atlantic Fleet]] dispatched [[destroyer]]s to the Philippines. The relations were strained until May 1916, when the British government decided to relax its aggressive policy and seek cooperation with the US. The ''China'' prisoners were released that month, but relations did not improve before November that year, with a number of exchanges{{clarify|date=June 2016}} through the rest of 1916.

The issue was ultimately addressed by [[Sir William Wiseman, 10th Baronet|William Wiseman]], head of British intelligence in the US, who bypassed diplomatic channels to give details of a bomb plot directly to the New York police. This led to the arrest of Chandra Kanta Chuckrevarty. As links became apparent, within the Chuckrevarty papers and the Igel papers, the investigations by federal authorities ultimately expanded to cover the entire conspiracy. The US agreed to pass on evidence so long as Britain did not seek admission of liability for Breaches of Neutrality. At a time that Diplomatic relations with Germany were deteriorating, the Foreign Office directed the Embassy to cooperate with the investigations. These ultimately resolved the Anglo-American diplomatic disputes just as America entered the war.<ref>{{Harvnb|Dignan|1971|p=}}</ref>
