|date=12 November 2007 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191104190310/https://www.derryjournal.com/news/opinion/maybe-it-s-time-for-a-green-poppy-instead-1-2117641 |archive-date=2019-11-04}}</ref><ref name="andersonstown">{{cite news |first=Roisin |last=McManus |url=http://www.belfastmedia.com/news_article.php?ID=2242 |title=PSNI wearing poppies in West Belfast for political reasons: RFJ |work=[[Andersonstown News]] |publisher=Belfast Media Group |date=28 October 2008 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110724153509/http://www.belfastmedia.com/news_article.php?ID=2242 |archive-date=2011-07-24}}</ref><ref name="westtyronesf">{{cite web |url=http://www.westtyronesinnfein.com/news/15040 |title=BBC's Poppy Wearing Policy Offensive to Majority of Nationalists and Republicans |work=West Tyrone Sinn Féin |date=11 November 2009 name="irishind">{{cite news |first=Tomas |last=Walsh |url=http://www.independent.ie/opinion/letters/lest-we-forget-who-they-honour-1218939.html |title=Lest we forget who they honour |work=[[Irish Independent]] |date=14 November 2007}}</ref><ref>{{cite news| url=https://news.bbc.co.uk/1/hi/northern_ireland/502290.stm | work=BBC News | title=Westlife poppy backing 'not their decision' | date=2 They argue that it [[Journalism ethics and standards|breaches impartiality]] and points out that political symbols are banned in workplaces in Northern Ireland. They also say that the BBC, as a publicly funded body, should broadly reflect the whole community.<ref name="westtyronesf"/><ref>{{cite news |first=Tom |last=Cooper |url=http://www.newsletter.co.uk/news/bbc-presenters-should-be-banned-from-wearning-poppies-1-7042455 |title=BBC presenters should be banned from wearning{{sic|nolink=y}} poppies |work=[[The News Letter]] |date=1 November 2015 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151105032134/https://www.newsletter.co.uk/news/bbc-presenters-should-be-banned-from-wearning-poppies-1-7042455 |archive-date=2015-11-05}}</ref> Likewise, the director of [[Relatives for Justice]] has condemned the wearing of poppies by [[Police Service of Northern Ireland|police officers]] in Catholic neighbourhoods, calling it "repugnant and offensive to the vast majority of people within our community, given the [[Operation Banner#Controversies|role of the British Army]]".<ref name="andersonstown"/> In the ''[[Irish Independent]]'', it was claimed that "substantial amounts" of money raised from selling poppies are used "to build monuments to insane or inane generals or build old boys' clubs for the war elite".<ref name="irishind"/> On Remembrance Day 2010 the [[Social Democratic and Labour Party|SDLP]]'s [[Margaret Ritchie (politician)|Margaret Ritchie]] was the first leader of a nationalist party to wear one.<ref>{{cite news |url=http://www.belfasttelegraph.co.uk/news/local-national/northern-ireland/ritchie-poppy-is-act-of-moving-on-15003906.html |title=Ritchie poppy 'is act of moving on' |work=[[Belfast Telegraph]] |date=2010-11-14}}</ref>

===Outside the Commonwealth===
The Royal British Legion and Royal Canadian Legion also distribute remembrance poppies to several non-Commonwealth countries. In 2010, the Royal British Legion's Poppy Factory distributed three million poppies to over 120 countries, primarily to British expatriate communities and British embassies.<ref name=wherebbc/> The RBL also distributes remembrance poppies to their international branches, including their Hong Kong branch.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://branches.britishlegion.org.uk/branches/hong-kong/poppy-appeal|title=The Poppy Appeal in Hong Kong |publisher=The Royal British Legion |access-date=20 May 2016}}</ref> Canadian remembrance poppies are also distributed at several embassies, including the Canadian embassy in South Korea.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.koreaherald.com/view.php?ud=20171107000366|title=Armistice Day, Remembrance Day commemorations in Korea|date=7 November 2017|last=Mckay|first=Anita|website=www.koreaherald.com|publisher=Herald Corporation|access-date=18 November 2022}}</ref>

====Albania====
In Albania, government representatives, including Prime Minister [[Edi Rama]], wore remembrance poppies during the commemoration ceremonies for the 70th anniversary of [[Liberation Day (Albania)|Liberation Day]].<ref>{{cite news |url=http://www.shekulli.com.al/web/p.php?id=61467&kat=88 |title=70-vjetori i Çlirimit/ Krerët e Shtetit, homazhe te Varrezat e Dëshmorëve (FOTO) |archive-url=https://archive.today/20141215114113/http://www.shekulli.com.al/web/p.php?id=61467&kat=88 |archive-date=15 December 2014 |work=[[Shekulli]] |language=sq |date=29 November 2014}}</ref>

====Ireland====
[[File:RBLI poppy pin 2020 on book cover.png|thumb|RBL Ireland "shamrock poppy" pin 2020]]

During World War I, all of Ireland was part of the United Kingdom and about 200,000 Irishmen fought in the British Army (see [[Ireland and World War I]]). During World War II, some 70,000 citizens of the [[Republic of Ireland|Ireland]], by then independent, served in the British armed forces, and a Roll of Honour in [[Trinity College Dublin]] lists 3,617 people from the Republic who died on active service in the war.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.irishexaminer.com/lifestyle/arid-20350818.html|title=In service to their country : moving tales of Irishmen who fought in WWII| work=Irish Examiner|first=Geoffrey|last=Roberts|date=29 August 2015|access-date=11 May 2021}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.tcd.ie/news_events/articles/roll-of-honour-acknowledging-irelands-contribution-in-world-war-ii-presented-to-tcd-library/ |title=Roll of Honour Acknowledging Ireland's Contribution in World War II Presented to TCD Library |author=<!--Not stated--> |date=16 June 2009 |website=Trinity College Dublin News and Events |publisher=Trinity College Dublin |access-date= 4 Aug 2021|quote=The list details the 3,617 people from the Republic of Ireland and the 3,890 from Northern Ireland who died on active service during the Second World War.}}</ref> The RBL has a branch in the Republic and holds a wreath-laying ceremony at [[St Patrick's Cathedral, Dublin]], which the [[President of Ireland]] has attended.<ref>{{cite news |url=http://www.newsletter.co.uk/news/local/republic_gets_behind_poppy_appeal_1_1873137 |title=Republic gets behind Poppy Appeal |work=[[The News Letter]] |date=29 July 2008 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111104101451/http://www.newsletter.co.uk/news/local/republic_gets_behind_poppy_appeal_1_1873137 |archive-date=2011-11-04}}</ref>

The Republic has its own [[National Day of Commemoration]] in July for all Irish people who died in war. As in other non-Commonwealth countries, poppies are not often worn and are not part of the main commemorations.<ref>{{cite news |first=Liam |last=Nolan |url=http://www.thejournal.ie/readme/column-is-it-time-to-start-wearing-the-poppy-275814-Nov2011/ |title=Column: Is it time to start wearing the poppy? |work=[[TheJournal.ie]] |date=10 November 2011}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |first1=David |last1=McKittrick |first2=Michael |last2=Brennan |url=http://www.independent.ie/irish-news/government-defend-taoiseach-decision-not-to-wear-poppy-28895378.html |title=Government defends Taoiseach decision not to wear poppy |work=[[Irish Independent]] |date=12 November 2012}}</ref> This is partly due to the British Army's role in fighting against Irish independence, some of its actions during the [[Irish War of Independence|War of Independence]]<ref>{{cite web |first=Sean |last=Welan |url=http://www.nga.ie/news-press_release-Wearing_of_the_British_Poppy.php |title=Wearing of the British poppy |publisher=[[National Graves Association]]}}</ref> and its role in Northern Ireland during [[the Troubles]].

In the years following the War of Independence, the poppy was particularly controversial, with Irish nationalists seeing it as a provocative symbol of British imperialism. In Dublin, British Legion marchers often had poppies snatched from their lapels, which led to street fights. In response, some poppy-wearers hid razor blades in their poppies.<ref>{{cite book |last=McGarry |first=Fearghal |title=Republicanism in Modern Ireland |publisher=University College Dublin Press |date=2003 |page=66 |isbn=978-1-900621-94-6}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |first1=Martin |last1=Evans |first2=Kenneth |last2=Lunn |title=War and Memory in the Twentieth Century |publisher=Berg Publishers |date=1997 |page=66 |isbn=978-1-85973-194-9}}</ref> According to historian Donal Fallon, "as the 1930s progressed, 'Poppy Day' lost much of its violent edge in Dublin, but the wearing of the symbol also became less commonplace in subsequent decades".<ref>{{cite web |first=Donal |last=Fallon |url=http://comeheretome.com/2015/11/04/poppy-snatching-in-dublin/ |title=Poppy-snatching in Dublin |work=Come Here to Me |date=4 November 2015}}</ref>

In 2017, [[Leo Varadkar]] was the first [[Taoiseach]] to wear a "shamrock poppy" in the [[Dáil]].<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/world-europe-41910166|title=Irish PM wears 'shamrock poppy'|date=8 November 2017|work=BBC News|access-date=8 November 2017}}</ref>

==== Palestine ====
According to [[Nasser Abufarha]], the poppy flower been used in popular Palestinian representations to symbolize the blood in the land of the ''[[Palestinian fedayeen|Fida'i]]'', the "heroic warrior sacrificer"; the ''[[Martyrdom in Palestinian society|Shahid]]'', the "victim youth sacrificer"; or the ''[[Palestinian suicide attacks|Istishhadi]]'', "moving the ''Shahid'' from victim to hero and asserting the intentionality of the sacrifice."<ref name=":2">{{Cite journal|doi=10.1080/10702890802073274|issn=1070-289X|volume=15|issue=3|pages=343–368|last=Abufarha|first=Nasser|title=Land of Symbols: Cactus, Poppies, Orange and Olive Trees in Palestine|journal=Identities|access-date=2024-01-25|date=2008-05-30|url=https://doi.org/10.1080/10702890802073274|url-access=subscription}}</ref> Abufarha describes these figures as icons of the "three distinct periods in the contemporary [[Palestinian political violence|Palestinian resistance]] to Israeli occupation and rule," referring to the [[guerrilla warfare]] of the [[Palestinian fedayeen]] in the 1960s and 70s, the [[First Intifada]] (1987–93), and the [[Second Intifada]] (2000–05)—the blood and sacrifice of all of whom Palestinians have represented with the poppy.<ref name=":2" />

In popular Palestinian narrative dating back to [[Canaan|Canaanite]] and [[Phoenicia|Phoenician]] times, the red color of flower's petals is from the blood of martyrs in the land.<ref name=":2" /> The narrative is related to the story of the [[Greek mythology|Greek mythological]] figure [[Adonis]], a boy representing the [[Masculine beauty ideal|ideal of male beauty]] who was killed by a [[wild boar]] in the forests of Lebanon and whose blood nourished the land from which the red anemone grew.<ref name=":2" /> Abufarha notes that the flower thus came to represent "renewal, resurrection, and life."<ref name=":2" />  It has appeared in Palestinian [[protest art]], especially as a symbol of [[Martyrdom in Palestinian society|sacrifice]] or [[Palestinian right of return|return]].<ref name=":1">{{Cite journal |last=Abufarha|first=Nasser|date=2008-05-30|title=LAND OF SYMBOLS: CACTUS, POPPIES, ORANGE AND OLIVE TREES IN PALESTINE|url=http://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1080/10702890802073274|journal=Identities|language=en|volume=15|issue=3|pages=343–368|doi=10.1080/10702890802073274|issn=1070-289X}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Maira|first=Sunaina|date=2021|title=Two Red Poppies, Possibly More|url=https://escholarship.org/uc/item/3hj65144|journal=Journal of Visual Culture|language=en|volume=20|issue=2|pages=386–389|issn=1470-4129}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last=Arafat|first=Zaina|last2=Eid|first2=Kholood|date=2024-05-14|title=The View from Palestinian America|url=https://www.newyorker.com/culture/photo-booth/the-view-from-palestinian-america|access-date=2026-03-26|work=The New Yorker|language=en-US|issn=0028-792X}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last=Iscoe|first=Adam|date=2023-12-04|title=Among the Protesters|url=https://www.newyorker.com/magazine/2023/12/11/among-the-protesters|access-date=2026-03-26|work=The New Yorker|language=en-US|issn=0028-792X}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2023-12-15|title=Artists Display 20,000 Poppies Outside NY Stock Exchange|url=https://hyperallergic.com/artists-display-poppies-outside-new-york-stock-exchange/|access-date=2026-03-26|website=Hyperallergic|language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Homage to Ghassan Kanafani {{!}} Dalloul Art Foundation|url=https://dafbeirut.org/collection/samia-halaby/homage-ghassan-kanafani|access-date=2026-03-26|website=dafbeirut.org}}</ref>

====South Korea====
Remembrance poppies are usually used for the [[Remembrance Day]] ceremony at [[United Nations Memorial Cemetery]] in [[Busan]] to honour [[Korean War]] veterans from [[South Korea|Korea]] and [[United Nations Command|UN Force]] members. Wearing poppies was introduced by Vincent Courtenay, a Canadian veteran of the conflict.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.koreaherald.com/view.php?ud=20211110000158|title=S. Korea to honor fallen UN Korean War veterans in 'Turn toward Busan' event|date=10 November 2021|author=Yonhap|website=www.koreaherald.com|publisher=Herald Corporation|access-date=18 November 2022}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.koreatimes.co.kr/www/nation/2022/11/281_339670.html|title='Turn Toward Busan' remembers Korean War veterans|website=[[The Korea Times]]|publisher=The Korea Times|access-date=18 November 2022|date=11 November 2022|last=Dong-hwan|first=Ko}}</ref>

====Ukraine====
[[File:Ніколи Знову 02.svg|thumb|Never Again symbol from [[Ukraine]]]]
Since 2014, Ukrainians have worn the poppy as a symbol of the [[Victory Day over Nazism in World War II|victory over Nazism]] and commemoration of the victims of World War II. It has largely replaced the [[Ribbon of Saint George]], which became associated with [[2014 pro-Russian unrest in Ukraine|pro-Russian separatists]] and Russian military aggression. A poppy logo was designed by Serhiy Mishakin and contains the text "1939–1945 Never Again".<ref>{{cite web |first=Andrew |last=Foxall |url=https://www.forbes.com/sites/realspin/2014/05/14/poppies-vs-ribbons-the-war-of-symbols-between-ukraine-and-russia/ |title=Poppies vs. Ribbons: The War of Symbols Between Ukraine and Russia |work=[[Forbes]] |date=14 May 2014}}</ref>

====United States====
[[File:Photograph of Poppy Presentation to President Harry S. Truman.jpg|thumb|A remembrance poppy being presented to U.S. President [[Harry S. Truman]] from the president of the [[American Legion Auxiliary]].]]

In the United States, the [[Veterans of Foreign Wars]] conducted the first nationwide distribution of remembrance poppies before [[Memorial Day]] in 1922.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.vfw.org/Community/Buddy-Poppy/|title=Buddy Poppy |publisher=Veterans of Foreign Wars|access-date=20 May 2016}}</ref> The poppy was named the official flower of the [[American Legion]] 27 September 1920,<!-- https://www.legion.org/honor/261738/national-poppy-day-friday --> although the legion only began their own national distribution program of remembrance poppies in 1924.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.legion-aux.org/poppy|title=ALA Poppy Program}}</ref> The [[American Legion Auxiliary]] distributes<!-- https://www.legion.org/sites/legion.org/files/legion/documents/2022-Poppy-Day-Toolkit.pdf --> crepe-paper poppies and then requests a donation, around Memorial Day and [[Veterans Day]] (''National Poppy Day'', the Friday before Memorial Day<!-- https://www.legion-aux.org/national-poppy-day -->).<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.legion-aux.org/Programs/Poppy/|title=Poppy|publisher=American Legion Auxiliary|access-date=20 May 2016|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130221092320/http://www.legion-aux.org/Programs/Poppy/|archive-date=21 February 2013}}</ref><ref name="legion.org">{{cite web|url=http://www.legion.org/troops/216371/legion-family-flower-remembrance|title=Legion Family flower of remembrance|work=The American Legion|access-date=20 May 2016}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |publisher=United States Department of Veterans Affairs |url=http://www1.va.gov/opa/vetsday/vetday_faq.asp |title=Veterans Day Frequently Asked Questions |date=10 November 2009 |access-date=23 February 2011 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110228162109/http://www1.va.gov/opa/vetsday/vetday_faq.asp |archive-date=28 February 2011 }}</ref>

Use of remembrance poppies in the U.S. has diminished since their introduction in the 1920s, although remembrance poppies are sometimes worn on [[Memorial Day]]. On [[Veterans Day]], a red, white, and blue ribbon was a more common lapel adornment by the early 2010s.<ref name=wherebbc/>

==Cultural adoption of the symbol==
[[File:Connor Joe (47946316383) (cropped).jpg|thumb|An [[Oklahoma City Dodgers]] baseball player with a remembrance poppy shoulder patch on his uniform in commemoration of [[Memorial Day]]]]
To commemorate Remembrance Day, several professional sports leagues have emblazoned the remembrance poppy symbol onto their uniforms. Many British professional football clubs create special edition kits with the remembrance poppy featured on their shirts.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.cnn.com/2022/11/11/football/james-mcclean-ireland-poppy-remembrance-day-spt-intl/index.html|title=Remembrance Sunday: For one dissenting voice, this is his most dangerous day|date=11 November 2022|access-date=4 February 2023|website=www.cnn.com|publisher=Cable News Company|last=Howorth|first=Alasdair}}</ref> Canadian professional and junior ice hockey teams wear remembrance poppy sticker emblems on their helmets.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://waxers.com/Articles/7406/Peewee_AE_White_Honour_Canadian_Service_Members/|title=Peewee AE White Honour Canadian Service Members|access-date=4 February 2023|website=waxers.com|publisher=Markham Waxers Hockey}}</ref> Remembrance poppy patches are also worn by American [[Major League Baseball|Major League]] and [[Minor League Baseball]] teams, although these are worn to commemorate Memorial Day in May, as opposed to Remembrance Day.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.mlb.com/news/mlb-memorial-day-2022-fact-sheet|website=www.mlb.com|date=30 May 2022|access-date=4 February 2023|title=MLB observing moment of remembrance on Memorial Day|publisher=MLB Advanced Media}}</ref>

In 2007, [[Air Canada]] emblazoned 20 of its jets with the remembrance poppy symbol in partnership with the Royal Canadian Legion.<ref name=aircan>{{cite web|url=https://nationalpost.com/news/canada/air-canada-bans-flight-crews-from-wearing-poppies-then-immediately-regrets-the-decision|website=nationalpost.com|date=7 November 2016|access-date=4 February 2023|title=Air Canada bans flight crews from wearing poppies, then immediately regrets the decision|publisher=Postmedia Network}}</ref>

==Controversy and protest==
===In Canada===
In November 2016, Air Canada released an internal memo that "strongly encouraged" its staff not to wear poppies while in uniform. After several hours of employee and union pushback, a second memo was distributed, reversing the earlier position and stating that the "wearing of poppies is supported" by the company.<ref name=aircan/>

In November 2019, [[Don Cherry]], a prominent ice hockey pundit known for his appearances on ''[[Hockey Night in Canada]]'', made a controversial complaint on-air that he rarely saw people he believed were new immigrants to Toronto wearing a remembrance poppy. His remarks caused widespread condemnation from the ice hockey community, and several complaints were filed against him through the [[Canadian Broadcast Standards Council]]. Cherry was later fired by [[Sportsnet]] for his comments.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.bbc.com/news/world-us-canada-50241256|title=Don Cherry: Canadian hockey pundit fired for poppy rant|website=www.bbc.com|publisher=British Broadcasting Corporation|date=11 November 2019|access-date=4 February 2023}}</ref>

In November 2020, U.S.-based grocer [[Whole Foods Market]] briefly banned its employees from wearing remembrance poppies at its 14 Canadian locations, as they did not conform to the company's updated uniform policy of not wearing symbols that were "supporting a cause". Whole Foods reversed its decision on the poppy several days later after receiving complaints from Prime Minister [[Justin Trudeau]], veteran affairs minister [[Lawrence MacAulay]], Ontario Premier [[Doug Ford]], and several Royal Canadian Legion branches.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/ottawa/whole-foods-poppies-allowed-1.5793069|title=Whole Foods backs down on banning poppies at Work|date=6 November 2020|access-date=4 February 2023|website=www.cbc.ca|last=Hwang|first=Priscilla Ki Sun|publisher=Canadian Broadcasting Corporation}}</ref>

===In the United Kingdom===
In 1993, The Royal British Legion complained that ''[[Cannon Fodder (video game)|Cannon Fodder]]'', a video game with an anti-war message, had planned to use a poppy on its cover. The Legion, along with some politicians, called it "offensive to millions" and "monstrous".<ref name="star">Jonathan Guy, ''[[Daily Star (United Kingdom)|Daily Star]]'', 26 Oct, 1993</ref> The cover was changed before the game was released.<ref name="rockpaper">{{citation|author1-last=Gillen|author1-first=Kieron|author1-link=Kieron Gillen|title=Retrospective: Cannon Fodder|work=[[Rock, Paper, Shotgun]]|date=2007-11-11|access-date=2011-12-03|url=http://www.rockpapershotgun.com/2007/11/11/retrospective-cannon-fodder/|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090506001741/http://www.rockpapershotgun.com/2007/11/11/retrospective-cannon-fodder/|archive-date=2009-05-06}}</ref>

[[File:Jon Snow, June 2007.jpg|thumb|[[Jon Snow (journalist)|Jon Snow]] in 2007. The [[Channel 4]] newsreader caused controversy in 2006 after he described the pressure to wear a remembrance poppy as "poppy fascism".]]

Within the United Kingdom, there has been growing controversy over the Poppy Appeal. Some—including a few British Army veterans—have argued that the Poppy Appeal has become excessive, that it has been used to marshal support for British military activities, and that poppy wearing has become seen as compulsory for public figures.<ref name=poppyveterans>{{cite news |url=https://www.theguardian.com/uk/2010/nov/05/poppy-appeal-subverted-veterans-complain |title=Poppy appeal's original aims being subverted, veterans complain |last=Bates |first=Stephen |work=[[The Guardian]] |date=5 November 2010}}</ref><ref name=harrysmith>{{cite news |first=Harry Leslie |last=Smith |url=https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfree/2013/nov/08/poppy-last-time-remembrance-harry-leslie-smith |title=This year, I will wear a poppy for the last time |work=The Guardian |date=8 November 2013}}</ref> In 2006, [[Channel 4]] newsreader [[Jon Snow (journalist)|Jon Snow]] described the pressure to wear a poppy as "poppy fascism".<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/uknews/1533751/I-wont-bow-to-poppy-fascists-says-Jon-Snow.html|title=I won't bow to poppy fascists, says Jon Snow|last=Pook|first=Sally|date=10 November 2006|publisher=[[Daily Telegraph]]|access-date=5 November 2009 | location=London}}</ref> Columnist Dan O'Neill wrote in 2011 that "presenters and politicians seem to compete in a race to be first – poppies start sprouting in mid-October while the absence of a poppy is interpreted as absence of concern for the war dead, almost as an unpatriotic act of treachery."<ref name=danoneill1>{{cite news |url=http://www.walesonline.co.uk/news/columnists/2011/11/09/dan-o-neill-s-outrage-as-politicians-send-more-to-war-while-they-wear-poppies-91466-29743917/ |title=Dan O'Neill's outrage as 'politicians send more to war while they wear poppies' |work=Wales Online |date=9 November 2011}}</ref> Likewise, [[Jonathan Bartley]] of the religious think-tank [[Ekklesia (think tank)|Ekklesia]] said "Public figures in Britain are urged, indeed in many cases, required, to wear ... the red poppy, almost as an article of faith. There is a [[political correctness]] about the red poppy."<ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/uknews/1533752/A-time-to-remember-but-should-we-wear-a-more-Christian-white-poppy-or-a-PC-red.html
|title=A time to remember, but should we wear a more 'Christian' white poppy or a 'PC' red?
|last=Petre|first=Jonathan|date=10 November 2006|publisher=[[Daily Telegraph]]
|access-date=11 November 2011 |location=London}}</ref> Journalist [[Robert Fisk]] complained in 2011 that the poppy had become a seasonal "fashion accessory" and that people were "ostentatiously wearing a poppy for social or work-related reasons, to look patriotic when it suited them."<ref>{{cite news |last=Fisk |first=Robert |url=https://www.independent.ie/opinion/analysis/blood-spilled-in-war-is-now-a-fashion-accessory-26789192.html |title=Blood spilled in war is now a fashion accessory |work=[[Irish Independent]] |date=5 November 2011}}</ref>

In 2010, a group of British Army veterans issued an open letter complaining that the Poppy Appeal had become excessive and garish, that it was being used to marshal support behind British military interventions, and that people were being pressured into wearing poppies.<ref name=poppyveterans/> In 2014, the same group protested by holding an alternative remembrance service: they walked to [[The Cenotaph, Whitehall|the Cenotaph]] under the banner "Never Again" with a wreath of white poppies to acknowledge civilians killed in war. Their tops bore the message "War is Organised Murder", a quote from [[Harry Patch]], one of the last surviving veterans of World War I.<ref>{{cite news |first1=Samuel |last1=Clement |first2=Joe |last2=Krishnan |url=https://www.independent.co.uk/news/uk/home-news/never-again-anti-war-veterans-to-carry-white-poppy-wreath-to-cenotaph-9833246.html |title='Never again': Anti-war veterans to carry white-poppy wreath to Cenotaph |work=[[The Independent]] |date=2 November 2014}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |first=Georgina |last=Ryall |url=http://veteransforpeace.org.uk/2014/war-weary-veterans-hold-aternative-remembrance-sunday-event/ |title=War-Weary Veterans Hold Alternative Remembrance Sunday Event |publisher=Veterans for Peace |date=11 November 2014}}</ref>

[[File:Dmitry Medvedev in South Korea 11 November 2010-3.jpeg|left|thumb|British Prime Minister [[David Cameron]] wearing a remembrance poppy in 2010.]]

[[Prime Minister of the United Kingdom|British Prime Minister]] [[David Cameron]] rejected a request from Chinese officials to remove his poppy during his visit to [[Beijing]] on Remembrance Day in 2010. The officials had deemed the poppy offensive because they assumed it to be connected with the [[Opium Wars]] of the mid-19th century.<ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.bloomberg.com/news/2010-11-09/cameron-risks-spat-with-chinese-by-wearing-poppy-during-visit-to-beijing.html|title=Cameron Risks Spat With Chinese by Wearing Poppy During Visit |date=9 November 2010 |publisher=Bloomberg LP |access-date=12 November 2011 |first=Robert |last=Hutton}}</ref>

A 2010 Remembrance Day ceremony in London was disrupted by members of the extremist [[Muslims Against Crusades]] group, who were protesting against the British military presence in [[War in Afghanistan (2001–present)|Afghanistan]] and [[Iraq War|Iraq]]. They burnt large poppies and chanted "British soldiers burn in hell" during the two-minute silence. Two of the men were arrested and charged for threatening behavior. One was convicted and fined £50.<ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/uk-england-london-12664346 |title=Man guilty of burning poppies at Armistice Day protest |work=BBC News |date=7 March 2011}}</ref> The same group planned to hold another protest in 2011, but was banned by the [[Home Secretary]] the day before the planned protest.<ref>{{cite news|last=Casciani|first=Dominic|title=Muslims Against Crusades banned by Theresa May|url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/uk-15678275|work=BBC News|access-date=11 November 2011|date=10 November 2011}}</ref> In 2014, a campaign was begun to encourage Muslim women to wear poppy [[hijab]]s. Some criticised it as a "shrouded loyalty test" implying that Muslims needed to prove their loyalty to Britain.<ref>{{cite news |last=Allen |first=Chris |url=http://www.newstatesman.com/politics/2014/11/poppy-hijab-just-islamophobia-floral-motif |title=The poppy hijab is just Islamophobia with a floral motif |work=[[New Statesman]] |date=3 November 2014}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |first=Simon |last=Hooper |url=http://www.aljazeera.com/indepth/features/2014/11/split-uk-opinion-over-poppy-hijabs-20141196523894487.html |title=Split UK opinion over 'poppy hijabs' |work=[[Al Jazeera English|Al Jazeera]] |date=9 November 2014}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |first=Atika |last=Shubert |url=https://edition.cnn.com/2014/10/31/world/europe/poppy-hijab-controversy/ |title=Poppy hijab honours Muslims, sparks controversy |work=CNN |date=1 November 2014}}</ref> Some [[Far-right politics in the United Kingdom|far-right]] groups have used the poppy as a symbol of militant [[British nationalism]], while some British Muslims have begun to reject it, seeing the poppy as a "symbol of Western imperialism".<ref name="fox"/>

In November 2011, people were arrested in Northern Ireland after a picture of two youths burning a poppy was posted on [[Facebook]]. The picture was reported to police by a member of the RBL.<ref>{{cite news| url=https://www.theguardian.com/uk/2011/nov/03/poppy-burning-northern-ireland-arrests?newsfeed=true | location=London | work=The Guardian | first=Henry | last=McDonald | title=Poppy-burning image leads to Northern Ireland arrests | date=3 November 2011}}</ref> The following year, a young [[Canterbury]] man was arrested for allegedly posting a picture of a burning poppy on Facebook, on suspicion of an offence under the [[Malicious Communications Act]].<ref>{{cite news|last=Rawlinson|first=Kevin|title='Poppycock': Man's arrest for posting image of burning poppy on Facebook is condemned by civil liberties activists|url=https://www.independent.co.uk/news/uk/crime/poppycock-mans-arrest-for-posting-image-of-burning-poppy-on-facebook-is-condemned-by-civil-liberties-activists-8306784.html|work=[[The Independent]] |access-date=4 February 2013|location=London|date=12 November 2012}}</ref>

In 2012, [[The Northern Whig]] public house in [[Belfast]] refused entry to a man wearing a remembrance poppy.<ref>{{cite news | url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/uk-northern-ireland-20208930 | title=Northern Whig bar apologises after poppy-wearer refused entry | year= 2012 | work= BBC News | access-date=12 March 2015 }}</ref> Although the owners apologised, the customer took the matter to court, supported by the [[Equality Commission for Northern Ireland]] (ECNI).<ref>{{cite web | url=http://www.equalityni.org/Footer-Links/News/Individuals/Sample-headline-text-(3) | title=Refusal of man wearing poppy | year= 2013 | publisher= Equality Commission for Northern Ireland | access-date=5 August 2017 }}</ref> The case was significant for the decision supporting the view of the ECNI that "the poppy, although not directly linked to a specific religious belief or political opinion, would historically have been associated to a greater extent with the Protestant or unionist community in Northern Ireland".<ref>{{cite news | url=http://www.irishnews.com/news/2013/11/27/news/poppy-refusal-discrimination-76888/ | title=Poppy refusal discrimination | date= 27 November 2013 | work= The Irish News | access-date=5 August 2017 }}</ref>

In 2018, ''[[The Independent]]'' reported that both the Royal British Legion and Lady Haig's Poppy Factory had, since 2015, held contracts with One3One Solutions, the commercial arm of the [[Ministry of Justice (United Kingdom)|Ministry of Justice]], for prisoners at [[HM Prison Ford]] to manufacture the plastic central button and green stem of the poppies, for which they earned on average £10 a week. The RBL also confirmed that it had a contract with [[HM Prison Whitemoor]] for the refurbishment by inmates of its collecting tins, buckets, trays and boxes.<ref name="Independent 2018">{{cite web |last=Wyatt |first=Tim |url=https://www.independent.co.uk/news/uk/home-news/royal-british-legion-poppy-appeal-prisoners-prison-hmp-ford-war-want-remembrance-day-a8617146.html?amp |title=Royal British Legion criticised for using prisoners earning £10 a week to make poppies |website=theindependent.co.uk |publisher=[[The Independent]] |date=4 November 2018 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://archive.today/20211103194810/https://www.independent.co.uk/news/uk/home-news/royal-british-legion-poppy-appeal-prisoners-prison-hmp-ford-war-want-remembrance-day-a8617146.html?amp |archive-date=3 November 2021}}</ref> The executive director of the charity [[War on Want]] described the use of inmate labour in the production poppies as the "exploitation of cheap labour",<ref name="Independent 2018"/> and Faith Spear, former member of the [[Independent Monitoring Board]] at Hollesey Bay prison, describing the repetitive and unskilled manual labour typically involved in prison labour as "mind numbing" and "akin to mental torture".<ref name="Corporate Watch">{{cite web |author=<!--Staff writers - no by-line--> |url=https://corporatewatch.org/poppies-prison-labour-and-the-war-machine/ |title=POPPIES, PRISON LABOUR AND THE WAR MACHINE |website=corporatewatch.org |publisher=[[Corporate Watch]] |date=1 November 2018 |access-date=4 November 2021 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://archive.today/20211104110152/https://corporatewatch.org/poppies-prison-labour-and-the-war-machine/ |archive-date=4 November 2021}}</ref>

====In media====
In the British media, public figures have been attacked for not wearing poppies. British journalist and newsreader [[Charlene White]] has faced racist and sexist abuse for not wearing a poppy on-screen. She explained "I prefer to be neutral and impartial on screen so that one of those charities doesn't feel less favoured than another".<ref>{{cite news |first=Shane |last=Hickey |url=https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2013/nov/13/charlene-white-itv-news-presenter-remembrance-day-poppy |title=ITV news presenter hits back after abuse for not wearing poppy |work=[[The Guardian]] |date=13 November 2013}}</ref> Newsreader Jon Snow does not wear a poppy on-screen for similar reasons. He too was criticised and he condemned what he saw as "poppy fascism".<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.standard.co.uk/news/newsreader-jon-snow-rails-against-poppy-fascism-7263001.html|title=Newsreader Jon Snow rails against 'poppy fascism'|date=9 November 2006|work=Evening Standard|access-date=20 May 2016}}</ref> Well-known war-time journalist Robert Fisk published in November 2011 a personal account about the shifting nature of wearing a poppy, titled "Do those who flaunt the poppy on their lapels know that they mock the war dead?".<ref>{{cite news |first=Robert |last=Fisk |url=https://www.independent.co.uk/voices/commentators/fisk/robert-fisk-do-those-who-flaunt-the-poppy-on-their-lapels-know-that-they-mock-the-war-dead-6257416.html |title=Do those who flaunt the poppy on their lapels know that they mock the war dead? |work=[[The Independent]] |date=5 November 2011 |access-date=4 November 2014}}</ref> While all newsreaders in the UK are expected to wear the remembrance poppy, those on the [[BBC World News]] service are told not to. The BBC say this is because the symbol is not widely recognised overseas. The Royal British Legion condemned this, insisting that the poppy is the "international symbol of remembrance".<ref>{{cite news |url=http://www.scotsman.com/news/uk/mp-s-fury-at-bbc-ban-on-poppies-1-584905 |title=MP's fury at BBC ban on poppies |work=[[The Scotsman]] |date=3 November 2001 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160508105857/http://www.scotsman.com/news/uk/mp-s-fury-at-bbc-ban-on-poppies-1-584905 |archive-date=2016-05-08}}</ref>

In a November 2020 episode of ''[[Jeremy Vine (TV programme)|Jeremy Vine]]'', activist [[Femi Oluwole]] questioned why BBC presenters were still permitted to wear poppies, following new impartiality guidance warning against "[[virtue signalling]], no matter how worthy the cause", which had previously prevented staff from expressing support for [[Black Lives Matter#United Kingdom|Black Lives Matter]] and [[LGBT rights in the United Kingdom|LGBT rights]].<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.pinknews.co.uk/2020/11/03/femi-oluwole-poppy-lgbt-pride-black-lives-matter-bbc-jeremy-vine/|title=Political activist Femi Oluwole questions why BBC presenters can wear poppies if they can't support Black or gay rights|last=Milton|first=Josh|date=3 November 2020|work=[[PinkNews]]|access-date=4 November 2020}}</ref>

====In sport====
In the run-up to Remembrance Day, it has become common for UK [[Association football|football]] teams to play with artificial poppies sewn to their shirts, at the request of the Royal British Legion. This has caused some controversy.
[[File:Celtic team - November 2010.jpg|thumb|right|Football clubs commonly wear jerseys with a poppy emblazoned on, as [[Celtic F.C.|Celtic]] controversially did in 2010.]]
At a [[Celtic F.C.|Celtic]] v [[Aberdeen F.C.|Aberdeen]] match in November 2010, a group of Celtic supporters, called the [[Green Brigade]], unfurled a large banner in protest at the team wearing poppies. In a statement, it said: "Our group and many within the Celtic support do not recognise the British Armed Forces as heroes, nor their role in many conflicts as one worthy of our remembrance". It gave [[Operation Banner]] (Northern Ireland), the [[War in Afghanistan (2001–present)|Afghanistan War]] and the [[Iraq War]] as examples.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.etims.net/index.php?option=com_content&task=view&id=3038&Itemid=29 |title=Green Brigade Statement on the Poppy Protest |date=9 November 2010 |work=ETims Online Celtic Fanzine |access-date=5 January 2011 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20101112085000/http://www.etims.net/index.php?option=com_content&task=view&id=3038&Itemid=29 |archive-date=2010-11-12}}</ref>

Irish footballer [[James McClean]], who has played for several English teams, has received [[death threat]]s and abuse since 2012 for refusing to wear a poppy on his shirt during matches.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.theguardian.com/football/2012/nov/18/sunderland-james-mcclean-death-threat|title=Sunderland's James McClean receives death threat over poppy protest|first=Dominic|last=Fifield|date=18 November 2012|work=[[The Guardian]]|access-date=28 October 2018}}</ref> McClean said he does not wear one because the Poppy Appeal supports British soldiers who served in Northern Ireland, and he believes it would disrespect those killed in his hometown, [[Derry]], on Bloody Sunday.<ref>{{cite news |first=Claire |last=Williamson |url=http://www.belfasttelegraph.co.uk/news/local-national/northern-ireland/wigan-player-james-mcclean-explains-why-he-will-not-wear-a-poppy-30730556.html |title=Wigan player James McClean explains why he will not wear a poppy |work=[[Belfast Telegraph]] |date=10 November 2014}}</ref>

In November 2011, it was proposed that the [[England national football team|England football team]] should wear poppies on their shirts in a match against [[Spain national football team|Spain]]. [[FIFA]] turned down the proposal; their decision was criticised by [[Prince William, Duke of Cambridge|Prince William]].<ref name=guardian-fifa-2011>{{cite news |url=https://www.theguardian.com/football/2011/nov/09/david-cameron-outrageous-poppy-ban?newsfeed=true |title=Prince William calls on FIFA to overturn ban on England shirt poppies |work=[[The Guardian]] |date=9 November 2011}}</ref> FIFA subsequently allowed the English, Scottish and Welsh teams to wear poppies on black armbands.<ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.bbc.com/sport/football/15666769 |title=FIFA allows England, Scotland and Wales to wear poppy |work=[[BBC News]] |date=9 November 2011 |access-date=12 November 2011}}</ref>

On 11 November 2017, the third day of the test cricket  match held at [[North Sydney Oval]] as part of the [[English women's cricket team in Australia in 2017–18|Women's Ashes]], the Australia and England players wore poppies to mark 99 years since the end of World War I.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Collins |first1=Adam |last2=Ehantharajah |first2=Vithushan |title=Ellyse Perry scores 213 for Australia on day three of Women's Ashes Test match – as it happened |url=https://www.theguardian.com/sport/live/2017/nov/11/australia-v-england-womens-ashes-test-match-day-three-live?page=with:block-5a067dfb437a7d06e9058660 |access-date=11 November 2018 |work=[[The Guardian]] |date=11 November 2017}}</ref>

During the [[2018 FIFA World Cup qualification|2018 FIFA World Cup Qualifiers]], the England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland football teams were fined for displaying the poppy during matches. FIFA rules forbid the display of "political or religious symbols".<ref name="IndependentDec2016">{{cite news|last1=de Menezes|first1=Jack|title=England just got fined £35,000 for defying Fifa's poppy ban|url=https://www.independent.co.uk/sport/football/international/fifa-poppy-ban-england-fine-35000-scotland-a7484296.html|access-date=26 July 2017|work=The Independent|date=19 December 2016}}</ref><ref name="Independent23Nov2016">{{cite news|last1=de Menezes|first1=Jack|title=Fifa take action against Wales because 'fans were wearing poppies'|url=https://www.independent.co.uk/sport/football/international/fifa-poppy-ban-northern-ireland-wales-england-scotland-poppies-a7433511.html|access-date=26 July 2017|work=The Independent|date=23 November 2016}}</ref><ref name="Telegraph19Dec2016">{{cite news|last1=Law|first1=Matt|title=FA could take Fifa to Court of Arbitration for Sport over £35,000 fine for poppy use|url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/football/2016/12/19/fifa-fine-football-associations-england-scotland-northern-ireland/|access-date=26 July 2017|work=The Telegraph|date=19 December 2016}}</ref> The decision was strongly criticised by prime minister Theresa May, and the Welsh and English football associations appealed against the fine, with the English Football Association threatening to bring the matter to the [[Court of Arbitration for Sport]].<ref name="Telegraph19Dec2016" /><ref name="EurosportNov2016">{{cite news|title=England and Scotland to defy FIFA poppy ban|url=http://www.eurosport.com/football/world-cup-qualification-caf/2018/england-and-scotland-to-defy-fifa-poppy-ban_sto5937190/story.shtml|access-date=26 July 2017|work=Eurosport|date=2 November 2016}}</ref><ref name="WalesOnline">{{cite news|last1=Abbandonato|first1=Paul|title=Wales appeal against FIFA fine over poppies|url=http://www.walesonline.co.uk/sport/football/wales-launch-appeal-over-fifas-12585392|access-date=26 July 2017|work=Wales Online|date=10 February 2017}}</ref>

In November 2018, Manchester United's Serbian midfielder [[Nemanja Matić]] refused to wear a poppy on his shirt for a match against Bournemouth.<ref name="bbc.com">{{cite web |url=https://www.bbc.com/sport/football/46099843 |title=Nemanja Matic: Man Utd midfielder explains why he will not wear poppy |date=5 November 2018 |publisher=BBC |access-date=5 November 2018}}</ref> After the match, Matić was castigated and received threats from a number of people via social media.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.thetimes.com/article/memory-of-bombing-raid-is-why-ive-stopped-wearing-poppy-says-matic-zqch809b3 |title=Memory of bombing raid is why I've stopped wearing poppy |date=5 November 2018 |work=[[The Times]] |access-date=5 November 2018}}</ref> Matić stated that he would not wear a poppy because his village of [[Vrelo (Ub)|Vrelo]] was hit by the [[NATO bombing of Yugoslavia]] in 1999.<ref name="bbc.com"/>

==Other commemorative poppies==
===White poppies===
{{more|White poppy}}
[[File:Anzac poppies.JPG|thumb|A white remembrance poppy left on [[Anzac Day]] in New Zealand, 2009]]
Some people choose to wear white poppies as an alternative to the red poppy. The white poppy and white poppy wreaths were introduced by Britain's [[Co-operative Women's Guild]] in 1933.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.ppu.org.uk/whitepoppy/white_cwg.html |title=White Poppies for a Culture of Peace |publisher=[[Peace Pledge Union]] |access-date=23 February 2011 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171201031843/https://www.ppu.org.uk/whitepoppy/white_cwg.html |archive-date=2017-12-01}}</ref> Today, white poppies are sold by [[Peace Pledge Union]] or may be home-made.<ref name="ppu"/>
The white poppy is worn alone or alongside the red poppy. According to the Peace Pledge Union, it symbolises remembrance of all casualties of war, including civilian and non-British casualties, to stand for peace, and not to glamorise war.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.ppu.org.uk/remembrance-white-poppies |title=Remembrance & White Poppies |date=30 July 2018 |publisher=[[Peace Pledge Union]] |access-date=28 October 2018}}</ref> Some women in the 1930s lost their jobs for wearing white poppies, with some veterans having felt that the white poppy undermined their contribution and the lasting meaning of the red poppy.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/remembrance/how/poppy.shtml|title=Why the Poppy?|work=1918–2008: Ninety Years of Remembrance |publisher=BBC |access-date=28 October 2018}}</ref> The Royal British Legion has stated it has no objection to the white poppy being worn alongside the red poppy.<ref>{{Cite news |date=2015-11-09 |title=Five reasons people don't wear poppies |language=en-GB |work=BBC News |url=https://www.bbc.com/news/magazine-34720464 |access-date=2022-11-06}}</ref>

=== Black poppies ===
On Remembrance Sunday 1999, a [[Merseyside]] group protesting against sanctions and war on Iraq laid a wreath of black poppies on the cenotaph in Liverpool.<ref>{{cite news |title=Military veterans refuse mayor's salute |work=[[Morning Star (British newspaper)|Morning Star]] |date=15 November 1999}}</ref> In 2014 the black poppy was embraced as an anti-war symbol by the [[Stop the War Coalition]] which reported 'anti militarists' in Glasgow distributing 16,000 black poppies in memory of World War I conscientious objectors.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.stopwar.org.uk/article/why-no-remembrance-day-black-poppies-for-16-000-first-world-war-refusers/|title=Why No Remembrance Day black poppies For 16,000 First World War Refusers|website=[[Stop the War Coalition]]|access-date=6 November 2018}}</ref>

In 2010, a different initiative proposed the use of a "Black Poppy Rose" that was "created to be a symbol that represents the contributions made by the African/Black/West Indian/Caribbean/Pacific Islands & Indigenous communities to various wars since the 16th century".<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.blackpoppyrose.org/about-us/|title=About Us - BlackPoppyRose|access-date=11 November 2023}}</ref> The symbol was worn in 2023 around the time of Remembrance Day by [[King Charles III]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/uk-67356103|title=King Charles finds his Seoul food in the suburbs|access-date=11 November 2023}}</ref>

=== Khadi poppies ===
Introduced in the 2018 centenary year by [[Jitesh Gadhia]] and the Royal British Legion, the [[khadi]] poppy is intended to represent specific gratitude for the contribution of 1.5 million people from undivided India, as well as [[Commonwealth of Nations|Commonwealth]] nations more generally, to the [[First World War]]. These poppies are identical to the Legion red poppy except the petals are made of khadi, a spun cotton cloth popularised by [[Mahatma Gandhi]] on his spinning wheel.<ref name="'Khadi' poppy marks India's WW1 servicemen">{{cite news |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/av/world-46113115 |title='Khadi' poppy marks India's WW1 servicemen | date=7 November 2018 | work=BBC News |access-date=9 February 2020}}</ref> Jitesh Gadhia has stated that "the khadi poppy is a hugely symbolic and highly appropriate gesture to recognise the outsized contribution of Indian soldiers during WWI."<ref>{{cite web|last=ABPL|title=Lord Gadhia joins Royal British Legion to unveil "Khadi" Poppy during India-...|url=https://www.asian-voice.com/Community/Lord-Gadhia-joins-Royal-British-Legion-to-unveil-%E2%80%9CKhadi%E2%80%9D-Poppy-during-India|access-date=2020-11-16|website=www.asian-voice.com|language=en-GB}}</ref> It has been worn by British Prime Minister [[Theresa May]], and by cricketers [[Joe Root]] and [[Virat Kohli]] before a test match between England and India in September 2018.<ref>{{cite news |first=Adam |last=Smith |title=Theresa May promises to wear a cotton khadi poppy to honour Indian WWI heroes |url=https://metro.co.uk/2018/11/01/theresa-may-promises-to-wear-a-cotton-khadi-poppy-to-honour-indian-wwi-heroes-8096378/ |work=[[Metro (British newspaper)|Metro]] |date=2018-11-01 |access-date=20 December 2018}}</ref><ref name="India, England cricket teams unite to unveil Khadi poppy">{{cite news |url=https://timesofindia.indiatimes.com/sports/cricket/india-in-england/india-england-cricket-teams-unite-to-unveil-khadi-poppy-in-uk/articleshow/65734568.cms | title=India, England cricket teams unite to unveil Khadi poppy in UK | date=8 September 2018 | agency=PTI | newspaper=The Times of India |access-date=9 February 2020}}</ref>

=== Purple poppies ===
{{more|Purple poppy}}
[[File:Purple Wreath at the Cenotaph, London in 2018.jpg|thumb|A wreath made of [[purple poppy|purple poppies]] laid at [[The Cenotaph, Whitehall|the Cenotaph]] in London]]
To commemorate animal victims of war, [[Animal Aid]] in Britain has issued a [[purple poppy|purple remembrance poppy]], which can be worn alongside the traditional red one, as a reminder that both humans and animals have been – and continue to be – victims of war.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.animalaid.org.uk/h/n/CAMPAIGNS/living//2256/|title=Purple Poppy: Commemorating the Animal Victims of War |publisher=[[Animal Aid]] |access-date=31 October 2012|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130121070658/http://www.animalaid.org.uk/h/n/CAMPAIGNS/living//2256//|archive-date=21 January 2013}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|url=https://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/8333733.stm|title= The dos and don'ts of poppy etiquette |work=BBC News |access-date=28 October 2013|date=30 October 2009}}</ref> The purple poppy was replaced by a purple paw symbol that can be worn all year round. This was because people saw the poppy as implying animals had given their lives as heroes in the service of human beings, whereas Animal Aid regards animals as having their lives taken by the abuse of humans in war.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.animalaid.org.uk/the-issues/our-campaigns/living-without-cruelty/the-purple-poppy/|title=The Purple Poppy|publisher=Animal Aid|access-date=5 May 2017}}</ref>

=== Rainbow poppies ===
In 2019, a listing appeared on [[eBay]] in the [[United Kingdom]] selling [[Rainbow flag (LGBT)|LGBT rainbow]] poppies. The Royal British Legion stated that the rainbow poppy was not endorsed by them. While the eBay listing stated that the money raised by sales of the rainbow poppy would "go towards helping charity", it was not clear which charities would benefit from sales.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://metro.co.uk/2019/11/07/war-heros-anger-lgbt-rainbow-poppy-isnt-actually-poppy-11055899/|title=War hero's anger at LGBT rainbow poppy that isn't actually a poppy|last=Roberts|first=Joe|date=7 November 2019|work=[[Metro (British newspaper)|Metro]]|access-date=8 November 2019}}</ref> This led to widespread criticism online, with some accusing the seller of "hijacking" the poppy appeal. Supporters of the poppy responded by [[Twitter|tweeting]] examples of famous [[LGBTQ]] people who had played a significant role in conflicts, such as [[Alan Turing]].<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.pinknews.co.uk/2019/11/07/rainbow-poppy-brexit-party-backlash-nicholas-goulding-twitter-remembrance-day/|title=To the surprise of absolutely nobody, the Brexit Party is kicking off about the 'rainbow poppy'|last=Milton|first=Josh|date=7 November 2019|work=[[PinkNews]]|access-date=8 November 2019}}</ref> The listing was removed by the original user, due to negative feedback.<ref name="Coventry Telegraph">{{cite news|url=https://www.coventrytelegraph.net/news/coventry-news/lgbt-rainbow-poppy-17210285|title=Rainbow Poppies: The truth behind the online controversy|last=de Souza|first=Naomi|date=8 November 2019|work=[[Coventry Telegraph]]|access-date=8 November 2019}}</ref>

title: Return of the Mayflower
wikitext:
{{Short description|1918 painting by Bernard F. Gribble}} {{Infobox artwork | image_file=Return of the Mayflower painting.jpg | image_upright = | title=Return of the Mayflower | artist=[[Bernard F. Gribble]] | year=1919 | type=[[oil painting|oil on canvas]] | height_metric= | width_metric= | height_imperial=60 | width_imperial=84 | museum=[[U.S. Naval Academy Museum]] {{small|(original)}}
[[Home of Franklin D. Roosevelt National Historic Site]] {{small|(second original)}} | city= }} '''''Return of the Mayflower''''', also known as '''''"We Are Ready Now" Return of the Mayflower''''', is a 1919 [[oil painting|oil on canvas painting]] by British artist [[Bernard F. Gribble]]. The painting portrays [[United States Navy]] [[destroyer]]s that had been sent to assist [[Great Britain]] during [[World War I]] approaching Ireland's [[Cobh|Queenstown]] on 4 May 1917. The name of the work is a reference to [[Mayflower|the ship that transported the Pilgrims]] from England to the New World in 1620. ==Historic context== [[File:Lot-7882-9 (28528279712).jpg|thumb|Photograph of US destroyers arriving at Queenstown, Ireland on May 4, 1917]] During [[World War I]], the [[Imperial German Navy]] adopted a strategy of [[unrestricted submarine warfare]], using [[U-boat]]s to cut Britain off from maritime imports in an effort to starve the country into defeat.{{cite journal |last1=Steffen |first1=Dirk |title=The Holtzendorff Memorandum of 22 December 1916 and Germany's Declaration of Unrestricted U-boat Warfare |journal=The Journal of Military History |date=2004 |volume=68 |issue=1 |pages=215–224 |id={{Project MUSE|50680}} |doi=10.1353/jmh.2003.0412 |s2cid=159765016 }}See [http://www.gwpda.org/naval/holtzendorffmemo.htm The Holtzendorff Memo (English translation) with notes] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20050309235031/http://www.gwpda.org/naval/holtzendorffmemo.htm |date=March 9, 2005}} On 6 April 1917, the United States joined the war against Germany.{{Cite web |title=Milestones in the History of U.S. Foreign Relations |url=https://history.state.gov/milestones/1914-1920/wwi |access-date=August 10, 2025 |publisher=[[Office of the Historian]]}} Four days later, Britain's [[First Sea Lord]] [[John Jellicoe]], believing that German U-boat attacks were close to defeating Britain, appealed to US [[Rear admiral (United States)|Rear Admiral]] [[William S. Sims]], who sent a message to [[Washington, D.C.|Washington]] four days later requesting [[destroyer]]s to aid the [[Royal Navy]]. Three weeks later, a [[flotilla]] of six destroyers arrived from the United States to British waters.{{cite web |title=Return of the Mayflower Returns to the Home of FDR |first=Frank |last=Futral |date=May 31, 2017 |publisher=[[National Park Service]] |url=https://www.nps.gov/hofr/blogs/return-of-the-mayflower-returns-to-the-home-of-fdr.htm}}{{cite web |title="The Return of the Mayflower" – Arrival of Destroyers at Queenstown |publisher=[[US Navy]] |date=May 2017 |first1=Dr. Dennis |last1=Conrad |first2=S. Matthew |last2=Cheser |url=https://www.history.navy.mil/browse-by-topic/wars-conflicts-and-operations/world-war-i/history/destroyers.html |work=Naval History and Heritage Command}} ==About the painting== The original ''Return of the Mayflower'' was a {{convert|5|x|7|ft|m|adj=on}} [[oil painting|oil on canvas]] painting painted in 1919,{{cite news |title=Paintings fit for a president |newspaper=[[Dorset Echo]] |url=https://www.dorsetecho.co.uk/news/5404523.paintings-fit-for-a-president/ |date=January 20, 2001}} while a smaller version was later painted for [[Franklin Delano Roosevelt]]'s personal collection at his request. Both paintings depict the 4 May 1917 arrival of the first [[United States Navy]] destroyers ({{USS|Wadsworth|DD-60|6}}, {{USS|Porter|DD-59|2}}, {{USS|Davis|DD-65|2}}, {{USS|Conyngham|DD-58|2}}, {{USS|McDougal|DD-54|2}}, and {{USS|Wainwright|DD-62|2}}) to the [[European theatre of World War I|European war zone]] for service during [[World War I]]. The paintings also depict fisherman welcoming the destroyers from their own boat.{{cite web |title=KN-215 (Color) Return of the Mayflower, 4 May 1917 |url=https://www.history.navy.mil/content/history/nhhc/our-collections/photography/numerical-list-of-images/nara-series/kn-series/KN-00001/KN-215.html |access-date=February 9, 2026 |publisher=[[US Navy]]}} Roosevelt paid $105 {{USDCY|105|1919}} for his painting. The paintings were meant to commemorate [[American entry into World War I|America's entry into World War I]] on the side of the [[Allies of World War I|Allies]]. They also came to symbolize the successful British and American co-operation throughout the war. Their title, a phrase that existed prior to [[World War I]], references the {{ship||Mayflower}}{{cite web |title=“The Return of the Mayflower” |url=https://voyagingthroughhistory.exeter.ac.uk/2019/01/19/the-return-of-the-mayflower/ |publisher=[[University of Exeter]] |work=Voyaging Through History – The Mayflower and Britain |date=January 19, 2019}} and was suggested by Roosevelt. The paintings are also referred to with the title ''"We Are Ready Now" Return of the Mayflower'', "We are ready now" being Commander [[Joseph K. Taussig]]'s response when asked how long it would take for the destroyers to deploy after arriving in British waters.{{cite web |title="We are ready now" return of the Mayflower--4 May 1917 |url=https://cdm16630.contentdm.oclc.org/digital/collection/p16630coll2/id/2822/ |publisher=[[U.S. Naval Academy Museum]] |via=[[Pritzker Military Museum and Library]] |access-date=February 9, 2026}} Gribble also painted a companion to this piece, ''[[Surrender of the German Fleet to the Grand Fleet at Scapa Flow with Admiral Sims and Rodman on the U.S. Flagship "New York"]]'', both in the original size and smaller version for Roosevelt. This piece commemorates the surrender of the German Fleet on 21 November 1918. The original ''Return of the Mayflower'' and its companion are on display at the [[U.S. Naval Academy Museum]] in [[Annapolis, Maryland]].{{cite news |title='The Return of the Mayflower' |newspaper=[[Norfolk Virginian-Pilot]] |via=[[Virginia Chronicle]] |date=October 22, 1939 |volume=155 |url=https://www.virginiachronicle.com/?a=d&d=NVP19391022.1.37&e=-------en-20--1--txt-txIN---------}} The smaller ''Return of the Mayflower'' and its companion were both painted for [[Franklin Delano Roosevelt]], then an assistant secretary in the US Navy, who was said to be entranced when he first saw them. According to a January 1921 correspondence between Roosevelt and Gribble, Roosevelt first displayed the paintings at [[Home of Franklin D. Roosevelt National Historic Site|his home]] in [[Hyde Park, New York]]. He also displayed this painting in the [[New York State Executive Mansion|New York Governor's Mansion]], presumably when [[Governorship of Franklin D. Roosevelt|he was governor]] from 1929 to 1932.{{cite web |title=Gov. Franklin Delano Roosevelt |url=https://www.nga.org/governor/franklin-delano-roosevelt/ |publisher=[[National Governors Association]] |accessdate=February 9, 2026}} In 1933, Roosevelt loaned these and other paintings to the [[Corcoran Gallery of Art]] in [[Washington D.C.]] After their exhibition, these paintings were moved to the [[Oval Office]], where they can be seen in many photographs. In 1942, Roosevelt moved both paintings back to his home, where they remained until his death three years later. After Roosevelt's death, his son [[John Aspinwall Roosevelt]] removed the paintings from the home. [[Eleanor Roosevelt]] owned them until her death in 1962, at which point her heirlooms were divided amongst family members, with the paintings going to "an anonymous New York collector" that was later revealed to be John.{{cite news |title=Roosevelt Legacy Goes on the Block |newspaper=[[Chicago Tribune]] |date=February 11, 2001 |url=https://www.chicagotribune.com/2001/02/11/roosevelt-legacy-goes-on-the-block/}} In 2001, John's widow auctioned ''Return of the Mayflower'', its companion painting, and numerous other works to the [[National Park Service]] and the [[National Archives]] for $300,000 {{USDCY|300000|2001}}. The Park Service then returned ''Return of the Mayflower'' to Roosevelt's home, where it was placed in the same location Roosevelt displayed it during his final years. ''Return of the Mayflower''{{'}}s companion piece was placed on display in Roosevelt's study at the [[Franklin D. Roosevelt Presidential Library and Museum]]. ==In popular culture== ''Return of the Mayflower'' is discussed in [[Erik Larson (author)|Erik Larson]]'s 2015 non-fiction novel ''[[Dead Wake]]'', about the [[sinking of the RMS Lusitania|sinking of the RMS ''Lusitania'']] and the [[American entry into World War I]].{{cite book |title=[[Dead Wake: The Last Crossing of the Lusitania]] |first=Erik |last=Larson |authorlink=Erik Larson (author) |date=2015 |publisher=[[Crown Publishers]]}} ==References== {{Reflist}} [[Category:World War I]] [[Category:Franklin D. Roosevelt]] [[Category:1919 paintings]] [[Category:Maritime paintings]] [[Category:War paintings]] [[Category:Oil paintings on canvas]] [[Category:Flags in art]]

title: Reversed bullet
wikitext:
{{Short description|World War I German anti-tank bullet}}
[[File:Cartridge 7.92x57mm Mauser CC BY-SA 4.0 by Grasyl.jpg|90px|thumb|right|[[7.92×57mm Mauser]] cartridge used by the [[Gewehr 98]] rifle]]

A '''reversed bullet''' was a German [[Anti-tank warfare|anti-tank]] method for penetrating the armor of the [[British heavy tanks of World War I]].

==History==
At their inception in 1916, the British [[Mark I tank]] proved nearly impenetrable to standard rifle fire.  The first attempt at boosting the power of German infantry rifles was the "reversed bullet".  This used the same case and bullet as a normal round, except with the bullet seated backward and additional propellant added to the [[7.92×57mm Mauser]] [[Cartridge (firearms)|cartridge]].  When fired, the blunt end of the bullet hit the target first.  The bullet did not as readily deflect or break apart against armor plating as a normal bullet would, but transferred most of its kinetic energy to the steel plate on impact.<ref name="Chisholm 1922, pp. 204–205">{{Cite EB1922 |wstitle=Armour Plate |volume=30 |pages=204–205}}</ref>  Used against World War I tanks, the reversed bullet sometimes penetrated into the tank compartment, but more often it severely indented the plate armor of the tank.  This caused a spray of metal fragments ([[spall]]) that injured or killed the crew of the tank as effectively as full penetration into the tank compartment.<ref>{{cite book |last=Paschall |first=Rod  |year=1994 |title=Defeat of Imperial Germany, 1917-1918 |publisher=Da Capo Press |page=113}}</ref>  At short range, armor required a minimum thickness of {{cvt|.50|in}} in order to stop a reversed bullet.<ref name="Chisholm 1922, pp. 204–205" />   The allies spread stories that reversed bullets were illegal, improvised, expanding bullets used by Germans against French infantry at short ranges.<ref>{{cite news |title=A New Dumdum Charge |year=1915 |newspaper= New York Times |url=https://query.nytimes.com/gst/abstract.html?res=9E0CE5DA1538E633A2575BC2A9679C946496D6CF&scp=1&sq=a+new+dumdum+charge&st=p}}</ref>  German reversed bullets were, however, factory loaded and offered no advantage over non-reversed bullets if used against infantry.

The reversed bullet sometimes damaged German rifles, often injuring its users. This made it unpopular with German infantry.<ref name="Chisholm 1922, pp. 204–205" />
Later in World War I, the Germans developed the armor-piercing [[K bullet]] for use against heavier British tanks.

title: Role of geography in World War I
wikitext:
{{Short description|none}}
{{Unfocused|date=June 2022}}

Geography greatly affected the events and outcomes of [[World War I]]. As [[World War I]] was one of the first true global conflicts, it was shaped by the influence of multiple nations and each country's unique problems. Other factors helped shape the war and changed the course of fighting. With the rise of [[imperialism]] and a desire for resources, the war involved almost all European nations, and was therefore fought on several fronts. Geographic barriers created diversions and weather patterns helped in leading the Allies to victory. Also, the new spread of technology along with trench warfare and disease eventually led to the defeat of [[Germany]] and [[Austria-Hungary]].<ref>Stearns, Peter N., Michael Adas, and Stuart B. Schwartz. World Civilizations, The Global Experience. 5th. Longman, 2007.</ref>

==Background==
[[Imperialism]] before World War I had been on the rise since the mid-nineteenth century because [[industrialization]] had caused a growing need for natural resources. Regions like Africa and India had been settled by European countries in order to make profit and extend power.<ref>Wood, Ethel. AP World History, An Essential Coursebook. Reading, Pennsylvania: Woodyard, 2008. 466-495. Print.</ref> Tensions began to rise as nations formed alliances with one another to improve their strength. Due to geographical closeness, Germany, Austria-Hungary, and Italy came together as the [[Triple Alliance (1882)|Triple Alliance]] and later became the [[Central powers]] due to their central positioning in Europe.{{citation needed|date=January 2012}} France and Britain became allies along with Russia in order to defend their borders and support each other in case of war. Conflicts in the Balkans grew steadily, and after the [[Assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand of Austria|assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand]], alliances drew almost all European nations and colonies into what would become known as World War I.

==The Fronts== 
Due to the geographical positioning of the [[Triple Entente]], the Central Powers were faced on all sides by their enemies. Once Italy had joined in on the side of the Allies, the war became a three front war. The big Western front was in France, and Italian Front in the mountains of Italy, and the Eastern Front was on the border of Russia.<ref>"McMURRY,FRANK M. ." THE Geography of The Great War. N.p., n.d. Web. 2 Jan 2012.<http://freepages.military.rootsweb.ancestry.com/~worldwarone/WWI/TheGeographyOfTheGreatWar/</ref> Because Germany and Austria-Hungary had to split their armies, they were severely weakened.  While the Schlieffen Plan intended for Germany to send ninety percent of their army to France and quickly overtake it then move to Russia, they were held up by fierce fighting at the [[First Battle of the Marne]].<ref>Spartacus Educational, . "Schlieffen Plan." n. page. Web. 2 Jan. 2012. <https://spartacus-educational.com/FWWschlieffenP.htm>.</ref>

==Battles== 
Throughout major battles in the war, geography influenced the method of fighting and often the victor. At Ypres, many men died by drowning in thick, liquid mud and fighting conditions were awful<ref>"Major Battles of World War I." Ypres. Web. 2 Jan. 2012. <http://home.zonnet.nl/rene.brouwer/majorbattles.htm.</ref> The [[Gallipoli Campaign]] involved the death of many Australian Allied soldiers because of the positioning of the peninsula. The Ottoman soldiers were able to position themselves at the top of a hill while all of the Allied soldiers remained at the bottom. In order to defeat the Central Powers, they had to get to the top of the hill without getting shot. Very few men ever made it up the hill, and if they did, they were shot shortly after. The Gallipoli Campaign was a devastating loss for the Allies.<ref>Burke, Garry. Under the Cover of Darkness Interview. Print. <http://web.ebscohost.com/src/detail?vid=6&hid=15&sid=6aa38f11-af19-452f-81b2-effd72396253@sessionmgr14&bdata=JkF1dGhUeXBlPWlwLGN1c3R1aWQmY3VzdGlkPXM4NDU1ODYxJnNpdGU9c3JjLWxpdmU=</ref>

==Geographic Barriers== 
Fighting on the Italian Front involved the Swiss Alps and other mountains. Rivers, such as the [[Isonzo]] were fought over, to gain access to supplies and resources. The domination of seas was important because naval fighting was also a true sign of power. The vastness of Russia made it difficult for the Germans to reach, and once they dropped out of the war their front was simply used to catch the Central Powers on both sides.<ref>Stearns, Peter N., Michael Adas, and Stuart B. Schwartz. World Civilizations, The Global Experience. 5th. Long man, 2007.</ref>

==Weather== 
Brutal winters diminished supplies and left both sides cold, starving, and wet. Lack of shoes and good clothes caused vulnerability and the spread of disease. Rain, snow, heat, and cold all played their role in World War One because of the giant amount of areas the war was fought in.<ref>Wood, Ethel. AP World History, An Essential Coursebook. Reading, Pennsylvania: Woodyard, 2008. 466-495. Print.</ref>

==Transfer of Knowledge== 
The Atlantic Ocean was home to submarines, naval ships, and also the transfer of goods. Domination on the seas was necessary for getting supplies, people, and weapons from place to place. With new technology, ideas were able to spread quickly and new warfare was created by both sides such as poison gas. Communication also played a role in getting the United States to join the war. The interception of the [[Zimmermann Telegram]] as well as [[Sinking of the RMS Lusitania|the sinking of the RMS Lusitania]] both helped persuade the US in joining the war.<ref>"Tunnelling." Spartacus Educational. n.d. n. page. Web. 2 Jan. 2012.<https://spartacus-educational.com/FWWtunnelling.htm>.</ref>

==The Trenches==
Trench Warfare was common during WWI, although it was not exactly the healthiest or morale-boosting experience for soldiers living in the trenches. They were constantly wet and water would often build up to several inches. Urine, body odor, poison gas, bad food, rats, little clothing, and misery all defined the trench lifestyle. Diseases such as      [[Trench Foot|trench foot]] emerged and close quarters caused the infection to be passed from one person to another and from rats and bugs to humans as well. Loud bombs often were the cause of deafness and long periods in the trench often led to mental illness such as shell shock (Now known as PTSD). While the Germans had running water, electricity, and had the moral support of the troops<ref>"Stories from the Trenches" https://www.loc.gov/vets/stories/wwi-trenches.html#stories</ref>

==Outcome and Effects== 
The geography of World War One helped it to play out the way it did. The brutal conditions, geographic landmarks, and outbreaks of disease as well as location helped in bringing the defeat of the Central Powers. After the war at the Treaty of Versailles, Austria-Hungary was broken up into two separate countries, and much of the German landscape was given away to France, Poland, and others. This angered Germany and set up tensions for another war of the worlds.<ref>"The Great War- Effects." Silva Pages. n.d. n. page. Web. 2 Jan. 2012.<http://www.pvhs.chico.k12.ca.us/~bsilva/projects/great_war/effects.htm>Silva</ref>

title: Rouge Bouquet
wikitext:
{{for|the 1918 poem by American poet Joyce Kilmer|Rouge Bouquet (poem)}}
[[File:EW-RougeBouquet-restored.jpg|thumb| "Rouge Bouquet" by [[Emmett Watson (illustrator)|Emmett Watson]].]]
'''Rouge Bouquet''' is a part of the [[Parroy|Forêt de Parroy]] near the village of [[Baccarat, Meurthe-et-Moselle|Baccarat]], France. It was the site of a German artillery bombardment of American trench positions on 7 March 1918 at 15:20 on the [[Chausailles sector]] of the [[Western Front (World War I)|Western Front]] during [[World War I]].<ref>National Archives and Records Administration - Washington, DC. ''CR Rouge Bouquet held by 2nd Btn 165th A.I.R. 7–8 March 1918, NA/RG 120: World War I Organizational Records: 42nd Division, Box 27, Folder—Rept. Of Events in CR Rouge Bouquet''</ref><ref name="FatherDuffysStory">Duffy, Francis Patrick. Father Duffy’s Story. (New York: George H. Doran Company, 1919), 350.</ref> The bombardment resulted in the burial of 21 men of the [[165th Infantry Regiment]] (originally the [[69th Infantry Regiment (New York)|69th Regiment]] of the [[New York National Guard]]), [[42nd Infantry Division (United States)|42nd Rainbow Division]] of whom only a few survived. The 22 men, including their platoon commander 1st Lieutenant John Norman, were assembled in a dugout when a German artillery shell landed on the roof of the dugout. Major [[William J. Donovan|William J. "Wild Bill" Donovan]] quickly began a rescue attempt to dig the men out, but the effort were hampered by mud-slides and continued enemy shelling.<ref name="FatherDuffysStory"/><ref name="HarrisDuffysWar">Harris, Stephen L. Duffy's War: Fr. Francis Duffy, Wild Bill Donovan, and the Irish Fighting 69th in World War I (Washington, DC: Potomac Books Inc, 2007).</ref>{{rp|pp.167–171}} Two men were rescued and five dead were recovered before efforts had to be halted. The voices of other men could be heard for a while, but the remaining fifteen men died before rescue efforts could resume.<ref name="HarrisDuffysWar"/>{{rp|pp.167–171}} Donovan was awarded the French [[Croix de Guerre]] for his actions during the attempted rescue.<ref name="HarrisDuffysWar"/>{{rp|pp.209–210}}

Poet and literary critic [[Joyce Kilmer]], a [[Corporal#United_States|corporal]] at that time, wrote the 1918 poem "[[Rouge Bouquet (poem)|Rouge Bouquet]]" (also called "The Wood Called Rouge Bouquet") as a eulogy to commemorate the soldiers in his regiment who died.<ref>{{cite book |last1=James |first1=D. Clayton |title=The Years of MacArthur Volume 1 1880-1941 |date=1 October 1970 |publisher=Houghton Mifflin Company |location=Boston, Massachusetts |isbn=978-0395109489 |page=158 |edition=1st |url=https://catalog.loc.gov/vwebv/search?searchCode=LCCN&searchArg=76108685&searchType=1&permalink=y |accessdate=1 January 2020}}</ref><ref name="HarrisDuffysWar"/>{{rp|pp.175–176}} The poem was first read by [[Military_chaplain#United_States|Chaplain]] [[Francis_P._Duffy#Service_as_an_Army_chaplain|Francis Duffy]] at "the funeral service held at the collapsed dugout, the tomb of the regiment's first men slain in battle" a few days later.<ref>{{cite book |last1=James |first1=D. Clayton |title=The Years of MacArthur Volume 1 1880-1941 |date=1 October 1970 |publisher=Houghton Mifflin Company |location=Boston, Massachusetts |isbn=978-0395109489 |page=158 |edition=1st |url=https://catalog.loc.gov/vwebv/search?searchCode=LCCN&searchArg=76108685&searchType=1&permalink=y |accessdate=1 January 2020}}</ref><ref name="HarrisDuffysWar"/>{{rp|pp.175–176}} It first appeared in print in the American servicemen's newspaper ''Stars and Stripes''—published two weeks after Kilmer died in combat in the [[Second Battle of the Marne]] on 30 July 1918.<ref>Kilmer, Joyce. "Rouge Bouquet" in ''Stars and Stripes'' (16 August 1918).</ref><ref>Mitgang, Herbert. ''Civilians Under Arms: The Stars and Stripes, Civil War to Korea''. (SIU Press, 1959), 146-148.</ref><ref>United States Army. Army Expeditionary Force, 1917-1919. (New York: G.P. Putnam's sons, 1919), 78-80.</ref>
