Australians expressed critical concern from 1919 onwards about the poor quality of the sculptures of soldiers on memorials, the blame being placed on the cheap reproductions by stone masons.<ref name="Inglis, p. 139"/> Their government responded by establishing advisory boards to discourage this trend.<ref>Inglis, p. 145.</ref> Britain also saw concerns over the "stereotyped designs" being supplied by firms of stone masons, and here again numerous bodies issued guidance on better practices, including the [[Royal Academy of Art]], the [[Church of England]]; the Civic Arts Association was formed specifically to help.<ref>King, pp. 71, 123.</ref> The opinion of professional artists and critics remained quite important for committees when choosing designs, however, and there was vigorous discussion between supporters of different styles and architectural traditions.<ref>King, pp. 109–110, 120.</ref>

Many designers were involved in the construction of memorials, but some became particularly well known for their work in this area. Many of the sculptors active on the memorials were established, Victorian-era individuals; the war had disrupted the training of a new generation, and many young sculptors had been killed.<ref>Borg, p. 79.</ref> Some attempts were made to give preference to designers who had fought in the war, but this was far from universal.<ref>Carden-Coyne, p. 121.</ref> In British circles, [[Edwin Lutyens]], [[Herbert Baker]], [[Reginald Blomfield]] and [[Charles Holden]] formed the core of the established artists; these were joined by [[Charles Sargeant Jagger]], [[Gilbert Ledward]] and [[Eric Gill]] from the younger generation.<ref>Borg, pp. xiii, 72–73. 80–81.</ref> [[Pietro Porcelli]] was a particularly prolific Australian designer.<ref>Inglis, p. 141.</ref> In Germany, [[Käthe Kollwitz]]'s memorial of a grieving mother at the Roggevelde cemetery was particularly famous, and based on her own loss of a son during the fighting in the war.<ref>Koshar, p. 96.</ref>

====Symbolism====
[[File:Cross of Sacrifice, Ypres Reservoir cemetery.jpg|thumb|upright|Sir [[Reginald Blomfield]]'s widely used [[Cross of Sacrifice]]]]

World War I memorials made extensive use of symbolism and [[allegory]].<ref>Borg, pp. 9–10.</ref> Some of these [[Allegorical sculpture|symbols]] were national in character, carrying a simple message about national victory – a [[Gallic rooster]] triumphing over a German, the {{lang|fr|[[Croix de Guerre]]}}, or the Romanians' symbol for their heroes' cult for example – but others, such as images of infantrymen, could be used in different ways, depending on how they were portrayed.<ref>Prost, pp. 18–19; Bucur (2004), p. 168.</ref> Some sculpture of French infantrymen, for example, aims to capture the spirit of French republicanism, while others are designed with more right-wing, nationalist attributes.<ref>Prost, pp. 18–20.</ref>

Major memorial themes, such as victory and death all had their symbols. Many Canadian and British soldiers are shown raising a hat or a rifle, a sign of victory first introduced into Boer War memorials.<ref>Vance, p. 18.</ref> The Greek goddess [[Nike (mythology)|Nike]] herself frequently appears on civic memorials, particularly in Britain and Canada, personifying victory, often pointing the way to soldiers: the image is far less common, however, on more sombre memorials in battlefields and graveyards.<ref>Borg, pp. 97, 99; Vance, p. 18.</ref> [[Personifications of death|Personifications of Death]] rarely feature on these memorials, however, probably because the emphasis is typically on the self-sacrifice of the soldiers involved, rather than their being taken or claimed by Death.<ref>Borg, p. 102.</ref> Death is more typically presented through images of widows, orphans and elderly parents on memorials, all popular inter-war allegorical forms for death and grieving.<ref>Prost, pp. 14–15.</ref> Figures of women often represented peace, civilisation or wider humanity.<ref>Carden-Coyne, p. 148.</ref>

By far the most important source of symbolism on memorials, however, is Christian imagery and icons. Religious imagery permeated many war memorials, even the secular.<ref>Winter, p. 90.</ref> The most important of these symbols was the [[Christian cross]], a widely used symbol of hope and suffering.<ref>Borg, p. 94; King, p. 129.</ref>{{refn|In countries such as England, the cross had only recently been considered unsuitable for displays because of its Roman Catholic connotations.<ref>King, p. 129.</ref>|group="nb"}} The cross could take multiple forms, from Catholic designs in France, to Orthodox crosses in eastern Europe.<ref>Bucur (2004), p. 168.</ref> [[Celtic cross]]es were popular in Britain and Ireland, partially because they avoided Catholic connotations, although they were considered vulgar by more classical architects such as Blomfield.<ref>Winter, p. 92; Borg, p. 93; King, p. 129.</ref> In France, ''les croix des bois'', wooden crosses, became popular symbols at memorials after [[Roland Dorgelès]]'s novel of the same name.<ref>Smith, Audoin-Rouzeau and Becker, p. 169.</ref> German memorials made extensive use of the image of the [[Virgin Mary]] tending her son Christ, following in the tradition of the ''[[pietà]]''.<ref>Winter, p. 90; Koshar, p. 101.</ref> The [[crucifixion]] was also a widely used symbol, as seen in [[Francis Derwent Wood|Derwent Wood]]'s [[Canada's Golgotha]], although Christ himself was relatively rarely typically seen on British memorials.<ref>Winter, p. 92; Borg, p. 101.</ref>

The widespread use of Christian symbolism led to questions about how to produce memorials suitable for non-Christians. Lutyens attempted to solve this problem for the IWGC through the design of the [[Stone of Remembrance]], or War Stone. This was a large, simple stone, intended to resemble an altar and evoke the theme of sacrifice.<ref name=GeurstP67>Geurst, p. 67.</ref> In practice, many commentators felt it resembled a sarcophagus.<ref name=GeurstP67/> Lutyens wanted it to avoid conventional Christian symbolism and based it on designs in Chinese [[Imperial Tombs of the Ming and Qing Dynasties|Ming tombs]].<ref>Winter, p. 107.</ref> One of Lutyens' arguments in favour of his design was that explicit Christian symbolism excluded the Indian and Jewish communities and atheists.<ref>Borg, p. 73.</ref> The IWGC designs for the Indian and Chinese war cemeteries in Europe deliberately did not use Christian imagery – although, as historian Xu Guoqi notes, the Chinese role in the Allied armies remains largely uncommemorated through memorials.<ref>Geurst, p. 67; Guoqi, p. 144.</ref>

====Classicism====
Many memorials drew on a [[Classical architecture|classical]] style of architecture to produce their effect. This had been a popular style for many pre-war memorials, such as those for the dead of the Boer War, and used Greek or Roman structures, styles and symbolism.<ref name=GlavesSmithP72>Glaves-Smith, p. 72.</ref> A key feature of the classical style was the concept of the "beautiful death"{{snd}}classical memorials might include figures of soldiers, sometimes dying in conflict, but always heroically and, ultimately, peacefully.<ref name=GlavesSmithP72/> Soldiers in these memorials were still frequently depicted as [[Homer]]ic warriors, rather than more realist figures.<ref>Carden-Coyne, p. 158; Miles, p. 102.</ref> The classical symbolism was often used to distance the event of death from the observer, appealing to allegories for sacrifice, justice and victory, in an attempt to make mourning easier to bear.<ref name=GlavesSmithP72/>

Some inter-war architects developed this approach further. Some traditional classical memorials had been criticised in both England and Germany as being fussy and overly ornate.<ref>Glaves-Smith, p. 72; Carden-Coyne, p. 155; Skelton and Gliddon, p. 150; Koshar, p. 103.</ref> Men such as Lutyens took the classical principles, but simplified them until the design became almost abstract.<ref>Borg, p. 75.</ref> These memorials used abstract, beautiful designs intended to remove the viewer from the real world, and focus them on an idealised sense of self-sacrifice, a continuation of the principle of a "beautiful death".<ref>Glaves-Smith, p. 72; Carden-Coyne, p. 155; Skelton and Gliddon, p. 150.</ref> In many ways the simplified, but still classical, forms of memorials like the Cenotaph meant that mourners could read their own thoughts and concerns onto the memorial.<ref>Winter, p. 104.</ref> Where dead soldiers were shown, they were depicted in an image of serenity and peace, often physically distanced from the viewer on a high platform, the entire effect reflected by the silence that traditionally surrounds ceremonies at the Cenotaph.<ref>Carden-Coyne, p. 156; Glaves-Smith, p. 72.</ref>

Many classical themes were used in this way. [[Thiepval Memorial]], for example uses the classical themes of a victory arch and an abstract pattern of diminishing arches to produce what historian Jay Winter has termed "an embodiment of nothing".<ref name="Winter, p. 105"/> The various Cenotaphs adopt the principle of [[entasis]]{{snd}}Greek method with apparently straight lines, that are in fact slightly curved.<ref name=BorgP74>Borg, p. 74.</ref> Many memorials and war cemeteries used [[religious precinct|precinct]] walls to mark out the memorial as special and sacred, originally a Roman feature made popular again in the 19th century.<ref>Borg, p. 131.</ref> Some features were more literally interpreted: the Victoria State Memorial in Australia, for example, was closely based on a Persian [[step pyramid]].<ref>Borg, p. 134.</ref>

Classical themes, like Christian symbolism, emphasised the sacred nature of the memorial sites.<ref>Winter, p. 102.</ref> Nonetheless, there was some criticism of classicism by those who wanted a clearer separation of pagan and Christian symbolism; this was played out in arguments in Germany over whether [[Iron Cross]]es or traditional Christian crosses should be used on memorials.<ref>Goebel, pp. 66–67; Koshar, p. 103.</ref> Similarly, Lutyens' War Stones were criticised for their blending of Christian and non-Christian design, while the London Cenotaph was critiqued by the ''[[Catholic Herald]]'' as being "insulting to Christianity".<ref>Winter, p. 107; King, p. 147.</ref> Some Christian symbols were redesigned in the simplified classical style, however, including the [[Cross of Sacrifice]]. This cross, in a classical style and featuring a white cross and an inverted bronze sword, was designed by Sir [[Reginald Blomfield]] for the War Graves Commission, widely used in Commonwealth countries.<ref>Gordon, pp. 162–163.</ref> The design was criticised by some who felt that it excluded other faiths from the memorial site, but nonetheless, over a 1,000 of these crosses were ultimately built.<ref>Borg, pp. 73–74.</ref>

====Medievalism====
[[File:Great War Memorial Windows, Guildhall, Derry.jpg|thumb|Medieval styled memorial window in [[Derry]], featuring the [[Red Hand of Ulster]] as part of the arms of the [[36th (Ulster) Division]] (l)]]

In some countries, particularly Germany and England, memorials used a [[Medievalism|medieval style]], reaching back to a more distant past. Some of these medieval styled memorials were set in existing medieval buildings, fusing older and newer themes. Memorial church windows, for example, could combine medieval and modern features, including armoured knights on horseback, modern weapons-including-tanks and aircraft-and modern national flags.<ref>Goebel, pp. 57–58; Winter, p. 91.</ref> Other memorials deliberately chose medieval themes and symbols, such as the Tomb of the Unknown Warrior in Westminster, where the language of the inscriptions was deliberately archaic, and the tomb itself made from a medieval chest, decorated with a [[Crusades|crusader]]'s sword.<ref name="Goebel, pp. 43–44">Goebel, pp. 43–44.</ref> England's patron saint, [[Saint George]], was a particular popular symbol in British designs, typically shown mounted and wearing armour.<ref>Borg, p. 100.</ref> The Arthurian [[Round Table]] and the medieval crusades proved popular themes in Canadian memorials.<ref>Vance, p. 39.</ref>

New memorial buildings could also adopt a medieval style. The [[Scottish National War Memorial]], for example, a [[Scots baronial]] styled memorial hall complete with stained glass in [[Edinburgh Castle]], attempts to blend in with the surrounding medieval fortress.<ref>Goebel, p. 58; Borg, p. 133.</ref> In Germany, the ''totenburgen'' usually looked to the past for their style; Tannenberg, for example, was heavily medieval in appearance, resembling a castle, albeit combined with a huge cross and mass graves.<ref>Goebel, pp. 36–38.</ref> The ''dolmen'' boulders used around the outside of many German memorials reinforced the archaic feel of the monuments.<ref name="Mosse, p. 101">Mosse, p. 101.</ref> In other cases Germans chose to preserve or rebuild real medieval buildings and architecture to form war memorials, such as parts of [[Dorsten]] and [[Dülken]].<ref>Goebel, p. 49.</ref>

Medievalism was popular with mourners because it reached back to the past, attempting to heal some of the discontinuities and ruptures of the war.<ref name=GoebelP39>Goebel, p. 39.</ref> In a period of great uncertainty, the style was reaffirming and apparently immutable, lost in a distant past.<ref name=GoebelP39/> By placing the recent dead alongside those who had fallen before, the style gave reassurance that the World War I dead would not be forgotten; in Westminster, the [[Herbert Edward Ryle|Dean of Westminster]], emphasised when he noted that the Unknown Warrior would be resting alongside his "Saxon and Norman, Plantagenet and Tudor" predecessors.<ref name="Goebel, pp. 43–44"/> The style was actively promoted by a number of extant artistic and architectural institutions and groups, such as the [[Victoria and Albert Museum]], the [[Arts and Crafts Movement]] and [[Gothic Revival architecture|Gothic revivalists]].<ref>Goebel, p. 58.</ref>

====Alternative styles====
[[File:Royal Artillery Memorial, outside Aspley House, London.JPG|thumb|The [[Royal Artillery Memorial]] in London, featuring an oversized stone replica of a [[BL 9.2 inch Howitzer|BL 9.2 inch Mk I howitzer]]]]

Only a minority of war memorials used some of the newer styles emerging in the inter-war period, such as [[Modern architecture|modernism]], [[Realism (arts)|realist]] and [[Art Nouveau]] approaches. As noted above, typically existing, traditional themes were preferred for memorials as a way of grounding mourning in a more familiar perspective. Nonetheless, some of the memorials to use the newer styles became particularly famous. There are a handful of memorials conducted in an Art Deco style, including the [[ANZAC War Memorial]] in Sydney which uses the delicate aspects of the Art Deco style to invoke sadness in the viewer, and is the only war memorial in the world to depict a naked soldier.<ref>Falconer, p. 174; Borg, p. 134.</ref> The Douaumont Ossuary also draws on Art Deco principles in its structural architecture, avoiding straight lines in favour of gentle, soft, intersecting curves.<ref>Borg, p. 135.</ref> Modernist principles were taken further in a small number of British memorials designed by [[Eric Gill]], characterised by their highly abstract, simplified forms.<ref>King, pp. 163–168.</ref>
[[File:Tour du Mémorial Interallié - le Phare de Liège.jpg|thumb|left|200px|alt=Tower of the Interallied Memorial of Cointe, Liège, Belgium|<div style= "text-align:center">Tower of the [[Interallied Memorial of Cointe]], Liège, Belgium</div>]]
Realism and early modernist principles were applied in Britain to produce a critique of the conventional classical approach and the concept of a "beautiful death", most notably by Charles Jagger.<ref>Glaves-Smith, p. 61.</ref> Jagger's later work during the inter-war period, most notably his [[Royal Artillery Memorial]], uses realism techniques to portray an oversized [[BL 9.2 inch Howitzer|BL 9.2 inch Mk I howitzer]] in detail, mounted on a huge, architecturally simple plinth with detailed carvings of military events involving ordinary artillerymen. The sheer size of the piece creates a dehumanizing impact, despite the portrayal of a team of artillerymen, including a covered corpse.<ref>Black, p. 141; Glaves-Smith, p. 21; Abousnnouga and Machin, p. 136; Miles, p. 102.</ref> Critiqued by much of the British press when unveiled in 1925, many veterans however felt that the style connected to them in a way that more classical themes could not.<ref>Miles, p. 102; Glaves-Smith, p. 72.</ref> While the Royal Artillery Memorial is unique, elements of the style can be seen in some other memorials, such as the [[Cameronians (Scottish Rifles) Memorial|Cameronians Memorial]] which includes a realist, almost tactile depiction of a machine gun position.<ref>Borg, p. 114.</ref>

Historical accuracy was important to many British designers, resulting in the use of genuine military equipment as models for memorials, and long discussions with committees over the details to be incorporated into designs.<ref>King, p. 159.</ref> In contrast, the British interest in accurately depicting real weaponry from the war was far less common on German monuments, where usually stylised medieval weapons and armour were used.<ref name="Mosse, p. 101"/>

==World War II and post-war==
[[File:Malta - Floriana - Triq Sant' Anna - War Memorial 02 ies.jpg|thumb|upright|The [[War Memorial (Floriana)|War Memorial]] in [[Floriana]], [[Malta]] was built in 1938 commemorating the dead of World War I. In 1949 it was rededicated to commemorate the fallen of both world wars.]]

The Second World War that broke out in 1939 consumed the attention of a new generation. Across most of the theatres of conflict, the participants attempted to respect the memorials to World War I. After the Second World War there was no equivalent mass construction of memorials to the war dead; instead, often local World War I memorials were adapted for use instead: additional names might be inscribed to the existing lists.<ref>Borg, pp. ix, 83.</ref> In some cases, this resulted in memorials losing their exclusive focus on World War I. The Tomb of the Unknown Soldier in Washington, for example, was expanded in 1950s to include corpses from the Second World War and Korea War, broadening the memorial's remit to commemorate most modern wars.<ref>Trout, p. 21.</ref> In other cases, such as the [[Australian War Memorial]], begun in the inter-war years but only opened in 1941, an essentially new memorial was formed to honour the multiple conflicts.<ref>Borg, p. 126.</ref>

In Italy and Germany, 1945 saw the collapse of Fascism; many memorials in Italian towns and cities were used to execute and display the bodies of the overthrown regime, and the inter-war Fascist pilgrimages and ceremonies around the memorials were abandoned and quickly forgotten.<ref>Dogliani, pp. 19–20.</ref> The World War I memorial sites continued to be used, but a combination of anti-war feelings and their residual Fascist links limited the attendance at their public ceremonies.<ref>Dogliani, p. 24.</ref> Due to the changes in national borders, in the post-war era some sites favoured by the Nazi government, such as the Tannenberg Memorial, found themselves in [[Poland]]; the demolition of Tannenberg began in 1949 and its stonework was reused for Soviet party buildings.<ref>Egremont, p. 179.</ref>

[[File:East Ilsley War Memorial - geograph.org.uk - 1659865.jpg|thumb|upright|left|War memorial in [[East Ilsley]], restored in 2008, and featuring combined original list of World War I and later [[World War II]] names<ref name=EastIlsley>''[http://www.warmemorials.org/search-grants/?gID=7 Showcase result]'', War Memorials Trust, accessed 19 February 2011.</ref>]]

Elsewhere, changes in post-war politics impacted considerably on the memorials. in Belgium, the Flemish IJzertoren tower had become associated with Fascism during the Second World War and was blown up in 1946 by anti-Flemish activists, leading to outrage.<ref>Shelby, pp. 118–120, 148; Conway, p. 257.</ref> Proposals were put forward to build a national monument on the site, but ultimately a second Flemish memorial was constructed instead.<ref>Shelby, pp. 118–122.</ref> In Romania, the Communist post-war government moved away from commemorations around Ascension Day, which was seen as carrying too many religious meanings.<ref>Bucur (2004), pp. 162–163.</ref> The Romanian ''Societata'' itself was abolished in 1948, pilgrimages to the memorials ceased and the focus of the Communist government was almost entirely placed on commemorating the sacrifices of the Soviet army during World War II.<ref>Bucur (2004), pp. 172–173.</ref> Unusually, political changes in Canada led to the construction of new World War I memorials; some of the inter-war tensions eased, and 35 new memorials were added in Quebec to the existing 68 in the post-war years, often built as combined memorials to later conflicts.<ref>Gordon, pp. 165–166.</ref>

As a whole, interest in the war memorials diminished considerably in the 1950s and 1960s, reflected in a reduced level of ceremonies and a simplification of the commemorative events around memorials.<ref>Saunders (2003), p. 156; Winter, p. 98.</ref> In the post-war years, for example, the separate official and veterans ceremonies at the Verdun memorials blended into one; in 1956, German and French ceremonies were also united into a single event.<ref name="ProstP60"/> Attendance at events like Anzac Day diminished.<ref>''[http://www.dva.gov.au/commems_oawg/commemorations/commemorative_events/anzac_day/Pages/legend.aspx History]'', Australian Government, Department of Veterans' Affairs, accessed 27 February 2012.</ref> Many memorials slowly deteriorated: in some cases the original inter-war funding had never included maintenance, in other cases the materials used to construct the memorials were not durable. In some towns and cities, the memorials were moved to less prominent locations as part of urban renewal projects, or hidden by new buildings. World War I memorials were commonplace in many countries and were paid little attention.<ref name="Borg, p. ix"/>

==Since 1990==
[[File:Memorial Rose-Garden 008.JPG|thumb|The [[Irish National War Memorial Gardens]], officially opened in 1995]]

In the 1990s, however, there was a resurgence of interest in World War I memorials. This was driven partially by a sequence of academic works on the social and cultural character of the conflict, aided by a sequence of artistic exhibits of some of more famous designers in the 1980s, and partially by generational change in many countries.<ref>Borg, p. xiii.</ref> As the generation who had lived and fought during the war died off, explaining the context of the memorials became more important.<ref>Prost, pp. 60–61.</ref> In France, veteran groups had begun to build memorial museums alongside the major monuments and battlefields from the late 1930s onwards.<ref>Prost, p. 61.</ref>

Similar efforts made at the end of the 20th century to create additional museums to explain the events of the war and the memorials; these initiatives have the support of the Commonwealth War Graves Commission – the successor to the IWGC – but caused concerns amongst British government officials, due to concerns that they might cheapen the symbolism of the memorials.<ref>Edkins, p. 25.</ref>   As old imperial links declined, in 1993, Australia decided to repatriate one of its unidentified war dead from the Western front to form its own Tomb of the Unknown Soldier in Canberra.<ref>Winter, p. 28.</ref>

Meanwhile, some of the political tensions of earlier generations faded, allowing new memorials to be built. In the Republic of Ireland, new war memorials were built, trips organised to war memorials in Europe, and the National War Memorial Gardens were restored and finally officially opened in 1995.<ref>McCarthy, pp. 25–26.</ref>

[[File:Lé Jour d'la Mémouaithe 2011 Saint Hélyi Jèrri 11.jpg|thumb|left|Temporary memorial for [[Remembrance Day]] in the Channel Islands, 2011]]

In Russia, the [[Memorial park complex of the heroes of the First World War]] was built on the site of the former Moscow City Fraternity Cemetery after the fall of Communism, opening in 2005 at a cost of 95 million roubles.<ref name="Petrone, p. 293">Petrone, p. 293.</ref> The park includes 12 monuments, amongst which was the only surviving headstone from the cemetery and a new memorial chapel.<ref name="Petrone, p. 293"/> In contrast, by the early 21st century, the numbers visiting the IJzertoren tower during the annual pilgrimages declined significantly as memories of the conflict faded.<ref>Shelby, p. 148.</ref>

In the late 1990s and start of the 21st century visitor numbers to the Western Front memorials have risen considerably, and Australian visitors to the memorials at Gallipoli have increased hugely in recent years; the Prime Ministers of Australia and New Zealand opened a new memorial at the site in 2000.<ref>Scates, pp. 62–53; Saunders (2001), p. 45; Macleod, p. 240.</ref>
World War I memorials remain in ceremonial use on [[Remembrance Day]]{{snd}}the post-World War II successor to Armistice Day – Anzac Day and other national occasions, while many utilitarian memorials are still in use by local communities in the 21st century.<ref>Borg, p. 139.</ref> Systematic efforts are being made to catalogue and record the memorials, with a number of individual restoration projects undertaken with public and private funding; the Liberty Memorial in the US, for example, was renovated and declared the country's national World War I museum in 2005.<ref>''[http://www.warmemorials.org/history/ History]'', War Memorials Trust, accessed 27 February 2012; ''[https://web.archive.org/web/20141209072901/http://www.nps.gov/nhl/find/statelists/mo/LibertyMem.pdf National Historic Landmark Nomination]'', National Park service, accessed 24 March 2017; Borg, p. xiii.</ref> During the [[First World War centenary]], the memory of the war became a major theme for scholars and museums.<ref>Reynolds, p. 424; Jones, pp. 287–291; Trout, pp. 1–3.</ref>  Many museums and historical societies set up special exhibits, websites, and multimedia exhibits.<ref>Reynolds, p. 424</ref><ref>Marsh, pp. 45–49</ref> Proposals were put forward to construct a new national US memorial to the conflict in [[Washington, D.C.|Washington]].<ref>[https://www.nytimes.com/2016/01/27/us/national-world-war-i-memorial-proposal-is-unveiled.html "National World War I Memorial Proposal Is Unveiled"], Nicholas Fandos, ''The New York Times'', accessed 29 January 2016.</ref>

title: World War I prisoners of war in Russia
wikitext:
[[File:Gorskii. Austrian prisoners of war in Olonets province.jpg|thumb|right|280px|Austrian prisoners of war in [[Olonets province]] (Russia).]] The '''Prisoners of war of the First World War in Russia''' included a majority of Austro-Hungarians (between 1,6{{sfn|Volgyes|1973|p=54}} and 2 million), 167,000 Germans, and 50,000 Ottomans.{{sfn|Sumpf|2014|p=187}} Along with Germany, Russia held the largest number of prisoners during this conflict. ==Causes== The large number of Austro-Hungarian prisoners, double that of Russian prisoners in Austria-Hungary, was the consequence of the disasters suffered by the [[Austro-Hungarian army]] at the beginning of the war, resulting from the priority given by the Russian General Staff to the Austrian front. Particularly during the [[Battle of Galicia]] (1914), the [[Siege of Przemyśl]] (1914–1915), and the retreat of the Austrian front in June 1916 during the [[Brusilov Offensive]] (1916), huge numbers of Austro-Hungarian soldiers were captured. A lack of fighting spirit and the failures of certain units also contributed to this disproportion. While the peoples of Austria-Hungary generally supported the general mobilization at the beginning of the war, cohesion subsequently weakened. For instance, the 28th Infantry Regiment from Prague surrendered to the Russians without a fight on 27 April 1915 ,{{sfn|Bled|2014|p=104}} and Ruthenian and Czech regiments surrendered or deserted during the battles of June 1916. An additional factor was the anti-war propaganda spread in the Austro-Hungarian army by Socialist and Bolshevik soldiers .{{sfn|Volgyes|1973|p=56}} In contrast, facing the German army, the Russian army was largely dominated and forced to retreat, abandoning a large part of its territory, resulting in a significant disproportion in the number of prisoners: the Germans captured a total of 1,434,000 Russians. ==Living Conditions== [[File:German & Austrian prisoners in Russia LCCN2014698318.jpg|thumb|right|270px|German & Austrian prisoners in Russia]] [[File:Murmansk Railway 1.jpg|thumb|right|270px|Austrian prisoners at the construction site of the Murmansk Railway.]] The high mortality rate of prisoners in Russia throughout the war, approximately 17.6%, significantly higher than that of prisoners in Austria (7%), France (5.3%), and Germany (3.5%),{{sfn|Sumpf|2014|p=137}} was primarily the result of Russia's unpreparedness for such an influx, the lack of available accommodation, which forced the initial use of various buildings such as barns, abandoned factories, and private homes, and harsh climatic and transportation conditions (long, exhausting marches, endless train journeys), but not of persecution or punitive policies.{{sfn|Sumpf|2014|p=137}} On the contrary, most former prisoners reported good treatment and a friendly welcome from the Russians.{{sfn|Sumpf|2014|p=137}}
However, some 300,000 prisoners died, mainly from typhoid, dysentery, exhaustion and hunger .{{sfn|Volgyes|1973|p=58-59}} From 1916 onwards, mortality declined following the establishment of camps and organizational changes that improved sanitary conditions, thanks also to the assistance provided by Austria-Hungary and Germany to their nationals. However, the situation deteriorated again, after the chaos caused by the [[February Revolution|February 1917]] and [[October Revolution|October 1917 Revolutions]] .{{sfn|Volgyes|1973|p=61-67}} Among the prisoners, Austro-Hungarians Slavs (Czechs, Slovaks, South Slavs), were given priority treatment and often housed separately. The Russians offered them the opportunity to enlist in brigades: approximately 10% of Slavic prisoners volunteered.{{Cite book|language=fr|author1=François Cochet|author2=Rémy Porte|title=Dictionnaire de la grande guerre. 1914-18.|location=Paris|publisher=Robert Laffont|year=2008|page=848|isbn=978-2-221-10722-5}} However, this discrimination had little effect due to the general poverty. Rations and living conditions, which varied greatly, depended more on the nature of the work and the chance of assignments than on ethnic origin .{{sfn|Sumpf|2014|p=141}} The prisoners were used in agriculture (460,000 in May 1916), on roadwork (140,000 in May 1916) ,{{sfn|Sumpf|2014|p=141}} and in industry (1,640,000) .{{sfn|Sumpf|2014|p=142}} Prisoners constituted a significant portion of the workforce in several sectors of the economy, like 60% in iron mines and 30% of foundry workers, due to low pay .{{sfn|Sumpf|2014|p=142}} ==Return of Prisoners== [[File:No-nb bldsa 6b010.jpg|thumb|right|230px|Map of Europe showing the number of prisoners of war returned from Russia during the period 1920–1922.]] The [[Treaty of Brest-Litovsk]] (March 1918) provided for the release of all prisoners from both sides. Those held in Russia, the majority Austro-Hungarians, numbering approximately 2 million, were repatriated starting in March 1918. This return was relatively slow (fewer than 500,000 by the beginning of the summer) .{{sfn|Bled|2014|p=351}}
The first released prisoners were reincorporated into the Austro-Hungarian army after a three-week quarantine, rigorous interrogation, and a four-week leave .{{sfn|Bled|2014|p=352}} This return to the army was accompanied by acts of disobedience, mutinies, and desertions, by soldiers who had hoped the war was over .{{sfn|Bled|2014|p=353}} Subsequently, [[the Russian Civil War]] delayed the repatriation of prisoners still present in Russia until 1922.
Many remaining former Austro-Hungarian prisoners of war participated in the Russian Civil War on both sides .{{sfn|Volgyes|1973|p=70-78}} Best known is the [[Czechoslovak Legion]], which fought against the Bolsheviks.Victor M. Fic, ''The Bolsheviks and the Czechoslovak Legion'' (New Delhi: Abhinav, 1978) p. 22–38. ==Well known WW I prisoners of war in Russia== *[[Josip Broz Tito]] (1892–1980), future President of Yugoslavia, captured on 25 March 1915, joined the [[Red Guards (Russia)|International Red Guard]] in November 1917, returned to Croatia in the autumn of 1920. *[[Béla Kun]] (1886–1938), captured in 1916. Fought for the Bolsheviks in the Russian Civil War. Leader of the [[Hungarian Soviet Republic]] (1919). *[[Imre Nagy]] (1896–1958), captured in 1916. Fought for the Red Army in the Russian Civil War. Prime Minister of Hungary and executed after the [[Hungarian Revolution of 1956]]. *[[Mátyás Rákosi]] (1892–1971), captured in 1915. De facto leader of Hungary from 1947 to 1956. *[[Máté Zalka]] (1896–1937), captured in 1917. Joined the Red Army. Fought against the Whites. Killed in the [[Spanish Civil War]]. *[[Said Nursi]] (1877–1960), captured in 1916. Turkish scholar of Islam *[[Ernst Mohr (gymnast)|Ernst Mohr]] (1877–1916), German olympic gymnast. Died in Russian captivity. *[[Karl Braunsteiner]] (1891–1916), Austrian soccer player. Died of typhoid fever. *[[Paul Wittgenstein]] (1887–1961), Austrian concert pianist. Captured in 1914. Had his right arm amputated. ==See also== *[[Prisoners of War in World War I]] == References == {{reflist}} ==Sources== * {{Cite book | language=fr | first=Jean-Paul | last=Bled | title=L'agonie d'une monarchie, Autriche-Hongrie 1914-1920 | location=Paris | publisher=Taillandier | year=2014 | pages =464 | isbn=979-10-210-0440-5}} * {{Cite book | language=fr | first=Alexandre | last=Sumpf | title=La grande guerre oubliée, Russie 1914-1918 | location=Paris | publisher=Éditions Perrin | year=2014 | pages=527 | isbn=978-2-262-04045-1 }} * {{Cite journal | language=en | first=Ivan | last=Volgyes | title=Hungarian prisoners of war in Russia, 1916-1919 | journal=Cahiers du Monde Russe et Soviétique | publisher=Cahiers du Monde Russe | year=1973 | volume=14 | pages=54–85 | doi=10.3406/cmr.1973.1171 | url=https://www.persee.fr/doc/cmr_0008-0160_1973_num_14_1_1171 }} * [[Gustav Krist]] (1936), ''Pascholl plenny!'' (Wien: L. W. Seidel & sohn), translated by E. O. Lorimer as ''Prisoner in the Forbidden Land''. * Reinhard Nachtigal and Lena Radauer (2014), [https://encyclopedia.1914-1918-online.net/article/prisoners-of-war-russian-empire/ International Encyclopedia of the First World War: Prisoners of War (Russian Empire)] {{World War I}} [[Category:Austria-Hungary in World War I]] [[Category:Russian Empire in World War I]] [[Category:World War I]] [[Category:World War I prisoners of war]] [[Category:World War I prisoners of war held by Russia]] [[Category:Austro-Hungarian prisoners of war held by Russia in World War I]]

{{Short description|Revolutionary movement during Austro-Hungarian rule in Bosnia and Herzegovina}} {{Use dmy dates|date=October 2024}} {{Infobox organization | name = Young Bosnia | native_name = Млада Босна
Mlada Bosna | native_name_lang = sr | image = Young Bosnia members.jpg | image_size = 200px | alt = | caption = Some of the members | map = | map_size = | map_alt = | map_caption = | abbreviation = | motto = | predecessor = | merged = | successor = | formation = 1904 | dissolved = After 28 June 1914 | merger = | type = [[Revolutionary movement]] | status = | purpose = Separation of Bosnia and Herzegovina from [[Austria-Hungary]] | headquarters = | location = | coords = | region = | services = | membership = | language = | sec_gen = | leader_title = | leader_name = | leader_title2 = | leader_name2 = | leader_title3 = | leader_name3 = | leader_title4 = | leader_name4 = | board_of_directors = | key_people = [[Vladimir Gaćinović]]
[[Dimitrije Mitrinović]]
[[Gavrilo Princip]] | main_organ = | parent_organization = | subsidiaries = | secessions = | affiliations = [[Narodna Odbrana]] and [[Black Hand (Serbia)|Black Hand]] | budget = | staff = | volunteers = | slogan = | remarks = | formerly = | footnotes = }} '''Young Bosnia''' ({{langx|sr|Млада Босна|Mlada Bosna}}) refers to a [[revolutionary movement]] active in the early 20th century, which sought to end the [[Austro-Hungarian rule in Bosnia and Herzegovina]]. Its members, primarily [[Bosnian Serbs]] but also [[Bosnian Muslims]] and [[Bosnian Croats]], were driven by various ideologies, prominently [[Yugoslavism]], the unification of [[South Slavs|South Slavic peoples]] into a single Yugoslav state.{{sfn|Tomasevich|2002|p=5}} The movement drew inspiration from a diverse range of philosophical influences, including German [[Romanticism]], [[anarchism]], and Russian [[revolutionary socialism]]. The most infamous act associated with Young Bosnia was the [[assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand]] of Austria in Sarajevo on 28 June 1914 by [[Gavrilo Princip]], one of its members. == Background == The region of Bosnia and Herzegovina, populated by Serbs, Croats and Muslims, was part of the [[Ottoman Empire]] until 1878. After the anti-Ottoman [[Herzegovina uprising (1875–1877)|Herzegovina uprising]], the region [[Austro-Hungarian campaign in Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1878|was occupied by Austria-Hungary in 1878]]. There was a small phase of modernization, however the region remained mostly underdeveloped, highly illiterate and agrarian. The new occupying authorities suppressed political opposition, though underground political opposition existed.{{cite journal |title='Union or Death!': Gavrilo Princip, Young Bosnia and the Role of 'Sacred Time' in the Dynamics of Nationalist Terrorism |author=Paul Jackson |journal=Totalitarian Movements and Political Religions |volume=7 |issue=1 |date=2006 |doi=10.1080/14690760500477935 |pages=51, 56}} In 1882, [[1882 Herzegovina uprising|an uprising]] broke out against the Austro-Hungarian occupation authorities, but was suppressed by force. There were a number of youth-oriented organizations before the rise of the movement Young Bosnia, such as [[United Serb Youth]] in the 1860s and 1870s. Defining membership and the vague idea of "youth" (omladina) was debated at length among South Slavic intellectuals. One major obstacle to defining and organizing the youth in Bosnia and Herzegovina was the educational system, which underwent major changes in the Habsburg period. By 1900, a small but growing number of young men from Bosnia were studying in Prague, Zagreb, Vienna, Graz, Istanbul, and Belgrade. This put them in touch with Serbian and Croatian nationalist circles.{{Cite book|last=Hajdarpasic|first=Edin|title=Whose Bosnia?: Nationalism and Political Imagination in the Balkans, 1840–1914|date=2015|isbn=978-0-8014-5371-7|location=Ithaca|pages=15, 127–160|oclc=922889410}} The rise to power of the popular [[Karađorđević dynasty]] in Serbia in the 1900s after the [[May Overthrow]] of the Obrenović dynasty by the Serbian Army in 1903, stimulated support by both Serbs and South Slavs for their unification into a state led by Serbia.{{sfn|Djokić|2003|p=59}} == Formation, membership and ideology == No unified organization was named Young Bosnia, while contemporaries rarely used the term.{{cite book |author=Robert J. Donia |title=Sarajevo: A Biography |publisher=University of Michigan Press |date=2006 |isbn=9780472115570 |pages=112–113}}{{cite book |title=The Sleepwalkers: How Europe Went to War in 1914 |author=Christopher M. Clark |publisher=Allen Lane |date=2012 |isbn=9780713999426 |pages=41–42}} It had no statute and a hierarchy.{{cite book |title=The First World War and the Balkans: Historic Event, Experience, Memory |chapter=Political Ideas of Young Bosnia: Between Anarchism, Socialism and Nationalism |author=Miloš Vojinović |publisher=Südosteuropa |date=2018 |url=https://www.academia.edu/40653109/Political_Ideas_of_Young_Bosnia_Between_Anarchism_Socialism_and_Nationalism |pages=165, 170, 181, 184, 188}} Young Bosnia had a decentralized structure consisting of small circles, connected only by designated intermediaries. The participants of Bosnian student movements did not have a common ideology, unified view of strategy or tactics, and were not part of an unified organization. Per writer [[Veselin Masleša]]: {{blockquote|[There is a] shortage of sources about Young Bosnia itself. Memoirs are weak, incomplete, and unreliable. All the participants of that movement who have written about it have fallen into one basic error: They have devoted more attention to their views at the time they were writing than to the movement itself.}} Young Bosnia was a revolutionary movement active in Bosnia and Herzegovina before World War I.{{cite journal |author1=Rok Zupančič |author2=Faris Kočan |author3=Janja Vuga |date=2021 |title=Ethnic distancing through aesthetics in Bosnia-Herzegovina: appraising the limits of art as a peacebuilding tool with a socio-psychological experiment |journal=Southeast European and Black Sea Studies |volume=21 |issue=1 |doi=10.1080/14683857.2020.1867410 |page=117}}{{cite book|author= Matjaž Klemenčič, Mitja Žagar |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=ORSMBFwjAKcC&pg=PA56|title=The Former Yugoslavia's Diverse Peoples: A Reference Sourcebook|publisher=ABC Clio|year=2004|page=56|isbn = 978-1-57607-294-3}} Young Bosnia has been also defined as "loosely connected secret student organisations based in Bosnia and Herzegovina" and "aggregation of groups and cells of revolutionary youth". Austro-Hungarian authorities referred to Young Bosnians as ''Jugoslawen'' (Yugoslavs). Young Bosnia started operating in 1904. On 6 October 1908, the region was annexed by the Austro-Hungarian authorities. The Austro-Hungarian annexation of Bosnia ignited the [[Bosnian Crisis]] in European politics and unrest in the province. The establishment of the [[Diet of Bosnia]] happened only in February 1910, and the [[1910 Bosnian parliamentary election]] in May the same year. In 1909, the Young Bosnia was a loose circle of mainly Bosnian Serb students whose interest in revolutionary and romantic Yugoslavism was prompted by the annexation.{{sfn|Lampe|2000|p=90}} [[Vladimir Gaćinović]] was the main ideologist of Young Bosnia{{cite journal |title=European Concept of the Young Bosnia Movement |author=Radoslav Gaćinović |journal=Serbian Political Thought |date=2014 |issue=2 |url=https://www.ceeol.com/search/article-detail?id=177409 |pages=54–57, 61–63}}{{cite book|author=Belgrade (Serbia). Vojni muzej Jugoslovenske narodne armije|title=Fourteen centuries of struggle for freedom|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=2m8MAQAAMAAJ|year=1968|publisher=The Military Museum|page=II }} and of [[tyrannicide]] as its method of political struggle.{{cite book|last1=Лесковац|first1=Младен|last2=Форишковић|first2=Александар|last3=Попов|first3=Чедомир|title=Српски биографски речник|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=ozYYAQAAIAAJ|year=2004|publisher=Будућност|page=634|isbn=9788683651627}} [[Petar Kočić]] led the most ardent anti-Austrian Serb nationalists and had ties to Young Bosnia.{{sfn|Banac|1988|p=191}} Per political scientist Radoslav Gaćinović, the term "Young Bosnia" was first used by Petar Kočić in the journal "Homeland" ({{lang-sh-Cyrl-Latn|Отаџбина|Otadžbina}}) in 1907. Allegedly, this was a mistake in the year of publication.{{cite book|title=Život|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=06lNAAAAYAAJ|year=1989|publisher=Svjetlost.|page=122|quote=И, подсећајући да му је то у писму са- општио Божидар Зечевић, наводећи погрешно 1907. годину... }} In June 1910, [[Bogdan Žerajić]] killed himself after failing to assassinate General [[Marijan Varešanin]], the Austro-Hungarian governor of Bosnia and Herzegovina. In 1911, Gaćinović published an article titled "Young Bosnia" in Almanac ({{lang-sh-Cyrl-Latn|Алманах|Almanah}}) published by [[Prosvjeta (1902)|Prosvjeta]].{{sfn|Dedijer|1966|p=831}} In the same year, he became a member of [[Black Hand (Serbia)|Black Hand]] and [[Narodna Odbrana]] (National Defense). Support for revolutionary [[Yugoslavism]] in Bosnia grew with the rise of the Serb-Croat Progressive Organization in 1911 which drew in support for the cause from Serbs as well as Croats and some Bosnian Muslims.{{cite book|author=Stevan K. Pavlowitch|title=Serbia: The History of an Idea|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=u46G_l3Cz20C|year=2002|publisher=New York University Press|isbn=978-0-8147-6708-5|pages=90–91}} The organization was a youth society led by [[Ivo Andrić]] that promoted unity and friendship between Serb and Croat youth and opposed the Austro-Hungarian occupation, but was decried by nationalists and harassed by the government.{{sfn|Dedijer|1966a|p=216}} The members were predominantly students,{{cite book|last=Stevenson|first=David|title=1914 – 1918: The History of the First World War|year=2004|publisher=Penguin Books|isbn=978-0-14-026817-1|page=11}} primarily [[Bosnian Serbs]] but also [[Bosnian Muslims]] and [[Bosnian Croats]].{{sfn|Djokić|2003|p=24}} Its members were also young peasants. Višnja Mosić used the cover of shepherding to transmit messages for Young Bosnia.{{cite web|title=Српска Православна Црква - Вишеград {{!}} Srpska Pravoslavna Crkva - Višegrad|url=http://www.crkva-visegrad.com/stari/novost.php?id=158|website=www.crkva-visegrad.com|access-date=27 April 2018|language=sr|archive-date=24 March 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180324101602/http://www.crkva-visegrad.com/stari/novost.php?id=158|url-status=dead}}{{cite web|title=Рат бабе Вишње против Аустроугарске {{!}} СРБИН.ИНФО|url=https://srbin.info/2014/09/28/rat-babe-visnje-protiv-austrougarske/|website=srbin.info|access-date=27 April 2018|language=sr}}{{cite web|title=Баба Вишња - Заборављена српска хероина • Фронтал.СРБ|url=https://frontal.rs/baba-visnja-zaboravljena-srpska-heroina/|website=frontal.rs|access-date=27 April 2018|language=sr|date=13 May 2014}} There were two main ideologies promoted amongst Young Bosnian members, Yugoslavism and [[Pan-Serbism]]. Historians have debated whether Young Bosnia was Serb nationalist or pan-Yugoslav.{{cite book|author=Neven Andjelic|title=Bosnia-Herzegovina: The End of a Legacy|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=YO64tcuC2aQC|year=2003|publisher=Psychology Press|isbn=978-0-7146-5485-0 |page=12}} Gaćinović did not favor Yugoslavism and he perceived it as "mixing the Croatian water with Serbian wine". His program articles mostly contained only the Serbian national idea. Unlike Gaćinović, a leading ideologist of the movement and Bosnian Serb [[Dimitrije Mitrinović]] advocated for Yugoslavism.{{cite book |title=Making Yugoslavs: Identity in King Aleksandar's Yugoslavia |author=Christian Axboe Nielsen |page=151 |publisher=University of Toronto Press |date=2014 |isbn=9781442627505}}{{sfn|Banac|1988|p=111}} Per historian [[Ivo Banac]]: "His utopian vision of Great Yugoslavia was a powerful indication of how the idea of Yugoslavism could be grafted unto Serbian expansionism."{{sfn|Banac|1988|p=111}} The goal of Young Bosnia was to promote the Yugoslav national idea among the locals, wanting to include all South Slavs into a Yugoslav federation.{{cite journal |title=Bosnian Daydreamers |author=Dejan Djokić |page=304 |journal=History Workshop Journal |volume=80 |issue=1 |date=2015 |doi=10.1093/hwj/dbv016}} Young Bosnia was inspired by a variety of ideas, movements, theorists, and events; such as German [[romanticism]], Italian national movement, [[Serbian nationalism]], [[anarchism]],{{cite web|author=Trivo Indic|url=http://www.katesharpleylibrary.net/1c5bbd|title=The anarchist tradition on Yugoslav soil|publisher=Umanità Nova|date=27 May 1990|access-date=17 October 2014}} Russian [[revolutionary socialism]], and [[anti-imperialism]].{{cite journal |title=Forging the Nation‐centric World: Imperial Rule and the Homogenisation of Discontent in Bosnia and Herzegovina (1878–1918) |author=Siniša Malešević |journal=Journal of Historical Sociology |volume=34 |issue=4 |date=2021 |doi=10.1002/johs.12350 |page=675}} Young Bosnians read works by [[Nikolay Chernyshevsky]], [[Mikhail Bakunin]], [[Alexander Herzen]], [[Fyodor Dostoevsky]], and [[Maxim Gorky]]. They were also inspired by the works of [[Friedrich Nietzsche]], [[Henrik Ibsen]], [[Oscar Wilde]], and [[Walt Whitman]]. The Young Bosnians romanticized South Slavic history, especially the [[Battle of Kosovo]]. The Young Bosnians used the [[Kosovo Myth]] to validate their self-sacrifice. They honored Bogdan Žerajić's attempted assassination. Young Bosnians believed that revolution was the only way to gain the liberation of Bosnia and Herzegovina from Austria-Hungary. They constructed their program on the theory of national sovereignty, believing that sovereignty comes from the people and that a government is illegitimate if the sovereignty is not from the people. Per Radoslav Gaćinović, the motto of the movement was: We want to either die in life or live in death. While Young Bosnia and the Black Hand struggled for national liberation, the two were different as Young Bosnia wanted to establish a South Slavic state, while its members were atheistic and young people with republican views. The latter wanted to create a pan-Serbian or Serb-dominated Yugoslav state, and supported authoritarian, militaristic, and clerical worldviews.{{cite book |author=Marie-Janine Calic |title=A History of Yugoslavia |publisher=Purdue University Press |date=2019 |isbn=9781612495644 |page=49}} The extent and significance of the influence from neighboring [[Kingdom of Serbia]] has been debated by historians, and it seems that the interactions between Young Bosnia and Black Hand agents (disguised as Narodna Odbrana representatives) were largely initiated by the former, rather than the latter. American historian [[Wayne S. Vucinich]] credited Young Bosnians with converting Black Hand members from [[Greater Serbia]] to Yugoslavism.{{sfn|Lampe|2000|p=90}} Young Bosnian activities were supported by the pan-Serbian secret society Narodna Odbrana.{{cite book |author=Bruce Hoffman |title=Inside Terrorism |publisher=Columbia University Press |date=2006 |isbn=978-0-231-51046-2 |pages=11–12}} == Assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand of Austria == {{Main|Assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand of Austria}} Archduke [[Assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand|Franz Ferdinand was assassinated in Sarajevo]] on 28 June 1914 by [[Gavrilo Princip]], a member of Young Bosnia. It received assistance from the Black Hand, a secret organization founded by members of the [[Royal Serbian Army|Serbian Army]]. During a Serbian [[court-martial]] in French-occupied [[Thessaloniki|Salonika]] in 1916/1917, Chief of Serbian Military Intelligence [[Dragutin Dimitrijević]], known as "Apis," claimed responsibility for organizing the assassination. Apis used his influence over the Serbian military and the Black Hand to smuggle weapons and assassins into [[Austro-Hungarian rule in Bosnia and Herzegovina|Austrian-occupied Bosnia]]. Following the trial's conclusion on 26 June 1917, Apis was executed by firing squad.{{sfn|Newman|2015|p=39}} Vladimir Gaćinović condemned the assassination in a letter after the [[World War I|First World War]] began, presumably to evade responsibility.{{sfn|Dedijer|1966|p=522}} During his trial, Princip said: {{cquote|The political union of the Yugoslavs was always before my eyes, and that was my basic idea... I am a Yugoslav nationalist, aiming for the unification of all Yugoslavs, and I do not care what form of the state, but it must be free from Austria.|author=Gavrilo Princip|source={{sfn | Halilovic-Pastuovic | 2020 | p=92}}}} People, including members of Young Bosnia, who participated in the assassination were: *[[Danilo Ilić]] (27 July 1890 – 3 February 1915) *[[Veljko Čubrilović]] (1 July 1886 – 3 February 1915) *[[Miško Jovanović]] (15 June 1878 – 3 February 1915) *[[Nedeljko Čabrinović]] (2 February 1895 – 20 January 1916) *[[Vladimir Gaćinović]] (25 May 1890 – 11 August 1917) *[[Trifko Grabež]] (28 June 1895 – February 1916) *[[Gavrilo Princip]] (25 July 1894 – 28 April 1918) *[[Muhamed Mehmedbašić]] (1886 – 29 May 1943) *[[Cvjetko Popović]] (1896 – 9 June 1980) *[[Vaso Čubrilović]] (14 January 1897 – 11 June 1990) An evening before the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand, Princip, Čabrinović and Ilić had visited the grave of Bogdan Žerajić for the last time.{{cite book|title=Stand To!: The Journal of the Western Front Association|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=gPAWAQAAIAAJ|year=2003|publisher=The Association|page=44|quote=On the evening before 28 June 1914 Princip, Cabrinovic and Ilic paid a last visit to the grave of Bogdan Zerajic in Sarajevo. Zerajic had planned an assault ...}} Žerajić's proclamation "He who wants to live, let him die. He who wants to die, let him live", was quoted by Gavrilo Princip in one of the songs he wrote ({{langx|sr|Ал право је рекао пре Жерајић, соко сиви: Ко хоће да живи, нек мре, Ко хоће да мре, нек живи}}).{{cite book|last=Marković|first=Marko|title=Članci i ogledi|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=1UYjAAAAMAAJ|year=1961|page=193}} == Legacy == [[File:Kapela Vidovdanskih heroja.jpg|thumbnail|[[Vidovdan Heroes Chapel]] in Sarajevo]] The first review article about Young Bosnians was published in August 1917 in the fourth issue of ''Zabavnik'' by poet and doctoral student of law in Paris, Božidar Purić, titled "Young Bosnia", where he wrote that "they had no doctrine, or established programme or statute. They had them in themselves. They were not created or unified by an à priori idea, but by their lively and atavistic feeling for freedom, for self abnegation and their impulse for greatness."{{cite journal |title=Coping with the Memory of Gavrilo Princip and the Symbolism of Vidovdan in Serbia and Yugoslavia |journal=The South Slav Journal |author=Slobodan G. Markovich |date=2015 |url=https://www.academia.edu/23971325/Coping_with_the_Memory_of_Gavrilo_Princip_and_the_Symbolism_of_Vidovdan_in_Serbia_and_Yugoslavia |pages=34-37, 39-41, 46}}{{cite journal |title=Млада Босна |journal=Hereticus |author=Božidar Purić |date=2015 |url=https://www.ceeol.com/search/article-detail?id=757318 |page=78 |language=sr}} After World War I, Gavrilo Princip's brother established a committee in Hadžići in 1919 to transfer Princip's remains to Bosnia. In the beginning of 1920, a new committee called "The Committee for the transfer of the bones of the Vidovdan heroes" was created in Sarajevo to transfer the remains of the participants of the assassination to Sarajevo. The remains of Princip and his associates were exhumed. In 1920, their remains were buried in Sarajevo. They were regarded as heroes in Czechoslovak media. A former member of the movement, Borivoje Jevtić, defended the act of the participants of the assassination on the cover page of the newspaper ''[[Politika]]'' on the 15th anniversary of the assassination in 1929. On 29 October 1939, the [[Vidovdan Heroes Chapel]] (where the remains of Princip and other Young Bosnian members have been preserved){{cite book |title=Crisis and Ontological Insecurity: Serbia's Anxiety Over Kosovo's Secession |author=Filip Ejdus |date=2019 |publisher=Springer International Publishing |isbn=9783030206673 |page=56}} was consecrated at the [[Serbian Orthodox]] cemetery in Sarajevo, [[Kingdom of Yugoslavia]], in the absence of Yugoslav officials, except for a military commander. Veselin Masleša published ''Young Bosnia'' in 1940, and [[Vladimir Dedijer]] published ''Road to Sarajevo'' in 1966. In his book, Masleša argued that Young Bosnia did not have "enough knowledge," and claimed that its politics "represented nothing more than the most ordinary aggregate of various ideas". He perceived the movement as an "inappropriate expression" of the people in Bosnia and Herzegovina.{{cite journal |title=1918 and a Hundred Years of Habsburg and Yugoslav Historiography |author=Miloš Vojinović |journal=Slavic Review |doi=10.1017/slr.2019.250 |page=926}} Dedijer described Young Bosnians in his book as "primitive rebels". Some historians have dismissed the movement as consisting of "frustrated, poor, dreary and maladjusted" adolescents. As Young Bosnian members were interested in literature and poetry, some of them became poets, writers, philosophers, and university professors. On 28 June 1953, the government of [[Federal People's Republic of Yugoslavia]] opened the Museum of Young Bosnia and Gavrilo Princip at the site of the assassination.{{cite web |title=Collection of the Austro-Hungarian period |url=https://www.muzejsarajeva.ba/en/zbirka-austrougarskog-perioda/ |website=Museum of Sarajevo}}{{cite book |title=The Causes of the First World War: The Long Blame Game |author=Annika Mombauer |date=2024 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=9781351168441 |page=222}} It displayed a red Cyrillic inscription: "From this place on June 28, 1914, Gavrilo Princip's shot gave voice to the national protest against tyranny and our nations' centuries‑long aspiration for freedom." Footprints were also added on the spot from which Princip had fired the shots, which were popular among tourists and locals. During the [[Bosnian War]], the museum was renamed to [[Museum of Sarajevo 1878–1918]] by the [[Sarajevo Canton Assembly]]. == References == {{Reflist|2}} == Sources == {{refbegin}} * {{cite book|last=Banac|first=Ivo|title=The National Question in Yugoslavia: Origins, History, Politics|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=KfqbujXqQBkC|year=1988|publisher=Cornell University Press|isbn=0-8014-9493-1}} * {{cite book|last=Dedijer|first=Vladimir|author-link=Vladimir Dedijer|title=Sarajevo 1914|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=QTdIAAAAMAAJ|year=1966|publisher=Prosveta}} * {{cite book | last = Dedijer| first = Vladimir| author-link = Vladimir Dedijer| year = 1966a| title = The Road to Sarajevo| publisher = Simon & Schuster | location = New York City| oclc = 400010}} * {{cite book|last=Djokić|first=Dejan|title=Yugoslavism: Histories of a Failed Idea, 1918–1992|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=ZMyZdvTympMC|year=2003|publisher=C. Hurst & Co.
